rrilE WARRINGTON EXTENSION AND WATER J. ACT, 1890. BOROUGII OF WARRINGTON. Whereas by the Warrington Extension and Water Act, 1890, it was provided that the extended Borough of Warrington should be divided into nine Wards with such names or dis- tinguishing numbers and boundaries as should be fixed and determined by a scheme to be made by a Commissioner to be for that purpose appointed by Her Majesty's Principal Secre- tary of State for the Home Department within three weeks ' from the passing of the said Act. And it was further provided by the said Act that the Com- missioner should by his scheme apportion all the existing Councillors among the Wards of the Borough as altered and state for which of the said Wards the five Aldermen assigned by the Council as Returning Officers on the 9th day of November 1889 should act and should also name an Alderman to act as Returning Officer to each of the remaining new , Wards. And the said Commissioner was empowered by the said Act to make all such provisions as might be necessary, or proper, in consequence of the extension of the Borough and of the division or alteration of the Wards. And it was further provided that the Borough should con- tinue to have nine Aldermen and twenty-seven Coun- cillors. And whereas the said Act was passed and received the Royal Assent on the 14th day of August. 1890, and on the 29th day of August, 1890. the Bight Honourable Henry Matthews, Her Majesty's Principal Secretary of State for the Home Department: did duly warrant and appoint Charles Neve Cresswell,Esquire, to be such Commissioner for the pur- poses of the said Act, and furthermore did, in exercise of the powers given to him by the 21st section of the said Act. fix the 30th day of September. 1890, as the day before which the said echeraeahould be completed. Now I. the said Charles Nave Cresswell, do hereby in pursu- ance of the said warrant and appointment 'fix and determine that the nine Wards of the Borough of Warrington as ex- tended shall be numbered, named, arid defined, as follows : Ward No. 1 otherwise Town Hall Ward. 2 „ Of 9. 3 if 4 „ 5 „ ~ 6 „ - Ward. 10 oo 7 PO 8 ~ 9 „ And I do hereby determine that the said Ward No. 1 other- wise Town Hall Ward shall comprise so 'ranch of the area of the extended Borough of Warrington as is contained within a line commencing from a point in the centre of the bridge erossing the London and North-Wesbern Railway, and known as Bank Quay Bridge. thence in an Easterly direction to and along the centre of Sankey-street, and Buttermarket-street. to a point opposite to the centre of Orford-street, thence in a Northerly direction to and along the centre of Orford-street, to a point opposite to the centre of Crown-street, thence to and along the centre of Crown-street, to a point in the centre of Win- wick-street. thence in a Northerly direction along the centre of se inwick-street, to a point opposite to the centre of Tanner's-lane, thence in a Westerly direction to and along the centre of Tanner's-lane to a point opposite to the centre of Bewsey-street, thence in a North-westerly direction to and along the centre of Bewsey-road, to a point in the centre of the bridge crossing the London and North- Western Railway and known as Bewsey Bridge, thence by a vertical line to the centre of the said Railway and thence in a Southerly direction,along the centre of the said Railway to the point of commencement aforesaid. And I do hereby determine that Ward No. 2 otherwise Whitecross Ward shall comprise so much of the area of the extended Borough of Warrington as is contained within a line commencing from the point aforesaid in the centre of Bank Quay Bridge, thence in a Westerly direction along the centre of Liverpool-road, Green-street. and Mill-lane to the Boundary of the Borough near Buttermilk Bridge thence in a Northerly direction along the said Boundary to the point of intersec- tion in the centre of Lodge-lane thence in a South Easterly direction along the centre of Lodge-lane and Bewsey-road to the Boundary of No. 1 Ward theuce in a Southerly direction along the said Boundary to the point of commencement afore- said. and I do thereby determine that Ward No. 3 otherwise Bewsey Ward shall comprise so much of the area of the ex- tended Borough of War:U:4(ton as is contained within a line commencing from the point in the Boundary of the Borough at the centre of Lodge-lane thence in a North Easterly direction along the said Boundary to the centre of the Bridge known as Longford Bridge in Winwick-road thence in a Southerly direction along the centre of Winwick-road to Winwick-street, thence to and along the centre of Winwick-street to,the Bound- ary of No. 1 Ward thence in a Westerly and North Westerly direction along the Boundary of No. 1 'Ward to the Boundary of No. 2 Ward thence along the Northern Boundary of No. 2 Ward, to the point of commencement aforesaid. And I do hereby determine that Ward No. 4, otherwise Orford Ward, shall comprise so much of the area of the ex- tended Borough of Warrington, as is contained within a line commencing from the point 1.). the Boundary of the Borough at the centre of Longford Bridge, thence in nn easterly direc- tion along the said Boundary so its intersection with the Cheshire Lines Railway at a point 70 yards south of Orford- lane, thence in a south-westerly direction along the centre of the said Railway to the centre of the bridge crossing Marsh House-lane, thence downward to the centre of Marsh House- lane, thence in a westerly direction along the centre of Marsh House-lane and Conie's Corner, to a point opposite to the centre of Orford-lane, thence in a south-westerly direction to and along the centre of Orford-lane and Pinners-brow to the Boundary of No.l Ward. thence in a northerly direction along the eastern Boundary of No. 3 Ward to the point of commence- ment aforesaid. And I do hereby determine that Ward No. 5. otherwise St. John's Ward shall comprise so much of the area of the ex- tended Borough of Warrington, as is contained within a line commencing from the point in the Boundary of No. 1 Ward, opposite to the centre of Crown-street, thence in a Northerly direction along the Boundary of No. 1 Ward to the Boundary of No. 4 Ward, thence in a North-easterly and Easterly direc- tion 'along the said Boundary to the point below the centre of Marsh House-lane Railway Bridge at the South-eastern corner of No. 4 Ward, thence upward to the centre of the said Railway, thence in a South-westerly direction along the cen- tre of the said Railway to the centre of the Bridge carrying the Railway over Battersby--lane, thence downward to the centre of the said Lane, thence in a Southerly direction along the centre of the said Lane, Brick-street, and Fennel-street. to a point in the centre of Church-street, thence in a Westerly direction along the centre of Church-street, Irlam-street, and Buttermarket-street. to the Boundary of No. 1 Ward, thence in a Northerly and Westerly direction along the Eastern Boun- dary of the said Ward to the point ot commencement aforesaid. And I do hereby determine that Ward No. 6, otherwise Fairfield Ward. shall comprise so much of the area of the ex- tended Borough of Warrington as is contained within a line commencing from the point in Church-street, opposite to the centre of Fennel-street, thence in an Easterly direction along the centre of Church-street. to a point opposite to the centre of Howley-lane. thence in a South-easterly direction to and along the centre of Howley-lane to the River Mersey, thence to a point in the centre of the bed of the said riser opposite to the mouth of asertain brook irs the Township of Warrington, 93 yards westwards of the Padgate Brook, thence in an East- erly direction along the centre of the bed of the river to the Borough Boundary, thence in an Easterly-nortkerly and Westerly direction along the said Boundary to the Boundary .of No. 4 Ward, thence in a South-westerly direction along the Boundaries of No. 4 Ward and of No. 5 Ward to the point of commencement aforesaid. And I do hereby determine that Ward No. 7, otherwise Howley Ward, shall comprise so much of the area of the extended Borough of Warrington as is contained within is line commencing from a point in the centre of Market-gate. thence in an Easterly direction along the Boundary of No. 1 Ward to the Boundary of No. 6 Ward, thence in an Easterly direction along the Boundary of No. 5 Ward to the Boundary of No. 6 Ward, thence in an Easterly and South-Easterly direction along the said Boundary to the Borough Boundary at Padgate Brook, thence in a Southerly and Westerly direction along the centre of the bed of the River Mersey to a point beneath the centre of Warrington Bridge. thence upward to the centre of the said bridge, thence in a Northerly direction to and along the centre of Bridge-street tothe point of commencement aforesaid. And Ido hereby determine that Ward No. 8. otherwise St. Austin's Ward, shall comprise so much of the area of the ex- tended Borough of Warrington as is contained within a line commencing from the point in the centre of Market-gate, thence in a westerly direction along the Boundary of No. I Ward to the point of intersection with the Boundnry of No. 2 Ward at Bank Quay Bridge, thence in a westerly direction along the Boundary of No. 2 Ward to the Boundary of the Borough, thbnce in a southerly, south-easterlyt,north-easterly, anct easterly direction along the said Boundary to a point in the centre of the bed of the river Mersey. 374 yards below Warrington Bridge, thence in a northerly direction along the centre of the bed of the said river to the Boundary of No. 7 Ward, thence in a northerly direction along the raid Boun- dary to the point, of commencement aforesaid. And I do hereby determine that Ward No. 9, otherwise Latchford Ward, shall comprise so much of the area of the extended Borough of Warrington as is coatained within the Township of Latchford And I do hereby apportion all the existing Councillors among the new Wards of the extended Borough, as follows To No. 1 Ward, otherwise Town Hall Ward. BROKE, BROKE, BROKE ! Broke, Broke, Broke! „ I have squandered the uttermost sou, And have failed in my efforts to utter One trivial, last 1.0. U. Oh, well for the infant in arms That for ducats he need not fret ; Oh, well for the placid corpse That he's settled his final debt. And dun after dun comes in, Each bringing his little account; And oh for the touch of a five-dollar bill,
----- - Or a cheque for a larger amount ! Broke, Broke, Broke! My course as a student is run; I'll back to my childhood's home, and act The role of the Prodigal Son. From Pirated Poeme.

div.p: Varittirs.

It isn't the taking the starch out of him that makes a man limp. It is when a fellow is broke that he most feels the need of change. To men about to strike : pause for reflection. The dressmaker does her work with mathematical accuracy. She is great on figures. A true word is often spoken in jest ; but we always like it to be about some other fellow. Charlie : " Will you be mine for ever and a day? " Susie : " Ye-e-es. At least—for the day. A man's love is the measure of his fitness for good or bad company here or elsewhere. It is getting to be the custom out West when a bank suspends to suspend the President also. Charity begins at home: but that is no excuse for treating one's family like a lot of paupers. Smokeless powder—the kind you generally have on your coat sleeve after a visit to your best girl. If the conceit was taken out of some people there wouldn't be enough of 'em left to hang clothes on. _ . . .
Be sure you're right, then

Elder sister: "Why don't you im-Prove your mind. Belle, instead of continually dawdling about;the house?" Belle: What's the use? I'm engaged." There are calm souls that never worry about any- thing, and nobody ever worries about them, I hope; but love—real love, would leave any heaven to save some
poor little lost earth. Smallness is often the disguise of the infinite. You may count the apples_ on the tree, but who can count
the trees in the apple? yon may reckon the acorns on the oak, but not the oaks in the acorn.

It was just after the Battle of Worcester, September 3, 1651, that Charles H. was forced to conceal himself in the oak tree at Boscobel. When he returned to England on his birthday, May 29. the oak leaf was displayed in memory of his adventure. A New York grocer, who recently took a trip to Coney Island, was sitting on the beach fooling in the sand with a small shovel. A friend seeing him, stopped, and bade him the time of the day. "Howdy," replied the grocer, absentmindedly, taking up a shovelful of sand, " How much sugar did you say?" American Business Man: "Now, sir, you have all the details of my new manufacturing scheme. If we suc- ceed, we'll make millions." Timid Capitalist: "But if we should fail!" American Business Man: "Fail? In -the bright lexicon of American enterprise there's no such word as fail—because whenever a thing don't pay we Can always unload it on an English syndicate.' Fond Mamma: "I am glad you enjoyed yourself at Mrs. Manners's, and I hope she noticed how carefully you had been brought up. You did not ask twice for pudding, did you ? " Small Son: "No, indeed, ma; I didn't have to. Every time I finished and began scrap- ing the plate with the spoon and smacking my lips, the servant came and brought me some more without say- ing a word." DISAPPOINTMENTS.—You are disappointed. —Do you re- member, if you lose heart about your work, that none of it is lost; that the good of every good deed remains, and breeds, and works on forever; and all that fails and is lost is the outside shell of the thing; which, perhaps, might have been better done, but, better or worse, has nothing to do with the real spiritual good which you have done to men's hearts; for which God will surely repay you in His own way and time.—Charles Kingsley. THE Maur CHORD.—On board a man-of-war any member of the ship's company touches his hat when he comes on deck. He would do so were there no superior . .

officer present. He "salutes the deck." The custom is typical of every sailor's sentiment of respect, admira- tion, and affection for his vessel, if the craft be hand- some and a first-class "sea-boat." The strength of this sailor loyalty was well understood by an English officer, . . . .

the late -Caitain Hall. Captain Hall was in command of a remarkably fine frigate on the South African station, which he always kept in exquisite order, and of which he and his crew were justly proud. The handsome bust on her beautiful figure-head was brightly gilded, and great care was taken of it. On one occasion the har- mony which usually prevailed on board was in some way disturbed. Instead of resorting to capital punish- ment, Captain Hall summoned the men aft, and in a simple, manly speech pointed out the impropriety of their conduct. He concluded thus:—" So now, my lads, if this be not put an end to, and hearty good will re- stored, I'll blacken your figure-head and put the ship in mourning." Had a bombshell fallen at their feet, the . . . .
men cod not have been more astonished. He had
touched the right chord. Have their figure-head - blackened I Not they—anything rather than that. . .
They at once resumed their wonted good behaviour and amiability.

THE KING OF ITALY AND HIS QITEEN.—A very cordial friendship exists between king and queen; and the former relies much on his wife's pidement, which is frequently clear and sound. Some pretty anecdotes are told of their domestic life. Thus the queen was anxious that her husband should follow the example of his _ _ _

father, and the fashion common among elderly Pied- montese officers, and dye his hair, which has become quite white. Her pleadings were in vain. Umberto's is an honest nature that does not love these subterfuges. Seeing petition was in vain, the queen had recourse to stratagem. he caused a quantity of fine hair-dye to be sent from Paris and put in the-king's dressing-room, together with directions for its use, making, however, no allusion to the subject. The king, too, said nothing, though he could not fail to see the pigments. Now the queen has a large white poodle of which she is very fond. What was her horror, a few days later, to see her pet come running into her room with his snowy locks of the deepest black hue. King Umberto had expended the dyes upon changing the colour of the poodle's hair! From that day forth the subject of hair-dyeing was

dropped between the Royal Couple. On yet an'other occasion the husband gave the wife one of those quiet rebuffs into which enters a sense of humour, and which are on that account less hard to bear. It appears that Umberto once asked one of the queen's secretaries what would be an acceptable Christmas present for her Majesty. This gentleman, a truer friend than courtier, had the courage to suggest to the king that the queen had a large number of unpaid milliners' and dress- makers' bills. The king took the hint, and begged that they should all be given to him. On Christmas morning ..ttenberto placed all these bills, receipted, under the s.tueen's table-napkin. There was no other present. It is said that she took the hint, and has been less extravagant since.—Leisure Hour.

MALAFROPOS.—Hostess : "Yes, thank you, Mr. Quoter, we are all very well but Johnnie and Willie, and the , doctor has sent some medicine for them." Mr. Quoter : ; "Sorry to hear it, but, er—er as Shakspere wrote, 'Throw physic to the dogs," and he never knew why she shunned him the remainder of the evening.— Chattering Lady, who enjoys the reputation of saying more in five minutes than any other woman in half an hour, to bored young man: "I'm sure you must be very tired of my foolish chatter, but I must tell you about a charming game we played at Mrs. Lund's the other day. 'Buried Proverbs.' What do you think was the proverb they set me to guess? So appropriate—you must guess it," Bored Young Man: " Ah, urn, well, Speech is silver, silenee is golden."—"Charley, my boy, you've ,heard the old saw, A- friend in need: is a friend in- deed." In fact, I got up early on purpose to:have a little talk with you. The early bird catches the worm, you know.' "—Mr. De Feat: "Yes, it was too much for me, and I fell." " Vicar (whose wife plays the organ in church) : "Mrs. So-and-So (naming another gentleman's wife) is going to take the organ next Sunday." Answer, "Glad to bear it; it will be such a treat."—Nell: "There was one of the ugliest men I have ever seen at Mrs. A.'s last night." Friend: What was he like?" Nell, "lie was just like your brother."—Visitor: "Oh, what a sweet baby !" "Mother (with red hair) : "Yes, isn't he—but I am afraid his hair will be the colour of mine." Visitor : "What a pity—l do hope it won't."—Charlie, with his dare amie and her mamma at the railway station bidding adieu to both: "Good-by. darling; 'Absence' truly 'makes the heart grow fonder !' "—Guest :to Jones : "Sorry to leave you, Jones, but, 'the best of friends must part you don't mind going down to the station to see me off?" Jones: " Oh ! not at all, I shall be delighted, for ' parting is such sweet sorrow.' " A CARD.—A Clergyman will send, free of charge, a prescrip- tion for a cure of all who suffer from nervous debility, physical exhaustion, and early decay. This great remedy was discovered by a Missionary in Old Mexico it saved him from a miserable existence and an early grave. Send a self- addressed, stamped envelope to Rev. JOSE2II HOLMES, Bloomsbury Mansions, Bloomsbury Square, London, WC Menton this paper.—Adet.
"CAPITAL CHAT."
At Bucharest the rumour is persistent that the Crown Prince of Roumania will shortly be betrothed to the Princess Victoria of Wales.

The Duke of Portland, I learn from the papers, is now engaged upon the almshouses which I stated some time ago that he intended to erect as memorial of his successes on the turf. I cannot help reflecting how much better it would have been for many winning owners in days gone by if they had set aside a portion of their gains in this way, and thus saved themselves from the eventual necessity of entering the workhouse.

The children of Prince Albert of Prussia are being taught to use their hands as well as their brains. Their father is as well versed in the mysteries of bookbinding as the Emperor Frederick was in car- pentering, and the two elder sons of Prince Albert have learned enough of masonry to be able to build a small pavillion under proper superintendence. Their younger brother is to be a joiner. Prince Albert takes more interest in this part of his sons' education than in any other.

Mr. Alderman Savory, who has just been elected to fill the office of Lord Mayor, is deservedly popu- lar in the City. He is a stoutish, ruddy-faced man, with black hair, no moustache, and slight whiskers. Ile is a member of the Goldsmith's Company. his residence is at Sunninghill, and his park adjoins the beautiful Virginia Water district of Windsor Forest. Mr. Savory was born at Elm Field, Upper Clapton, in 1843. Ile is a strong Tory in politics—another congenial qualification for the office.

A brewer writes to inform me that a short time since he received an application through his solicitor to advance .£l.lOO to the Salvation Army upon the security of the barracks at Crewe. He appears to think this strange. I cannot altogether agree with him unless I know a little more about the vellum of the security. General Booth may not anticipate that the transaction would be to the brewer's advantage. To spoil the Egyptians has always been considered a meritorious act.

The refusals to renew licenses which are taking place all over the country have created a panic in the public-house camp. In the course of a few days the Council of Licensed Victuallers will meet to con- sider the situation. There will, of course, be a battle in the law courts as to the legality of the action of the magistrates. The legal advisers of the publicans are by no means confident that the deci- sions of the licensing courts will be set aside. Should they be upheld, the prospect before the publican is somewhat alarming.

-- The Nonconformists are to have their Toynbee Hall movement. University men belonging to the Free Churches propose to establish a centre for reli- gious, social and educational work of all kinds among the poor of the East-end. Canning Town is the district selected, and Mansfield House, as the new settlement is called, in memory of Mansfield College, Oxford, will be brought into immediate co- operation with the Canning Town Congregational Church, of which the Rev. F. W. Newland, of Merton College, Oxford, is pastor.

Sir Peter Edlin has been ill for several days, and he mentioned in court yesterday that his indisposi- tion was due in a great measure to the polluted atmosphere of the badly ventilated Law Courts. This brought a daring young barrister to his feet with the remark, "The last things the architect thought of were light and air, m'lud." "Oh," snapped the judge, "did he confide that to you ?'' and that adventurous counsel realised, amidst the laughter of all present at his discomfiture, that Sir Peter resents rivalry in discontent.

Lord Wolseley has taken up the command of the army in Ireland, in. place of the serene German Prince who has just retired from the post. Lord Wolseley, although an Irishman, has little more sympathy with the Irish people than the foreigner, tor he is, it is understood, a strong opponent of liome Rule. Re has more than once made indis- creet political speeches. We shall await with in- terest to see what action our only general will take in Ireland. One who is so fond of dramatic displays and self-advertisement is not likely to remain quie- scent for long.

" His Lordship dwelt on the Church's clearness of vision and readiness for self-sacrifice." This is not a joke, but a quotation from the Bishop of Manches- ter's address to the Church Congress on social ques- tions. The Church's "clearness of vision" has been aopropriately testified by its virtual refusal to hear Mr. Tillett on the labour question and to regard him as a duly baptised Churchman and a member of the communion to which he clearly belongs. Its "readiness for self-sacrifice" is. shown by the man- ner in which its Archbishops, Bishops, and Deans adhere to their stipends.

The death is announced a Alphonse Karr, th rvenerable French novelist. M. Karr's works con- tinue to be read largely, but he belonged to the old romantic school of French novelists, and had grown rather out of date. He was once editor of tha " Figaro," and was always a contribntor to it. His best known works were published between 1835, and 1850. After the revolution of 1848 he left Paris, and went to live at Nice, but continued to produce many literary fragments and horticultural products—for, like our on Blackmore, he was an ardent gardener. His "Voyage autour demon Jardin " hae been translated into English. He was eighty-two.

Miss Borthwick, the young lady artist wbo assisted Mrs. Illingworth in doing ambulance duty at Tip- perary, is not related to Sir Algernon Borthwick, although she is a daughter of a very ancient and very Conservative Scottish family, and is nearly related to some of the most prominent Scotch Tories, including Lord Kingsburgh, the late Lord Advocate. Miss I3orthwick is very clever and very beautiful. Her classical profile and fair hair are known and admired in the artistic world. One of Miss Borth wick's sisters is Mrs. Malcolm Lawson, the wife of a Radical musician; from which it may be inferred that the venerable traditions of Scotch Toryism have not the influence they should have on the clever young ladies of our generation.

A measure against the adulteration of tea has been in operation in Russia now for upwards of a year. The Government undertakes to label pack- ages of tea, of various weights, if they are found to be genuine. The Government labels are affixed by persons employed by the Government, working un- der the control of official inspectors. The cost of the work is defrayed out of the money realised by the sale of the labels. The labelling is not imperative, but most of the tea merchants in the retail trade have had recourse to it to increase their sales, and her Majesty's Consul at St. Petersburg reports that in the two capitals the system has checked the traffic in adulterated tea. The provincial towns, however, are said to be still suffering from the adulteration .of tea and other commodities.

The cheAp press is triumphing everywhere. The " Nonconformist " has conle down Considerably in price since the days when, under the editorship of the late Edward Miall, it had a spirit and a force all its own. A short time ago it was joined on to the " Independent " under the title of the "Noncon- formist and Independent." This is now to be called the "Independent and Nonconformist," and by a polite fiction there will still be a Nonconformist itew.gthlpor, flit:hough actually there will only be the "Independent." That there is room for a weekly journal exclusively devoted to the Congregatioual body aeems to be the opinion of a great number of the leaders of the denomination, who have written to wish success to the new editor, Mr. F. Herbert Stead.

Mr. II J. Roby, who is the Liberal candidate for the Eccles division of Lancashire, and we hope soon to be the Liberal member, is a man of some note in the educational world. Not only is he the author of one of the best Latin grammars that were ever compiled, but he was for some years the secretary of the Endowed schools Commission, retaining that post until the Tory Government contrived to manoeuvre him out of it. After leaving his educa- tional work, in the course of which he left a real mark on the educational history of his country, he went into business and established the highly suc- cessful cotton mills of which he is now the proprie- tor. He is a very able man, is president, we think. of the Manchester Liberal Union, and is a solid and impressive speaker.

It cannot be questioned that the recent rise the Bank-rate, and the plausible representations of toilers in the market that money is extremely scarce, have provoked a general but undefined fear in the City that something dreadful is about to happen, which the City columns of a daily paper, by
. THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, OCTOBER 4, 1890

covert insinuation and the publication of shifting rumours affecting credit, have done much to foment. We have during the past few years more than once had occasion to complain of the lamentable readi- ness with which our contemporary lends itself to the manufacture of mare's nests, which, in the guise of mysterious financial and commercial conun- drums, set the whole City guessing the answer, and sow for a time the seeds of distrust broadcast over a large area of business activity. It is satisfactory, however, to know that the whole story was a bag of wind, and a pure invention of the enemy.

What a gratifying thing it is for all sorts and conditions of society that we have royal princes condescending enough to hold high commands in our fleets and armies ! The Duke of Edinburgh, after his turn of good things in other parts of the world, is now the naval commander-in-chief at Ply- mouth. His next brother is military commander- in-chief at Portsmouth. As if it were not enough that the biggest plums in the public service should be picked out for these two gentlemen, large sums are now being spent on their official residences—the house which would do for an ordinary admiral or general not being fit, of course, for a royal prince. To crown the whole thing, it appears that the Duke of Connaught has four months' holiday immediately after his appointment,because he can't live anywhere else in Portsmouth while his house is being got ready. And we call this a democratic age!

Attention is called to a matter of interest to the miners of England by what is said to be the law of Austria. Anyone there who takes out a search license is entitled to search for minerals on any- body's property. The proprietor has, ot course, to be indemnified, but if he be unreasonable in his de- mands, the searcher can obtain a compulsory lease or sale at a valuation price of the ground which he requires for sinking a pit or bore hole. This sys- tem, which appears to make a great breach in the generally accepted rights of property, is reported to have worked wonders in Austria. It is now pro- posed to adopt the Austrian system in some degree in Ilungary. The Hungarian Government wish to further mining operations in the same way, but the bill which has been drafted will, it is stated, affect only coal and petroleum, and the landowner is to receive a royalty, which is not the case in Austria, where the minerals become, the absolute property of the mining operator.

Now, Lord Penrhyn. We want your reply on the following very simple point:—You declared that the Prince of Wales's son refused to go to the Eisteddfod because party politics—that is to say, Liberal politics—had been introduced into it. To this statement Sir Francis Knollys on behalf of the Prince of Wales, gives the lie direct, and declares that the Prince of Wales's son declined to attend, not because the Liberals were trying to mix up party politics with a national celebration, but because you declined to attend on that account, and that the Duke of Clarence, being your guest, could not, in ccmmon politeness, go without his host. ' In other words, Sir Francis Knollys declaves that your conduct, and not that of the Prince of Wales or the Duke of Clarence, was the cause of the latter's non- attendance at the Eisteddfod. Now, as you have impertinently dragged the name of royalty into the arena of Tory politics perhaps you will kindly apologise to the Prince of Wales, to the Duke of Clarence, and what is very much more important than either, to the Welsh people.
RHYMES IN THE DIALECT.

THE MYSTERY OF THE COFFIN. We take the following from the reminiscences of Mr. Joseph Jefferson, the actor, in the September number of "The Century " The Gregory mansion was an interesting old house; the ivy had covered the walls long ago, and was now climbing upon the roof. The lawn was shaded with fine old oaks, planted by the original owner, and the grounds were tastefully laid out and kept in trim by an interesting Scotch gardener. His father and grandfather had been servants in the same house ; and he himself, then past seventy years of age, told me of many interesting events that had happened in the auld lang syne. My wife had been ill for some days, and we were quite alarmed at her low condition. One evening I was sitting by her bedside reading when my son came to look for some article in one of the closets at the far end of the room; he had a candle in his hand, and was peering at something that had attrac- ted his attention on the top shelf. Suddenly he gave a start and a half-suppressed cry of fear, and as he turned his face towards me I saw that he had grown quite pale, while his hair seemed to stand on end with fright. 1 was about to ask him what had shocked him, when he made a nervous motion for me to be quiet, and leaving the room hurriedly beckoned me to follow him. It was quite evident that something had startled him, and that he did not wish my wife to know what it was. When we were alone in the entry he gave me the light, saying, "Go back, and look on the top shelf of the closet." I took the candle from him, and, retiring to the room, sat down to read, so as not to attract my wife's attention. She asked me what had startled Tom, tc which I replied," Oh, nothing; it was only some of his nonsense." I waited anxiously until my wife dropped off to sleep. She was in a critical state of health, and the least excitement or shock might have killed her ;so 3 took up a light, and standing upon a chair saw, to my horror and surprise, a child's coffin. It had been put far backend well out of sight, which accounted for no one of the family having seen it before. I took it down, and walked stealthily out of the room with the burden under my arm. I went directly to the library with it, and calling my son , and a friend who was staying in the house with me I locked the door, and called a council as to what course it was best to pursue. The coffin was some- thing over two feet long, just about the size of one that would contain a new born-infant. We were somewhat puzzled, arid many plans were discussed. I thought over the reticence of the Scotch gardener in all matters connected with the family, conjuring up a suspicion that some dark mystery surrounded the house. We next thought of sending for the coroner, and placing the matter in the hands of the authorities. At last I determined on opening the coffin myself, rather than make any stir before I was sure that the case was one needing public at- tention. We got a screwdriver, and with some con- siderable agitation we began to. open the lid, and as we removed it we discovered the dead body of a large poll-parrot. We were elf dreadfully sold, and burst out laughing at the mystery and precaution , in which we had been lately indulging. It all came out the next day :: it was a favoured pet of Miss Gregory, and the gardener was to have buried it in her absence, but had forgotten it.
I.

div.p: A CHAMPION PRO._

Bi footbo lot co7d " we'd bin licked weel once or twice, An' th' way they chaffed au' snub'd us rued eawr teorn feel owt but nice ; Like sowjers, they'd o stiffen up, when us they chanced to see, An' stretched an' swaggered just like- some o' th' aristocracy. They sed as t' cause o' ther success wur him, 'at knocks
abeawt— A trampin' footbo player, Wl' his shin-booan tekken
eawt ; He'd gi'en adyice an' towd 'em heaw to tackle men an' t' bo, An' done 'ern rattlin' service, like a fost-class Pro.
When eawr Committee heeard o' thad, they tavrked a
neet or two Ad strapped a lot o' drink up at eawr.Clubtheawse von o' th' broo ; At last id wur decided theer, bi fifteen vooates to three, They'd hey a fost-ciass,player, too, wodeyer t' cost mut

. • Ae. t' landlord wur mart treasurer, an' sed he'd see us thro', Fhwr top nobs off to Seotland seet, to try wod they cud do; An' soon a tallygram wur sent fro' theer to let us know They'd dropt o' t' mon they wanted—a reight good Champion Pro 1 We went to t' station in a gang tha.d neet ea wr men coom in, An' when we clapt eawr een on himove cuddn'll help but grin; We o felt gradely satisfied—he seemed a likely chap— An' th' teom declared eawr deputies bed med a lucky snap! Ea wr players flashed thersels abeawt, an' bovrdiy towd ther skeoms, Heaw varra soon they'd rank thersels as one o' thr leodin' teoms. But neaw they wawk like mourners—melancholy, dull,

„ an' slow, For he isn'd wod they reckoned him—a Champion Pro! Pro's short fora professional,—av cooarse yoill a know thad ; But wod yon chap professes is, lust t' thing as meks us mad • It's true he is a player,—a rare good un—up to th' mark, An' never moons to kill hissel wi' bucklin' to hard wark. lie's a gret strappin' fella, full o' nowt but noisy- brag, For when he shoots for goal he sends t' b reight to t' corner flag. One kessend him ” Surpriser," an' soon geet a welt on t' jaw-, For at eytin' an' at feightie he's a Champion Pro! Th' fost day he went to practise he wur forrud on t reight wine, An' shaped at punchin' t' he, like Navvy Turn at th' Highland fling; We put him onto t' left wing then, but when he tried to "screw," He welly turned a somerset, an' med us o look blue! We tried him then i' t goal a bit,—a swift shot hit his nooase, He rooared just like a bull' at's mad, an' up his temper rooase, He whizzed his arras, like drumsticks, reawnd, an' shot eawt mony a blow, An' proved hissel among eawr lot a Champion Pro ! If he runs hawf a field length, he's done up an' eawt o puff, Then lays him deawn, but if we laff, he gods up rayther ruff, An' charges wild among us o' an' rattles at eawr knees, Till t' players are laid reawnd him like a lot o' deein' flees. Tiler's four o'th' teom this week bin sent inside th' In- firmary gates, An' teoms we owt to play, 'thro' him' hey cancelled o ther dates; But th' news we hey fro' Scotland puts a capper onto o, Ther's nod a teom o'er th' Border knows eawr Champion Pro! Ther's bin black looks an' discontent th' club for mony a day, We've getten a professional, an' dearly we've to pay; Eawr President an' Vice keep coin' one another foo's, An', to tell th' truth, between 'em ther's but little odds to choose. Th' Committee's gradely bad, an' th' teoms sitch a
_ nervous state, - They loyso i' every match they play, an' we korn'd ged a" gate." We've nowt to pay expenses wi' for th' Scotchmon's ta'en
- id o, An' t' club 'll soon be bankrupt thro' eawr Champion

Pro. Then when thad bad job happens, as id will i' tooathrT days, He'll go back to his " thussells" an' his "hither " an' his "braes." But he wern'd gooa empty-handed, for he's getter). lots o' brass, An' liv'd o' t' best o' meyt an drink, an' cooarted th' landlord's lass. ' Ther wern'd be mony tears shed when he teks hissel I
away. We'st profit bi his loss, an' feel med o'er again an' gay ; But them as wins con allus laugh, an' we've no room to Crow. For we've getten sucked in gradely wi' a stiff-backed Pro!
JACK ANN'S.

div.head: SIR GEORGE URNS. SOME OF HIS STORIES.
div.p: SIR GEORGE URNS. SOME OF HIS STORIES.

Although the death of Sir George Burns," The Patriarch of 14 emyss Bay," was announced but a few months ago, a biography of, his life has already been published by Mr. Edwin Bladder (Hodder and Stoughton, 27, Paternoster-row,. Sir George Burns was raised to the baronetcy at the ripe old age of 94, being the oldest recipient. of such an honour in the worl I's history. The story of his remarkable career includes the early history of Atlantic steam navigation, and the founding of the Cunard Com- pany. The volume is brimful of anecdotes, most of them being of a distinctly humorous turn. One of George Burns'. earliest and most intimate acquaintances was the-celebrated Dr. Chalmers, and the friendship between the two-men continued till ,Ideath parted them. Dr: Chalmers handwriting we ! are told, was notoriouslybad,. insomuch that When he wrote to his mother—so• the story goes—she would put the letter on.the shelf„saying, This is from Tam. I'll keep it till he comes hame, for him to read it himself." A good story is told of 'Norman Macleod and John Burns (a son of Sir George), when together with Anthony Trollope on a tour in the Highlands. On arriving at an inn in Oban,late at night, they had supper, and then told stories and laughed without stint half the night through.. lia the morning an old gentleman who slept in a.bedroom above them, complained to the landlord that he had not been able to sleep on account of the noise from the party below; and added his regret that such men should "take more than was good for them." "Well," re- plied the landlord, " Lam,boundi to say there was a good deal of loud talking and laughing; but they had nothing stronger; than, tea and herrings." "Bless me," rejoined the old gentleman, "if that is so, what would Dr. Macleod and Mr. John Burns be after dinner?" The same Mr. John. Burns once had the honour to propose Lord Palmerston as.ansember of the Gaiter Club. .Now, there is a rule of this club, which is to the effect that at "Gaiters,' there shall be no "up- right speaking." When it came. to. Lord Palmerston's turn to reply, he not only: did not rise but buried' half his body under the table and in that quaint, dry style which distinguished his humour, said,' among other good things—'Gentlemen, I am very, proud and flattered:to be associated with such a distinguished body,. I am informed, though gaiters have an intimate connection with legs, that-no gaiterman is allowed to speak upon his legs. Ile may speak about his, legs), but not upon his legs. Now, as we in these days never show our legainas- much as trousers would conceal even the gaiter. if we wore it, you will excuse me if lam very short in my thanks. Lean only assure you that whether I wear long gaiters-or short gaiters, my memory of; your kindness will belong, and not short." . .

- It is not surprising to and that Sir Georg s Burns,., whose personal recollections stretched from the battle of Trafalgar to the Parnell Commission, should have had his mind stored with innumerable anecdotes. Lord Shaftesbury was a great friend of the Duke of Wellington, and the former is Sir- George's authority for the following story :--" The duke told him (Lord Shaftesbury) of a very,singular ' occurrence which took place at Waterloo. At one moment in the battle. the duke was left aloncs-bi^ aides-de-camp having been dispatched ;with mes- sages, when a gentleman in plain clothes rode up tc. him and said,.' Can. Ibe of any use, sir 2', The. duke looked at hima and' instantly said. Ws, talz,tha'A' pencil note to the commanding officer,pointingfto a regiment, inthe very- heat of the engagementt. Tle gentleman. insmikdiately complied, and gllopird through the thick of the fight and delivered the note. After thilmttlethe duke made everrinqu3rY, but though he-for long used all the- means-in his power,he never could trace to whomlhe was-indolated, and he told Lord Shaftesbury that. he coasidered it one of the most gallent deeds that had over come under-his notice,.as. the gentlemnia.who did itcould have had no prospect of reward or honon"—From the 'Star."

CHAPTER, xxvrrw • A BRAVE RESCUE.

We win now proceed to relate the very extraor- dinary circumstances attending the arrival of Sit William Deane and :Captain Rushleigh from India, with the subsequent and concluding °yenta which will bring this history to a conclusion.

Cons along, uncle," said Minnie, who was wait- ing anxiously for George Collier to accompany her. "Come along. We sha/1 not have time to reach the next station unless you make haste." "Plenty of time, my dear. Don't you hurry. 1 never knew such a girl for the railways. No wonder they call you The Signalman's Daughter.' You are as fond of the line as if you you had been born on it."
"Mother says I was born at sea," replied Minnie; "but I am not a bit foncl:of the water." "Ml Britons should be fond of the sea,"remarked Collier.

_ _ "But I can't be English if I was born at sea. Can I, uncle ? " "Yes, my dear. Stepney is your parish. In London it is. All people born at sea belongs,'so I am told, to Stepney parish." "Who was my father, uncle P Did you ever see him? I suppose not, though." "Yes, I did," replied Collier, grimly. "lie was about here a good deal before he and.your mother went to India. Yes, I know'd him." "Ho was an officer, wasn't he—in the army—like Sir 'William Deane ? " • "Very like I should say," replied Collier ;• "but never mind, my dear, he's dead, poor gentleman." " Gentleman ! Was poor papa a gentleman ?" "Yes; officers are gentlemen, I suppose," said the signalman; "at least, they say so." "Am I like him, uncle ?" asked the girl. "Not a bit, my dear —not in face,l mean; and I don't know as you are like him in any other way, either." "I like you to talk to me," continnedllinnie ; "you always tell me what I want. o other never will say anything about me when I was a baby. She thinks me unkind if I ask her, and I am sure I don't mean to be."

"She can't think you unkind, dewy, . It is only natural, after all, that you should want to know all about yourself. There's many a one of us who doesn't know any more about himself than you, or not as much. It's a weary world, andTm.a-gellin' tired of it all."

"Oh, mud(); you getting tired of living? Non- sense!" cried Minnie, clasping his arm.. "You are tialking like an old man. You will live a long time yet, you know." " Who can'tell that!'" replied Collier: "I've had nanny narrow escapes, Minnie, on this very line, -when I was signalman, partiiularly; but I never had what people call warnings till last night" "Warnings, Uncle George! Warnings of what ?" "Of death, my dear. But you are too young to be talked to like this. Never mind: We'll do our business and come home as quick as we can. I don't feel over happy." Minnie pulled his face down to hers and kissed him. "There's a special one for you," she said, "and a warning you'll have no moredf you talk so sad/y." "Talkin. of specials," said the ex-signalman. "There's a special coming down to-day with Sir William Deane, the great soldier, and his friends. So rwe must remember that. Here comes the goods train; look how his dropping his Ere on the line. There's something wrong about the ash-pan, I expect." In fact the engine as it approachedfwas !letting fall large hot coals, which smoked, away and burnt the sleepers as they fell.. Collier shouted to the &liver, who made some answer and seemed aware of the fault in the machine, probably intending to remedy it at the next station., . . _

There were many incidents in that stroll along the line which Minnie remembered for many a day. The platelayers all :gave them a cheerful greeting, the engine men as they passed waved their hands and caps to the girl and her companion, and when they reached the cutting ..ev gang of men with pitoh and tar (with which .they had been lately barring the wooden viaduct over the gully previously mentioned in commotion with the, strike) entered into an animated conversationl with the inspector con- aerning the permanent way and' its defects. The birds sang and fluttered across the line, hopping familiarly upon the wires of the telegraph till Minnie in her ignorance wondered they .'t fall down dead from the electric) shock.

Her simple observation reminded the inspector ,of the trick he hid played upon Sandy Sam, and he told Minnie all about it, and how the man had tried to wreck the trains on thaelitidge they wcza now approaching. "We must mind the special does not mt um on that viaduct, Minnie. Thare,iit not much morn to stand up, I can tell you.e!" "We can lie down," tepliNt Minnie, half smiling; then remembering the anxiety she had mused, she added, "I will never pleymmr more triclm on the railway. lam so very sorryi.lincle George." He assured her that !,all'; was forgivem; and at length they turned the curve and came itt sight of , a very pretty bit of thalline—the limit of .Collier's inspection. In front the line ram-,gently into theinidst of a_ grove of trees which: sheltered it on both sides, the , foliage meeting overhemi,, and forming quite a. natural tunnel of. leaves. Just in front of this bower, so to speak..., the white tinfmrs of the, viaduct were plainly. visible where it spanned thek, little rapine leading te,the canal and the me.

The canal passeciA, aorass it at tan end, an4l beyond. that again at some, distance the seashore was distinctly visible through the spacg lox. the trees hid the view on the, right, and thN embanknuatt topped with more treos,on the left ("die enclosed tini Line for one or two,rniless It was a very chancing places and quite like a forest through which the, railway had beentilaid.. But there,was no lomat,— only an extensive..basf foliage, elliefly pines and. other eoniferoua treee... _

In this spot -ilia siipalman and; his " daugAter "' at down and rested,. chatting of aaany thinf;'s an& le4Plaft "What is, that smoke the uncle?" • asked Minnie, suddenly.. "How curioaa that there-slaould 1* any here ! "Someone inay have lighted si fire for tireppitah- kg, but they,aught to have put; it out," relied!the signalman. "We'll see to it presently." "But look :round, it is getting worse. The sun has set fire t,a,the grass, perhaps," said Mianie, "Not likaly,, ray dear; it i that careless, pach- gang—depend. won it. They have lefla the fire smouldering:, upon the line.. We'll go 3414. put it out.

The sign' alinsin and his young companion aaranced towards the viaduct, but as they approached, it was evident that the fire was n4t on the line but upon the bridge itself. As soon as this became evident to Collierhe hurried forward, and as he. came ;nearer the danger became very c‘vident. " Why the bridge is. burning, Mitinil'e. Good heavens the timbers ara•already on fire! Who has done this Look. ill); God, the tmai?salight ! The whole.thing will blasa up soon. Come, hurry up, and help me to put the fire out. Quick. Quick I " "'I see," cried Minnie. "Here in the worst place. It must have been, a coal from that engine that dzoppoil and burnedit first." "Very likely," assented Collier,. who was busy throwing gravel and. beating the•fire with a 'branch of air e. " Very likely. What am von doing P he shoutetl to his companion. Minnie paid =attention to Mtn. Alongside the line ran just there a tiny rivulet, which hurried along, and finally trickled through a drain-pipe down into the, ravine. Minnie had taken off a ; light shawl she wore, and had steeped it in the water before the inspector could step her. She ran bark to the bridge, and, by pressing the wet shawl upon the nearly blazing wood, managed„, after a thas,te subdue a very dangerous outbreak, /here was one beam—quite a small one—which, had it remained burning, would soon have blazed out, and, endangered the whole structure. But, notwithstanding- all their exertions, the firs would have gained tad not assistance arriived. Seeing that, unless George Collier could SLICCCtea in checking the flames„ the whole structure would be charred, and dangerous, and perhaps give tvq, when a train passed overt it, Minnie hurried forward up tho line, incited:by Collier "Run along, girl; take this red:handkenchiet and meet the spacial. Get round this corner as, quick as you can. The line is straight then for a good bit, and they will Bee yOu. Tell them to come slowly up to the bridge." Minnie needed no second bidding, " She hurried along, and soon after she lad turned the corner she perceived the cloud of steam and smoke in the dis- tance. The special train bearing Sir William Deane and his tried companion-in-arms, Captain Rushleigh, was rapidly approaching. The young girl still advaneed,Twaving her red handkerchief with all her. might.' The train still approached, and the engine was distinctly visible. Just as Minnie began to feel that the train would not pull up, the steam was shui" off, and Boated aside; and then a series pi- whistles told her practised eye that her *nal had. been seen and recognised. The train was palling up I

CHAPTER XXVIL LADY DEANE MEETS LUCY LAYTON.

WE must now endeavour to explain how it hapscnsd that Minnie had arrived at the Hall, and to do this wa must go back to the morning before her arrival. Mar- maduke Deane did not accept the punishment he had received in a manner at all befitting the high station in life he had to support. He was obliged to nurse his revenge, though, and that he would he revenged, those who knew him best were convinced.
Lady Deane had. reasoned with him upon the sin Of pugilism; had endeavoured to show him how very unbecoming his.whole_behaviour had been. _

"The ids, 'she said, "of your wishing to marry village girl. .Your father will be home 113 a few days, and to him we will appeal." Marmaduke had never seen this terrible father, who had been so often held up to him as a pattern; and felt rather awed at the near approach of the meeting. .

"A hey like you thinking of marrying at all is ridiculous,' continued Lady Deane. "Time enough when you are of age to think of such things." "I suppose Watson thinks of it - all men think oil getting married, don't they P" asked the young man. "I'm old enough." " All mer 4 yes—not boys like you. I will call upon this Mrs. Layton and advise her about her child. I cannot have this girl thrown at your head, as the phrase goes. She is no companion for you." "Lily Watson knows her," muttered the invalid. "Miss Watson is quite different. If you had any taste you would have preferred her. SAV is a ladY, and will have plenty of money. No one could: possibly object to Lily Watson," said Lady Deane., "I'll go and spoon' her if you like," said the' elegant youth. "I don't care a pin for her, but she might like me, and if the governor-doesn't come, and spoil sport it might come off." "You are really incorrigible, Marmeduke. I. cannot listen to such remarks. Where you have got such ideas I cannot uuderstand. Not from me— and certainly not from your dear father. will see this woman Layton to day." Lady Deane had made up her mind to speak to Lucy and endeavour to induce her to keep her daughter out of Marmaduke's way, but when it came to the point there was a dmlicacy about the question which Lady Deane could not break through. Under the circumstanrrs, her ladyship thought she would go up and ' call upon Lady Watson, and ex- plain her views to her sympathising friend. This would also be a good opportunity to find out whether there was any likelihood of any feeling for her Mar. madoke existing irr.Lily'e heart. So Lady Deane went up to "the Towers," and hoped to be fortunate enaegh to find Lady Watson at home.
Lady Deane determined' on this occasion to 'die pense with the carriage,..and took her way across , the fields and through the lane to consult the chair man's wife.

She did not reach "the Tdwers," though, upon that occasion. While crossing, the park she encountered Lucy Layton, who respectfully, if 'boldly, greeted her; and then it occurred to Lady Deane to make her remarks concerning Minnie to her mother, as she thought her. "Good morning, Mrs. Layton. lam glad 'te meet you; for I wish to speak to you. My FON, as you are aware, has been inured in defending yous daughter." . Mrs. Layton was understood to say it was,in defending himself, while- he had offended her daughter; but she did not, insist upon this vievt,of the else.

"No matter," said Ladpikane ; "but I wish it to be understou that Marmaduke must not be en. eouragod to associate with' your daughter. It is always best on these occasions to speak frankly; and you innst excuse me when I say that the girl ought not to encourage him." " She does not encourage him," said Lucy - Layton. _ _

" If she did not tolerate his visits the boy wonld' not go so often; you know- that as well as-I do- The young girl (her ladyship would not call dm' lady) is doubtless very winning, and were she in at proper sphere of life it might be permitted, but as it,

"As it is, Lady Deane, things must lake their chance. My daughter is quite capable of takinct care of herself, and, I 'think, Mr. Marmaduke iu likely- enough to have his own way. I shalt not; interfere."

"-nn take very high ground in th Mts.. Layton. I have befriended you in some- respects,. and was not prepared for any resistance on • your- part-to such a very obvious arrangemeat.' I wilt forbid my son to gooup to your cottage inlature,, and 'when Sir Williarn-returus—"

"-He will see me righted," said Lucy.. "t' oars depanil upon him at, any rate. Ho wilt. eognik,e-- She suddenly stopped. Her reason for thttandia-- tillbag- a drop of poisonninto Lady Daniel' heartwaa not-clear even to herself. The failnre of her plangor her..sode marriage to.the heiress, or the chalaces of his succession at all; were becomina--faint. Sir William was on his way home, and if by any chance hen husband ever rreturned, and he blew thoir child was a by, wiaatwonld become ci.her then-2 33er apparently well-planned edifire.was. caturtla. nog slowly away, and would soon leave her home. less and unshelterelarter all her cars,- and; iactwith- standing the well-arranged meshes to catch others, her own feet were-not to be tripped up;, " Sir William will recognise niaat 7". increSred Lady Deane, after n.,-pause, during which she strove to repress her anger. "Have you seen Sir Winiam Vefore ? " "Yes," replied. Tilley, boldly, "It haye—in and he will recognise me—and rap—claims."' "I do not understand you, woman," 'said Lady "It is quite impossible. that Sir William can in any way be imposed upon by, such. assertions any more than .I can. You are only adding insult to injury, Mrs- Layton, and I would suggest the pro- priety f yGem leaving your present abode. We cannot tohave ourAciu brought into 'contact with your child. The intimacy must cease."' “That will entirely depend upon, citeurustances," replied LuarLayton. "My child is quite as dear to me as yours is to you. If suath a marriage were, to take plc,eer son would nct be ashamed of reys, hild."

_ It is no.use speaking to ynur'said Lady Dear.ei, The'subject cannot be further discussed. between us. Where is your daughtsr "Minnie has, gone down to the railway to ier 'uncle,' as we call the inspector:' "I will endeavour to see her, and inform her that her meetings with. Marmadlike mast cease."

"Yew, Will, I trust, do, no, such thing, Lady Deane: Lam quite able to .manage my own affairs and hers.. Ii you do so far forget yourself—"' Mrs,.Laytm checked fferself in, time. She very nearly had.told all.

" Leannat-seibniit tat-kegs- I will act as seems best to myself. Good. morning. You will not expect to, see me agaadnnor shall I permit Marma- dule—my son—to meet your daughter." "Are yon sure he ia youraon ?" said Lucy Layton, ering, a parting shot.. "What do you mean, woman?" exclaimed her ladyBl4. "You have moire than once, 'thrown out Mysterious hints. Explain yourself." Enty Layton vouchsafed no reply,, but, turnin way, proceeded homewards. Lady Deane, who re, traeced her steps, with very mingled &clings. Neither had got very far upon their homewarde Ways when a man overtook Mrs. Layton with a message that caused her to prceeed, at once towards, the railway station ; and a telegram, which had Lady Ded eaannehour before, was at Isagth delivered to .She opened it as she went along. It was from Sir William announcing his speedy arrival by Special train with Captain Ruahleigh. The massage to Lucy Layton was to the effect that Minnie was going down the line with her "Uncle George," and would not be back till dark, This arrangement did not snit Mrs. Layton, and she made up her mind to bring Minnie home, She was half inclined to take the girl to the Hall, and tell the whole truth. She was getting very tired el Planning, and at present things looked very badly tor her. But when she got to the station she discovered that Minnie and Collier had gone away some dis. tan Ce. His business was to inspect the line, and he had taken the girl with him. It was a very fortunate thing that he did so, fed an accident happened, which would have cost many lives -had not Minnie been present. It was this occurrence which led to Mirmie's sad. den and unexpectedappearance at the Ada:as already related, after Marmaduke's interview with Mn. Layton, which took place after Lady Deane had, as a more vulgar person would have expiated it, give* 01q.Layton a piece of her mind.

But another train which had come in the 01,P"eliA direction also pulled up and stopp.hl close to where Minnie, with her red handkerchief was waiting to tell her news. The up express train and the down special) arrived together, and Minnie was eagerly questioned. "It might have been a deal worse," said the driver of the up-train, "and it's a mercy it isn't. I couldn't pull up sooner,. could we, Fred?" we did all we could.. Let us get back again. You needn't come, miss.":_:: ...ie., - He nodded:sigiaifleantly- as he spoke to:the driver a the special train, wbamodded in reply, "You come in here, Miss," said the guard.. "We'll take ye on the viaduct. The compenr ought to reward ye well." "George Collier deserves the reward." said, Minnie; "he told me to coma en , I must see hire' for a mine." "You needn't go now," said the guard.' 7" The gentlemen in the train wish to speak to you. Come' in here, we will carry you safely back to the station.... Minnie, of course, could not refuse. The door of the reserved saloon carriage was opened, and she was greeted very kindly 13; two gentlemen. One' of the occupants immediately attracted her attention, and she equally attracted the attention of the other., "'Well, my girl, so you have saved our train, I hear. You are very brave, and I am sure' we are very thankful such a plucky little lady happened to' be near. 'What is your name, my dear ?" The General—for the person who thus addressed Minnie was'. Sir William Deane himself—uncon- sciously found himself becoming more familiaras his, address proceeded. He perceived.in a moment that- the girl was no labourer's; child. "My name ,is Minnie Layton," replied the girl. simply. The General's companion started violently•:. "Great Jove, is it possible !" he exclaimed • “*.Lw —no—it cannot be!' "What's the matter, Rushleigh ? Did the name strike you? I'confess the circumstance is curious but, let me see—was your mother ever in India, naY. dear ?"" "I don't know; never was," replied the child. "I belong to Stepney, Uncle George says!' "Stepney. You are are a Londoner, then-,--a cockney ?" replied the General, smiling kindlV. "I don't know what you mean,' said Minnie. "George Collier says so." Captain Rushleigh rose hastily, and went to the window, . where he remained looking out.. The train was slowly crossing the viaduct; the -timber's of which were charred and smoking. He noticed a bundle of something on the up-line, and shilddered. The train was, stopped, and, it was put into the. rear van.. Meantime the General was chattering lasniliszll with Minnie, who took a great fancy to the old soldier, and permitted him to hold her band familiarly in his own. • " So George Collier is your uncle," imid ,Captain Rushleigh, suddenly coming back to lhis:sear. "IS he very old, now P" "Not very, but he is not my own uncle.. We call him uncle. He brought me with him to-daYO and sent me on to warn the train, sir. He is still en the lisle. . He is an inspector now." p‘ Captain Rushleigh continued to stare" at Minnie as intently that at at she blushed deeply under his prolonged scrutiny. Minnie disliked being stared at very much, and, after a more than usual]: long look,,she turned away, murmuring— " Well, I 'hope you'll know me again." ' The General laughed and rebuked his younger friend. " You shOuld,not embarrass the girl so, Rnshleigh• What makes you stare at her ? " "Is it possible you do not .see the likeness, General', You must perceive it. Leek again!' "No, 'roan- distinguish nothing ;very remark- able in that 'way-, but I can see that ;this girl is far above her uncle's station in life. She has a natural grace and ladylike manner which impresses me veal much. Your, mother's name is Layton,7 he C0,,,n- -1 tinued.. "la her husband a soldier ? • Was father in the army??' "I never saw father," replied the girl«. "He diel 'refore I was born." "And you were born in London, you say P" asked Oaptain:Rushleigh. "Not .at sou I was:born omboard ship," motl3el says.. " But --youcsaid Stepney," continued the captain. Then,, suddenly recollecting'; himself, ho added, ...of course, yes. All people horn at sea are said to belong te.Stopney, General. I seelt now." " Yes,asentedlMinnie, quickly. ."Uncle George • told sue so." "HOw.strangel” exclaimelßushlaigh, mnsinel "(Where do you live, my dear f"-he said. " Neardlie Hall at Woodbine Cotter. It belong; to Lady Deane. Sir Williamds— "Here,"'fmterrupted the General, taking her ban. ct kindly, "you' must come home with me first. Ye?, are, tired; and Lady Deanomust thank you at least, headded. "Meantime try this on."' He handed her a plain Indian geld ring which he tools Irene his little finger-and placed it on Minnie's middle finger of the right land. " That willeerve to remember rne by," said . Sir William, kissing her affectionately, for he felt & great, interest in the girl already. 06" Oh, but 'I cannot have 'this," she exclaimed- ',Mother will not let me wear rings, I'm sure.'!' "It will see your mcther and, obtain her permis- sion. Here we are. Now, Rushleigh. Coma with

_ us, my dear. I must insist." - Minnie could not disobey the !find, nice, old gentle- man, who talked to her as ifi he were her-father. She. wished he had been,. was so kind and affec- tionate that all her heart went out to him at once. They hurried her away to the General's Xixriage' amid the wonderment of th.e people at the station... and drove away to the Hall, untidy and dishevelled,- aa she was. She had been, se occupied that she Ilea forgotten to ask about her Uncle Collier, 'tor did she- make any remark when the train stopp on ed the viaduct. "I shall see hi_Mpto.maarrow," thought 31.11aa114 "and give him .the rhig, He will weAr it, for ,vba' deserves But poor George Collier would never wear ringg-' again. He had met Ilia reward already. Ran °vex.' by the up express, he had been killad on the linet at the very time he had been so unselfishly fetaa. upon the safety of others. Minnie was quite unconscious of his fate, and regretting his absence, had no idea that she and her dear" uncle "---Aindl„ good, faithful George Collier-- had passed away for ever, and that his inelancia4 presentiment aftclesith had proved alas, LOU true.-

div.head: DISASTROUS RAILWAY COLLISION.
div.p: DISASTROUS RAILWAY COLLISION.

EIGHT LIVES LOST. A disastrous collision occurred, on Sunday, between an East-end and a West bound goods train, on the kalti- More and Ohio line, near .Zanesville. Instructions had been given for the trains to pass each other at Black- bank, but the operator there tailed to deliver the order, and, perceiving his blunder too late, telegraphed to the •operatn. at Zanesville that a collision was unavoidable, and then left his post. The two trains met with a fear- ful crash, the cars being pilled up in a confused heap, a d eight persons were killed.
THE TRADES CONGRESS PARLIAMEN-
TARY COMMITTEE.

At the quarterly meeting of the representatives of the Amalgamated Society of Cotton Spinners of Lancashire and adjoining counties, held in Manchester, on Satur- day, the delegates to the Trades Congress presented their reports, and whilst the general question of the relation of The Cotton Operatives' Society to the Congress was left over for future consideration it was agreed that as many of the resolutions passed by the Congress were of a char- acter which the amalgamated society could not support, The general secretary (Mr. Mawdsley) should be recom- mended to resign his seat on the Parliamentary Com- mittee.
A MOTHER AND FIVE CHILDREN MURDERED IN TEXAS.

Another desperate affair has been added to the annals of crime in Texas. A man named Albert Nutting, a rough character, called on Saturday morning at the farmhouse of a respectable family named Elwell, almost a mile east of San Antonio. The husband was away, but his wife, with her six children, ranging from two years old up to fifteen, was at home. The man demanded Money, which was refused. Without at least warning he put a bullet through the mother's head, and fired the contents of four other barrels of the revolver at four of children, and killed another with a jack knife. The eldest, a girl of 15, managed to escape and alarm the neighbourhood. They found Mrs. Elwell lying dead in the hall, and besides her the bodies of her five children. A posse has been organized and is in pursuit of Nutting, who will be lynched when caught.

div.head: SIR G. 0. TREVELYAN ON POLITICAL REFORMS.
div.p: SIR G. 0. TREVELYAN ON POLITICAL REFORMS.

Sir George Trevelyan, addressing an open-air meeting at Golspie, near Inverness, on Tuesday, advocated the Payment of members of Parliament and shorter Partia- l:l:Lents. fie held that a imribund Parliament should not commit the nation to an obligation of £200,000,000 for compensation to the liquor interest. In next session they must see that such a parliament did not com- mit them to buy the land of Ireland. What a prospect there was for the country. Two years more of dis- appointment, expectation, and reforms deferred for England, Scotland, and Wales. Did any man believe that if we had a new Parlia:nent the prison door would be closed on Mr. Dillon : that another Irish duke would Ret off with a quarter of a million of their money; that the Welsh Church would stand ; that the. Crofters Act Would remain inoperative ? Let the Liberal electors of the country give expression to their views, and show what they thought of four years of Tory rule.

div.head: EVILS OF PROTECTION.
div.p: EVILS OF PROTECTION.

THE AMERICAN TARIFF BILL. The Conference Committee of the Senate and House of Representatives having come to an agreement upon the Tariff Bill, that measure was on Saturday passed by the the House, and this ensures the enactment of the new Tariff. It was estimated by members of the Conference that the effect of the new Tariff will be a reduction in the Customs revenue of sixty million dollars, but others interested calculate that it will instead produce an in- crease to that extent. Nothing, however, is definitely known as to the nett effect of the change in the Tariff, owing to its raising and lowering thousands of duties. All financial authorities welcome the adjournment of Congress on Wednesday next to afford an opportunity- to consider the important charges affected by the new Bill. Commerce is for the moment seriously affected, owing to the impossibility of fathoming the results of the new Tariff. Whilst some trades are languishing, others are Spurred into unnatural activity, which introduces a new anxiety into the commercial world. Imports of an un- precedented amount cram the bonded warehouses, and how to distribute these without disturbing the markets IS a problem which merchants find it difficult to solve.

div.head: CHANNEL FLEET AT LIVERPOOL
div.p: THE CHANNEL FLEET AT LIVERPOOL

Shortly before noon, on Saturday, the Channel Fleet, consisting of the Camperdown (flagship), the Rodney, Tlowe, Aurora, Immortalite, Curlew, and Speedwell entered the Mersey, where they are to remain, until next Tuesday, open to the public. The arrival of the fleet was witnessed by a vast concourse of people, who lined the piers on both sides of the river, whilst the landing Stage was crowded with sightseers. The vessels were thrown open to the public after arrival, and crowds Paid the shilling which the various tug companies have arranged as the charge for the cAnveyance to and from the fleet. During the whole of the afternoon the river 'was kept very lively by the tug boats with their crowds •of passengers for the fleet. The Dock Board tender, having on board Mr. A. B. Forwood, Secretary of the Admirality ; Sir W. B. Forwood, his brother ; Mr. Alfred bolt, chairman of the Dock Board ; the Mayors 4141.iiverpool and Birkenhead, Mr. William Laird, and Others, went out to meet the fleet. The morning was very tine, and the sight was most imposing as the vessels tame majestically up the river. The Mayor of Liverpool entertained the Officers at dinner in the evening. Though The weather on Sunday was somewhat threatening, there Was an immense number of visitors to the fleet. It is calculated that at least 20,000 were conveyed in the Various tags and ferry-boats, the arrangements working most satisfactorily. On Sunday, as on Saturday, when 11,000 visited the fleet, the flagship Camperdown was the g'reatest attraction. The Fleet left the Mersey on Wednesday for Greenock During the three days the vessels have been lying in the- river they have been visited by 55,000 persons.
