It is understood that Sir Charles Dilke intends to ap- peal to the Superior Courts to reverse the decision of a revising barrister, at Guildford, in striking Lady DRke's name off the list of county voters. At the Tamworth Revision Court, on Tuesday, the name of Lady Emily Peel was struck off the voter's list, the revising barrister stating that as a married woman she could not vote.

div.head: SUICIDE IN ST. PAUL'S
div.p: THE SUICIDE IN ST. PAUL'S

CATHEDRAL. An inquest was held by the London coroner, on Wed- nesday, on Edward Easton, 38, surveyor's clerk, who shot himself, in St. Paul's Cathedral, last Sunday. The evidence showed that he had suffered from ill-health, and his physician had apprehended a suicidal tendency also. The death resulted instantaneously. The jury found that he was temporarily insane.

div.head: ATTEMPTED DOUBLE MURDER.
div.p: ATTEMPTED DOUBLE MURDER.

On Saturday morning a man named Rollitt, residing in Thorton-road, Bradford, attempted to murder his wife and child with a coal-rake. The child lies in a pre- carious condition, and with the mother is under the care of two medical men. Rollitt has been arrested. To a neighbour who, after a severe struggle, succeeded in get- ting the child from him he said, " I had meant finishing it." He was in Menston Asylum for six weeks until a week ago, when, on .the representation of the asylum authorities that he was all right, his wife brought him back.

div.head: MR. MORLEY AT HAWARDEN.
div.p: MR. MORLEY AT HAWARDEN.

On Tuesday morning, Mr. John Morley, M.P., arrived at Chester General Railway Station shortly before 11 o'clock from St. Helens, and left by the quarter to 12 o'clock train for Sandycroft. He was afterwards driven to Harwarden Castle, to pay a visit to Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., and Mr. Henry Gladstone are at present staying at the Castle. On Wednesday Mr. John Morley left Hawarden for London shortly after noon. In the morning at ten o'clock, Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Morley walked' through the park to the new library which Mr. Gladstone has erected for the benefit of the villagers of Hawarden. THE STRIKE AT ST. HELENS.

The strike at the Cowley Hill Plateglass Works of Messrs. Pilkington Bros., remains unsettled. The cast- ing-hall men, who ceased work 14 weeks ago on the firm declining to grant an increase of wages, do not manifest any signs of returning to work on the old terms. They are receiving weekly support from the funds of the 'United Plateglass Workers Society, and the contributions from other trades and the public generally ars such as to create the impression that the dispute will be prolonged for an indefinite period. The hands engaged in the other departments of —he works, however, suffer keenly from the effects of the strike. On Sunday, a meeting of the workmen employed by Messrs. Pilking,ton Bros., at their "bottom" works, was held in the coach-house, Gotham- et. As on the previous Sunday, the building was crowded, and many persons were unable to gain admis- sion_ Considerable enthusiasm prevailed. Mr. P. J. King. president of the Chemical and Copper Workers' Union., was the chief speaker, and after an address on the advantages of combination, over 50 new members were enrolled—On Tuesday afternoon, a deputation of the strike hands waited upon Colonel W. W. Pilkington in his office at the works. They informed that gentle- man that an intimation had been conveyed to them that he desired to see the men, but Mr. Pilkiagton stated that this was not correct. In the course of a brief conversa- tion, Mr. Pilkingtontold the men that they could resume work on signing the usu3l agreement and on the old terms, but the deputation replied that they never in- tended to return to work on the old conditions. The deputation then retired, and the result was afterwards reported to an informal meeting of the strike hands and lock-outs at the Angel Inn, Barrow-st. The action of the deputation was unanimously approved.

div.head: QUEEN OF ROUMANIA.
div.p: THE QUEEN OF ROUMANIA.
A DEMONSTRATION AT LLANDUDNO.

On the occasion of the welcome given by the women of Llandudno and the school children to the Queen of Roumania that town was on Monday gaily decorated. Business was suspended, and the day was observed as a general holiday. At three o'clock two thousand school children, carrying , flowers and banners, paraded the principal streets leading to the Marine Hotel, where "Carmen Sylva " and suit are staying. The Queen waved her handkerchief from the window for half an hour whilst the children passed and repassed her Majesty's rooms. On returning the children assembled before the hotel. General Greciano, the Minister in attendance upon the Queen, who has been seriously ill for many days, was bolstered up with pillows near the win- dow by the side of his sovereign. The children and their friends cheered vociferously. The procession was re- formed, and marched across the parade to tfie pier pavi- lion, where six thousand persons took part in the de- monstration. The Queen drove through the town amid enthusiasm to the pavilion, and was loudly cheered on ascending the platform, accompanied by Lady Augusta Mostyn and Lady Mostyn, the Hon. Henry F. and Mrs. Mostyn, Lady Neville, Sir Richard Bulkeley, Madame Varesco, Dr. Nicol, and Mr. Elias Jones, chairman of the Llandudno Commisioners. On Tuesday the Queen drove out to Gloddaeth Hall on a visit to Lady Augusta Mostyn. Her Majesty, expresses great pleasure and satisfaction at her visit to North Wales. Queen Elizabeth is now fully convalescent. The King of Roumania has abandoned his projected visit to England. 1 The Queen of Roumania on Wednesday concluded her five weeks' visit to North Wales, and left Llandudno in the evening for Balmoral. During the day Her Majesty was presented with addresses by the. Llandudno Town Commissioners and by the Bards, and at night the town was illuminated. The Queen of Roumania arrived at Balmoral, on Thurs- day, on a visit to the Queen. Before leaving Llandudno her Majesty gave a donation of £lO to the Lifeboat Institution and £lO to Sanatorium.

div.head: PUGILISTS AGAIN.
div.p: THE PUGILISTS AGAIN.

The pugilists Slavin and M'Auliffe, learning that war- rants were out for their arrest in connection with the glove contest of Saturday, voluntarily surrendered them- selves, on Monday, to the police. They were charged before Mr. Partridge at the Lambeth Police Court, and 1 remanded till Friday, each in his own recognisancesl of £l,OOO and two sureties of £2,000. Detective-in- spector Chisolme informed the magistrate that he was 1 present at the affair, and it was in no respect a scientific boxing match, but a fierce and furious fight. Slavin left the ring soon after it terminated, but M'Auliffe, who was sick and vomited, and had to have spirits administered by his seconds, was unable to leave for fully twenty minutes. In regard to the proposal of Mr. Fox that J. L. Sullivan should meet Slavin, the American pugilist say he does not care to fight. "Acting," remarks Sullivan, "pays much better than fighting. I have made barrels of money this season. You can bet your life that the stage is a bigger game than the ring." A BRUTAL EXHIBITION AT BARROW. A boxing contest had been announced to take place on Monday night, in the Drill Hall, Barrow, between Thotnas Smith, of Belfast, and David Main, of Sunder- land, under the Marquis of Queensberry's rules, for £3O, with four-ounce gloves. The police getting wind of the affair, the principals had to appear during the day before the Barrow magistrates, who, after a prolonged discus- sion, intimated that although not unanimous, they had I decided that there was no reason for inferfering at that stage, the responsibility for the meeting resting with the principals, the police to be present. A stage had been erected in the centre of the hall, and about 1,000 people were present. In the third round, Main got heavily on to Smith's face and chest, knocking him down. The fighting was now severe, both men show- ing signs of exhaustion and bleeding. With a violent blow Smith was knocked over the ropes just as time was called. It was quite evident DOW that Smith was quite exhausted, and before the fourth round had proceeded far Main again knocked him over the ropes, and as he was now thoroughly done his seconds threw up the sponge.

div.head: CONVERSATION BETWEEN LONDON AND MANCHESTER
div.p: CONVERSATION BETWEEN LONDON AND MANCHESTER

Telephonic communication has just been opened up by ' the National Telephone Company (Limited) between London and Manchester (a distance of 206 miles by the route adcpted), and is being continued further north. The line is not yet quite ready for use by the general public, but it was placed on Monday night by the cour- tesy of the officials at the disposal of the Manchester Field Naturalist's Society for a conference with London I friends on their work of planting trees in their smoky city. A company of 50, presided over by Mr. Alderman IW. H. Bailey (in the absence of the Mayor) and includ- ing many members of the Corporation, were present at the Manchester office of the Telephone Company, and a lively discussion took place on the effect of town fogs on animal and vegetable organisms between Dr. Bailey, of Owens College, and Mr. Oglesby (Manchester), and Colonel Mackenzie, Superintendent of Epping Forest, Dr. Chas. Roberts, Professor R. Meldola, F.R.S., and Mr. Philip Hartog, at the head office, Oxford-court, Cannon- et. It was proposed to take measures to make a syste- matic examination of the composition of the atmosphere, which, both in London and in Manchester, is becoming more and more unfit to support plant life. In the course of the evening refreshments were served, and the toast of "The National Telephone Company," was most cor- dially received by the members of the society. The Ber- liner (a modified Blake) transmitter and the Bell receiver were used, and the voices of the Manchester members were heard quite distinctly and were easily recognised. After the formal proceedings were over the London office was connected with the Princesses' Theatre, Manchester, and the Manchester office with the Savoy Theatre. London. We are imformed that the results were highly satisfactory. Owing to the use of " loop " lines (i.e., complete metallic circuits) a conversation can now be carried on between London and Manchester with- out any disturbing noises whatever.

div.head: TILE LICENSING QUESTION.-RENEWALS
div.p: TILE LICENSING QUESTION.-RENEWALS
REFUSED.

At the adjourned Ryde Licensing Sessions, on Mon- day, the police superintendent reported that a licensed house for which a renewal was asked was not needed, as there were three others fully licensed within 300 yards of it. There was a memorial against the renewal. The license was not renewed. Notice of appeal was given. The Bewdley licensing justices took a very decided line at the adjourned Brewster Sessions, on Monday. They declined absolutely to renew several old licenses on the ground that there were too many public-houses in Bewd- ley. They also declined to hear renewed applications for licenses for refreshment houses which had previously been made and refused. At the adjourned licensing meeting held at Sandwich, on Monday, an application for the removal of a full license from a house called the Three Compasses, at Ramsgate, to another of a better class, holding an off license in Victoria-road in the same borough, which was unanimously refused by the justices. The Chairman, however, said the would renew the license of the former house this year, but in 1891 the licenses of such houses as the Three Compasses would no doubt be generally dealt with according to a law that would presently be passed. Two other applications for new licenses were also refused. At Nantwich, on Monday, the Bench refused the re- newal of the license of Mrs. Tagg, of the Coach and Horses, Buerton. Mrs. Tagg was convicted of permitting drunkenness, and also of being drunk twice on her own premises. The Chairman said the magistrates had resolved" that the superintendent be requested to make efforts during the ensuing twelve months to ascertain how far the number of licenses in the district might be considered to be in excess of the existing requirements, and to report at the next Brewster Sessions." The magistrates wished this report to be prepared, in order that no undue hardship might occur to the owners of licenses the event of the magist rates seeing it their duty to modify the existing number of licenses.

The case which excited most notice at the Blackheath Licensing Sessions, on Tuesday, was that of the Norwich Arms, a prominently placed beerhouse close to Green- wich Pier, belonging to Messrs. Crowley, brewers. Evi- dence proved that the present tenant had been twice fiaed during tho past twelvemonths for selling beer at unlawful hours on Sundays, the license having, on the second occasion, been endorsed. Mr. Grain, however, stated that the brewers had no knowledge of the tenant's laches until after the endorsement, and that they had since made every endeavour to find a new tenant. They would undertake, if the license were renewed, to transfer it within seven days. It was true that the Bench had absolute power, but the fact had only just been realised, and there seemed to be a common understanding through- out the country, that the present year should be a year of grace, and that the arbitrary exercise of the new function should be deferred until next year.—Mr. Low : If we wait until next year we may not have Et convic- tion to justify us. There are seven public-houses and three beershops in the same street. The Bench refused a renewal of the license. All the other licenses were re- newed.

THE EXAMINER, SAT-LiII:WAY OCTOBER 4, 1890. • - NIGHT CLASSES Al RUNCORN BOARD I lIARNEST FESTIVALS. SCHOOL. The experiment of the Runcorn School Board in forming night classes for the teaching of the three R's and othezr subjects was put to a practical test, on Monday evening, when the school was opened, for the first time. About 35 students put in an ap- pearance, which may be considered a highly satis- factory number bra commencement. Mr. J. Pritchard the Chairman of the Board, was present and in a short address, said he was glad to see so many youths and young men anxious to improve themselves. It was the desire of the school Board to give every facility to help students forward in every way. The Education Depart- ment had arranged for the facilities to be given through- out the country, and they trusted that Runcorn would not be behind other towns in taking advantage of the privileges which were offered. He had no doubt the students would be joined by many others before long, and that they would have a very successful school of advanced education. The Board would make provi- sion for teachers according to requirements.—Mr. J. J. Howitt commenced a speech by an anecdote of George Stephenson the first engineer, which deeply interested the juvenile audience, and went on to speak of the advantages of education. Boys now-a-days had more reason to be thankful than they had when he was a boy. In his young days it was thought when they knew reading, writing, and arithmetic, and a little bit of grammar, and knew where their own coun- try was situated, that they were educated as far as they needed to be in the class to which he and they belonged. Be had, after finishing a day's work, sat up studying by candlelight until the early morning. Now boys who were not educated and wished to be, had the opportunity given them, and boys who had a knowledge of mathe- matics, mensuration, could write shorthand, knew a foreign language, and understood the sciences, would come to the front and make a position for themselves. He was certain that no boy would like to be kept at work for a small wage during the whole of his life. He urged them to study and not think of failure, and to encourage them in their work he would endeavour to get some small prizes for those who ;had succeeded the best after the sessions was over. (Applause.)—Mr. G. Moss, the clerk to the Board, and Mr. Moulton then announced the subjects to be taught, and how the classes would be conducted.

BOLD-STRBRT WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WARRINGTON. The harvest festival in connection with the Bold- st. Wesleyan Chapel was held on Sunday, when special sermons were preached, in the morning by the Rev. T. Ross, and in the evening by the Rev. A. Freeman. There was a large congregation at each service. There was as usual a good deal of tasteful decoration, which was deservedly admired. During the service the choir, under the conductorship of Mr. Fanshaw, rendered the anthems "0 Lord how manifold," and "The Lord is loving." In the even- ing, and prior to the sermon, the choir sang the an- them" Ye shall dwell in the land," the solos being taken by Miss Gunton and Mr. Fanshaw. Mr. Harri- son, as usual, presided at the organ. The following amongst others assisted with the decorations : the Misses Smith, Lawton, Weaver, Jones, Fanshaw, Collins, Linger& Kerry, Mrs. Gunnell, and Mrs. Hen- shall. During the day collections were taken on behalf of the circuit funds. CHRIST CHURCH, CROFT. The annual thankgiving services for the safe in- I gathering of the harvest were held in the above ' church on Sunday, when there were large congre- gations. The ladies and gentlemen who took the most prominent part in the work of decoration were Mrs. and Miss Kirkman, Mrs. and Miss Owen (of the Brewery), Mrs. and the Misses Carr, the Misses Maines, Miss S. A. Wild, Miss Hardy, the Misses Makeman, Mr. McCarthy, &c. The service commenced in the morning at half-past ten, the prayers being intoned by the preacher, the Rev. H. A. Hignett, M.A., vicar of Ringway, who also con- ducted the service in the afternoon. The lessons in the afternoon were read by Mr. T. E. Withington. The choir rendered the musical portion of the ser- vices in a creditable manner, especially the anthems, "Praise the Lord, 0 Jerusalem" and "Like as a father pitieth his children." The collections for the churchwardens' expenses amounted to .£9, includ-; ing donations.

div.head: WOMAN THROWN INTO THE MERSEY. NARROW ESCAPE FROM DROWNING.
div.p: A WOMAN THROWN INTO THE MERSEY. NARROW ESCAPE FROM DROWNING.

On Monday afternoon, a woman called Mary Lyons, had a narrow escape from drowning after being thrown into the river at Warrington by a man in whose company she was. The man referred to is named Thomas Hall and is employed as a puddler by Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co., and it seems that he and Lyons spent some time together on Monday. In the afternoon about two o'clock they wandered to a field by the river side near Mr. Cunliffe's tannery, at Howley, and it was here that the outrage took place. Hall after being taken into custody ex- plained the circumstances as follows. He and Lyons, he said, had fallen asleep on the grass and when he awoke he found her hand in his pocket and that she had taken therefrom a sum of 2s. 9d. This he demanded of her to return but as she refused, he became angry and threw her into Lila water. Whether this be the correct version or not there is no doubt that the woman was stuggling in the water when she drew the attention of a large number of people by her loud screams. A crowd very soon collected, and one of the workmen from the tannery bringing a long rake managed to draw Lyons from the water with it. Hall was de- tained till the police were brought, and he was then taken to the police station. Lyons was also taken to the police station and afterwards to the Work- house. She is a woman about 40 years of age, and, according to her own statement, she was born at Dunham Massey, but on Monday came from Bedford Leigh to see a sister who is ill in Warrington. She said that Hall and her had a quarrel, and he threw her into the river. She had already sunk once or twice when she heard some people on the bank shout," be sharp, be sharp." Sne struggled hard to keep afloat, and the man with the long rake was just in time to save her. On Tuesday morning, Hall was brought before Mr. S. Rigby, at the Occasional Court, but it was then stated that the woman had disappeared. She was left at the Workhouse, on Monday evening, ap- parently in an exhausted condition, but early on Tuesday morning she took her discharge and the police had not been able to lay their hands on her although they had made a very diligent search. There was nothing for it, in consequence, but to remand the prisoner and this was done for a week. As he left the Court room he remarked," I know I did it, but I was ill a passion." „

div.head: IRISH PROSECUTIONS.
div.p: THE IRISH PROSECUTIONS.

On Monday very little progress was made with the trial of Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien and their co-defend- ants before Mr. Irwin and Mr. Shannoa at Tipperary, and the proceedings were decidedly dull. The generally monotonous character of the business was only relieved by the revival of the defendants allegation of bias on the part of the Bernh, in connection with which Mr. Healy stated that he meant to apply to the High Court in Dublin for a conditional order to restrain further pro- ceedings in the case pending a raotion for a writ of pro- hibition. On this announcement being made, the Crown council obtained an adjournment for two hours to enable him to communicate with the Attourney-General as to the cburse to be taken. The result of the telegraphic consultation was that the hearing was resumed. On Tuesday the proceedings were again of a very un- interesting character. Large numbers of newspapers containing articles alleged to incriminate certain of the accused were put in, and the police note-taker gave evi- dence respecting the speeches delivered at the Limerick Junction meeting in May last. At one point Mr. Har- rington complained of the conduct of the other side in withholding information usually supplied to the defence. In two cases the bench ruled that papers tendered could not be admitted as evidence, because portions had been cut out. The trial of Wr. O'Brien, Mr. Dillon, and others, was resumed at Tipperary, on Wednesday. A police note- taker gave further evidence respecting the Limerick Junction meeting, and was being examined respecting the subsequent collision with the police, when Mr. Shan- non was present. when the Bench interfered, and de- clared the question to be irrevelant to the issue. A long argument ensued, in the course of which Mr. W. O'Brien described the ruling of the judges as an attempt to smother the case. In further cross-examination of the police note-taker, he admitted that after the Limerick Junction meeting, he ran down O'Brien-st. with a re- volver in one hand and a stick in the other, and that he struck four or five people. A stone had, he said been thrown at him in Church-st., but no one had struck him. He was in plain clothes, and on duty as a shorthand writer. In Dublin, on Wednesday, Mr. Justice Holmes refused the writ of prohibition to suspend proceedings at 'Tip, perary, on the ground of the alleged bias of Mr7Shannon- one of the resident magistrates.

THE ASSAULTS AT TIPPERARY. The summonses for assault against members of the Royal Irish Constabulary at the instance of Mr. Harrison, M.P., and others, in connection with the occurrences at Tipperary a week ago, were down for hearing on Thurs- day, but owing to the amount of opposed licensing business to he got through, were not reached until late in afternoon. Mr. Morphv, on behalf of the police, applied for an adjournment. Mr. Healy, M.P., protested against adjournment, and said that the reason why the summonses had not been served before was that a police- man had been smuggled out of the country with the con- nivance of the Government.—Mr. Morphy denied this. Ultimately the summonses were adjourned until next Thursday.

THE CONGREGATIONAL UNION At
SWASSEA.

The Congregational Union of Engoand and Wales, for the second time in its history, has made Swansea the scene of its deliberations. The autumn meetings com- menced there on Monday. The delegates, who number about 700, commenced to arrive on Saturday, but the bulk of:them did not reach Swansea until Monday. A number of Church clergy have reciprocated the hospita- lity shown by local Nonconformists when the Church Congress was held in Swansea and have thrown open their houses to members of the Union. The last visit made to Swansea was in 1871, when the late Thomas Jones was Chairman. On the present occasion the Rev. Thomas Green (Ashton-under-Lyne) presided. During the afternoon a reception was held in the Albert Hall (tastefully decorated for the occasion) by the Mayor of Swansea (Mr. Alderman Freeman), who is himself a Con- gregationalist, and who tendered a hearty welcome to the Union. Sir Hussey Vivian, M.P., also briefly ad- dressed the delegates. The annual meeting of the Con- gregational Total Abstinence Association took place on Monday evening, when it was stated that of 2,700 Con- gregational ministers upwards of 1,600 were teetotal- lers. The business commenced on Tuesday, under the pre- sidency of the Rev. Thomas Green, of Ashton-under-Lyne. The subject of the president's address was "The secular element in Church life." A paper by the Rev. T. Simon I on " The strength and progress of Congregationalisin," lin which he adopted a most pessimistic view of the future of the cause unless some serious defects were speedily remedied, led to a spirited protest from the Rev. Guinness Rogers, who claimed that never was Congrega- tionalism in a better condition for doin effectual Christian work. On the motion of the Rev. ' 1. P. Glad- stone (London), seconded by Mr. Walter Flazell, a resolu- tion in favour of international arbitration was carried, and on the receipt of an overture to the Union from the general assembly of Presbyterians in the United States, an addition to the motion was passed approvin., of its action in approaching the Christian governments'of the world. On Wednesday the transaction of business at the meet- ings of the Congregational Union was resumed at Swan- sea, when Professor Adeney, New College, read a paper on" Christ and the Social Problems of Modern Times." He urged forgetfulness of the hard ecclesiasticism of priests and the dismal dogmatism of schools and the return to Christ to discover that the Saviour of the World was the Saviour of Society as well as of souls. On Thursday, a resolution in favour of Sunday closing was adopted. The Rev. T. Robinson, of:Colchester, read a paper on" The decay of Sunday observance," and said the scdnes at the Pelican Club were sure signs of moral decay and lower civilision. It was decided that the Re- ference Committees hould draw up a definite resolution on the subject. The report on the Special Committee on Secondary Education among Nonconformists was adopted . The Rev. W. Spenseley, of London, carried a resolution strongly condemning gambling.

SHOCKING DEAIII OF MR. ENOCH HARVEY. Deep regret was expressed in business circles in Liverpool,on Wednesday,at the news that Mr. Enoch Harvey, the eminent solicitor, had met with a fatal accident as he was on his way to business from his home in Riversdale-road, Aigburth. It appears that Mr. Harvey, who was in his sixty-fourth year, was in the habit of travelling to town from the Mersey-road Station of the Cheshire Lines, and that when trying to catch a train about noon he was knocked down and instantly killed. It is stated that at the time that the train for Liver- pool was approaching the station, an express for the Metropplis, which left the Central Station some time before, was also coming in the opposite direction. When the train for Liverpool was pulling up to stop, Mr. .Jarvey was noticed coming along the platform, and efforts were made to attract his attention, but without result. He was just about to cross the metals when he was caught by the express train, which hurled him on one side, and when assistance arrived he was found to be dead. The painful facts of the case are increased by the circumstance that Mrs. Harvey and a daughter were in the same train, and did not hear of the shocking occurrence till after they had arrived in Liverpool. Mr. Harvey was well known in Warrington, as he was uncle to Mrs. Broadbent and the Misses Harvey, of Latchfo:d. He was, too, a director of the Whitecross Wire and Iron Co., Warrington ; and was the senior member of the firm of Messrs. Harvey, ALsop, Stevens, and Harvey, solicitors, Castle-st., having been in busi- ness about forty years. He served his articles in the office of his father, the late Mr. Thomas Harvey, and he was admitted as a solicitor in 1849, since which time he has been connected with the firm, so that he was one of the oldest and best known solicitors in Liverpool. His professional reputation stood very high, and he was among the gentlemen who were consulted as to the working of the Chancery Court in Liver- pool, when the Judicature Act was being pro- moted in Parliament with a view to the fusion of the business of law and equity proceedings. He had for years taken a deep interest in the progress of the Liverpool Law Society, of which he was president for a term. In years gone by he was a prominent advocate in local courts, especially in Admiralty cases; while as a conveyancer he was concerned in the transfer of very important property in Liverpool and the vicinity. Among the offices which he held was thatof solicitor to the Bank of Liverpool. The deceased gentleman had for many years taken an active part in political affairs, and was a prominent member of the Liberal party, engaging in all the great contests as they occurred, and notably in that in which Mr. Gladstone stood as a candidate for South- West Lancashire. He was always an acceptable council- lor in the deliberations of the old " Nine Hundred." Of late years he had been a declared Liberal Unionist. Mr. Harvey was a man of high cultivation and refined tastes. One of his favourite pursuits was the cultivation of orchids, and he enjoyed a considerable reputation as a botanical connoisseur. Mr. Harvey leaves three sons and two daughters, the youngest son being a member of the firm.

div.p: INQUEST.

The inquest on the body was held on Thursday, at the residence of the deceased gectleman, 12, Riversdale- road, Aigburth, before Mr. Samuel Brighouse, coroner for South-west Lancashire. It appeared that no one was to blame, and the jury returned a verdict of " Acci- dental death."

div.head: SUICIDE OF A GIRL AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: SUICIDE OF A GIRL AT ST. HELENS.

On Tuesday afternoon, the body of Annie Makin, 15 years of age, of 50, button-Bt., St. Helens, who had been missing since the 18th ult., was found float- ing in the old quarry pit, in Sherdley Park. On the date: named, the deceased accompanied her younger brother and sister on their way to school,and on parting Irons them, bid them " good-bye " She never returned home, and on search being made in the locality, her hat was found in the old quarry pit. The pit is between 30 and 40 feet deep, and was dragged for two or three days afterwards, but without success. On Tuesday afternoon, a man named Carney was walking along the footpath through Sherd by Delph, when he saw the body floating, and, on assistance being obtained, it was brought to the side and conveyed to the girl's late home. Her dress was found to have been turned up and pinned, and it is sup- Posed that she has committed suicide. It is stated that she had once or twice previously threatened to destroy her life. The occurrence has occasioned some excite- ment in the district.
INQUEST. -THE FATHER CHNSITHED!

Mr. Brighouse held an inquest at the Griffin Hotel, reasley Cross, on Thursday morning on the body of the deceased. James Makin, the father, a chemical labourer, of 50, Sutton-st. said the deceased acted as his housekeeper, his wife having been dead ten years. On the 18th of September he had scolded his daughter for baking cakes for some of her companions. He then ordered her to take two of her younger sisters to school, and to hurry back. She took the children to school, and he had not seen her alive afterwards. The Coroner ; Did you know that your daughter had threatened several times during the last month to commit [ suicide? Witness No, I did not. I had no idea that she had wished she were dead. Mary M'Namara, 14, said about a month ago Makin wanted her to drown herself with her in the delph, but she persuaded her away. At another time the deceased was going to drown herself in Roughdale's pottery delph, but she again got her away. It transpired that the police on several occa- sions had been attracted to the house when he was beat- ing his children, but they always found the door bolted. The jury returned a verdict of " Suicide while temporarily insane, but did not say what had produced the insanity. The Coroner called the father into the room and censured him. He told him that he was strongly of opinion that the girl had drowned herself through the father's mis- conduct. He (the coroner) was perfectly satisfied that the father had not behaved as he ought to have done. Children had delicate organisations,and could not bear to be threatened and ill-treated. It was a terrible state of affairs, and if one of his children took away her life under similar circumstances he felt that he should never for- give himself. Makin had several other children to bring up, and he hoped he would do better towards them than he had done to that one.

CURIOUS ENutilißATioN o SCDTCH SONGS.—To Sandy o'er the Les.—Dear Sandy :—After getting some Guild kail in Aberdeen, with John Roy Stewart, I accompanied him ta The house below the hill, where Graen grow the rashes, and where two er three of The merry lads of Ayr were taking their Bottle of Punch, having lately come from Doon-side ; the landlord was Johnnie M'Gill, you know he married the Soutar's daughter ; she gave as a hearty welcome, for Blithe was she but an' ben, and when She came ben she hobbit, and intro- duced us to Maggie Lander, Mary Gray, &c., &c., not forgetting the Bonny wee thing ; they were all waiting the arrival of Lucy Campbell from Within a mile o' Ediubro, for you must know Lucy is to be married to the Ranting Roaring Highlandman. So down we at to Cakes and ale, and were very happy, when up fiew the door, and in started a Soldier 'addle. I thought it had, been Johnnie Conlin', but na faith, says Peggy Bawn, that's John Anderson my jo, from Bonnie Dundee, for He would be a soldier. Moat of us knowing John, we invited him to a seat ; he took out his fiddle, and was beginning to touch The bush aboon Traquair, but was stooped by Duncan Gray, who begged he would first favour us with God save the King. Hang the King, says Charlie Stewart, who was immediately knocked down by Jack the ',tisk young drummer, who is a Bonny bold soldier. We all thought that Lewie Gordon would have interfered, who was standing in a neuk whistling Johnny Cope, when in came the Wandering sailor, singing Hearts of oak, with Black-eyed Susan in one hand, and The oak stick in the other; and poor Lewie did not like A' that an' a' that, but slunk away as pale as Hosier's ghost. Duncan Davidson was beginning to cry Kick the rogues out, when in the midst of the sculfie we had notice from Roy's wife of Aldivalloch of the arrival of the young couple from the Wanking o the fauld ; then the cry was Busk ye, busk ye ! Py let us a' to the bridal. By this you will under- atand that Johnny's made & wedding o't. We were just going when Jenny Nettles hinted that the Ale wife and her barrel must be paid, on which we bid The good wife count her law in'. So each of us had a Saxpence under our thumb, and Jennie's Bawbee made up the sum. On coming to The back of the change-house where the wedding was held, naar the Mill, mill, 0, we were met by The lads of Dunse gallanting the lasses of Stewar- ton. The best man was Rattling roaring Willie, and I assure you Willis is a wanton wag. The best maid was Katherine Ogie, who is the Bonniest lass in a' the world, except My jo, Janet. Our dinner consisted of the Roast Beet of Old England, Lumps of pudding, The haggis of Dunbar, Bannocka of barley meal, &c., &c. As for myself, There were three eggs in the pan, and after dinner we had Dribbles of Brandy; the whole cry was Fill the stoup an' had it clinking, and by no means Drink hooly an' fairly; then Come gie's a sang the lady cried, so Patio came up frae the glen, and Whistled o'er the lave o't, and sung Maggy's tocher. oif your had seen auld Rob Morris laughing at the Auld wife ayont the fire, singing 0 as I was kiss't yest'reen 1 We were now growing Sae merry as we twa ha'e been, and some of them began to Trip upon trenchers. So the dancing commenced, The bride cam' in free the byre, and led down with one of the Braw lads of Gala water, to the tune of the Campbells are coming. The glancing of her apron, Silken snood, and the Gawd in her garters, made my heart Gas pitty patty. I danced a reel with the Maid of the Mill and the Shepherd's Wife, to the tune I'll make you be fain. Andrew, wi' his catty gun, was at Kies me sweetly, with Bess the gawkie, whistling all the while Come kiss me in a corner. In short, we all danced heartily, but I observed Jennie dang the weaver, and Scoffed and scorned at him, saying 0 gin ye were sue and twenty, tam. After this we had a good night and joy; I came Todlin' hame, Not drunk nor yet sober, and expected a bonny wee house and a eanty wee fire, but I could not open the door till three, nor waken Sleepy Maggie. At last My kind dearie heard me, and She rose and let me in. By , this time I was a sleepy body, and got to bed by the light of The bonnie grey eyed morn.—Yours, WILLIE

AFTER DIARRIAQE. —One mistake into which women perhaps fall more frequently than men is that of expecting too much by Way of what, for want of a better word, I will call lovemaking. Too much love, truth, tenderness, devotion we cannot expect. Those qualities are what a noble love means—its spirit and its essence ; but the continued lover-like expression of love belongs to the unrest- ful days of wooing, or the half-a«iaaintanceship of early marriage, There comes a tune to men when the dearest and holiest things are rather lived than spoken, and the woman makes a mistake who feels herself unloved because the fervours of early utter- ance are absent from the speech of her hus- band. Men should remember that women hunger for words, and not wait, as Carlyle did, to breathe their vain remorse and despair beside a grave; and women should under- stand that a man's truth is not to be measured by his professions, and that the deepest emotion is perhaps too often silent. The only possible secrets between two married people should be those which are confided to either one of them by others. While some people, who call themselves worhlly-wise, will laugh at the idea of such perfect confidence as this implies, others still, especially the newly-mar- ried who have had small worldly experience' will be shocked that I should suggest the keeping of any kind of secret by either wife or husband from the other. I am not prepared to say that these last are not the wiser of the two. Only, in that case, when any confidence is proferred to either husband or wife, the recipient of it should make his or her Vsiiiott clearly understood, One frequent cause of trouble in ni:sried life is a want of openness in business matters. A busband marries a. pretty, careless girl, who hae been used Co taking no more thought as to how she rhould be clothed than the lilies of the field. He begins by not liking to refuse any of her requests. He will not hint, so long as he can help it, at care in trifling expenses ; he does not like to associate himself in her mind with disappointments and self-denials. And she, who would have been willing enough, in the sweet eagerness to please of her girlish love to give up any whims or fancies of her own whatever, falls into habits of careless extra- vagance, and fe9ls herself injured when at last a remonstrance comes. How much wiser would have been perfect openness in the beginning. Ideality is a good housemate.. That love lasts longer, as well as Tebel bizher, which idealises its object; yet th r ;re is one danie.i: ous direction ideality may take. If it deceives us into the belief that we are wedding perfection, then the revelation of human infirmities, which is an inevitable consequence of al/ marriage comes upon us with a shock which is sometimes perilous to contentment. The best antidote for this rude shock would be a little wholesome self-examination. The vainest of us can scarcely cherish a secret belief in our own perfection. We realise in our- selves, when we look within, the very faults of which we are most intolerant in others.—Louise C. Moulton.

How TOIL CONQCLII.EID PIZIDE. John ACkIEI6, the second President of the United States, used to relate the following anecdote: "When I was a boy I used to study Latin gram- mar ; but it was dull, and I hated it. My father was anxious to send me to college, and therefore I studied the grammar till I could stand it no longer; and going to my father I told him I did not like study, and asked for some other employ- ment. It WU opposing his wishes, and he was quick in his answer. Well, John, if Latin gram- mar does not suit you, try ditching ; perhaps that will. My meadow yonder needs a ditch, hnd you may put by Latin and try that.' This seemed a delightful change' and to the meadow I went, But soon I found ditching harder than Latin, and the first forenoon was the longest I ever experienced. That day I ate the bread of labour, and glad was I when night came on. That night I made some comparison between Latin grammar and ditching, but said not a word about it; dug next forenoon, and wanted to return to Latin at dinner ;:t but it was humiliating, and I could not do it. night toil conquered pride; and though it was one; of the severest trials I ever had in my life, I toldt my father that if he chose I would go back to Latin grammar. He was glad of it; and if I havaainoe gained any distinction, it has been owing to the. two days' labour in that ditch. -- THE kind off book which, as to size, is mcFt in favoar with tipplers is the quart-o. div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY. OCTOBER 4, 1890.

Mr. Morley Jr is a favour at any time for a con- at stituency to be addressed by Mr. St. Helens. JOHN MORLEY, but St. Helens was 'especially favoured, on Monday night, in having the opportunity of listening to the Liberal leader immediately on his return from Ireland, and from Tipperary above all other places in Ireland. There is such a lying spirit abroad as to what goes on in the sister isle, that it is an immense advantage to the cause of truth to have a plain unvarnished tale from the lips of an eye-witness whose veracity will not be impeached even by his enemies. Mr. MOR- LEY is not surpassed by any statesman in fairness of statement, freedom from party bias, and loftiness of aim ; and his speech on Monday, naked almost in its simplicity, will do much towards convincing the doubtful that Ireland will not be pacified, and ought not to be pacified, by such barbarities as have been recently inflicted at Tipperary. It was "the accident of an accident "—it was due to the inter- position of an Irish member—that Mr. MORLEY Was not himself struck down, so reckless and so indiscriminate are the Irish police in the exercise of their brutality. They have found that Mr. BAL- romt will swallow any lies they may tell him; and that they best please him by batoning those whom they ought to protect. He plays golf in Scotland Whilst they "play hell" in Ireland; but there is a time approaching when he and his party will be overwhelmed by the electors for their multituden- ous misdeeds. It was hoped that the Tories were having "a lucid interval" in the matter of coer- cion; but it is not in their nature to deal justly by Irishmen—except by accident, and we are therefore having a repetition of the crime and bloodshed which are the distinguishing features of what they call their "resolute government." Their reign as far as it has gone is a reign of tyranny and hypocrisy, following upon the oiliest professions of peace and good-will. It is enough to make the late Lord Carnarvon turn in his grave when Mitchelstown and Tipperary are cited as illustrations of his message of peace. He was, we believe, honest in his professions, and he did well In leaving an Administration which, he saw, was prepared to break its word and betray the country by substituting Coercion for Conciliation. What has been done is a crime against humanity; and another VICTOR HUGO will be needed to write its history. Mr. MORLEY has acted in his recital on the maxim that "an honest tale speeds best being plainly told," and what a tale he has to tell 1 There were a few knots of people when he and his friends arrived at Tipperary; and there was not the slightest sign of disturbance until "a' shrill cheer" was given in his honour as an ex-Irish Secretary who was beloved and not hated by the people. "Yet," he says, "this harmless cry seemed to excite the constabulary as if 5,000 men had come tearing down upon that army with shillelaghs." It was alleged that there was a multitude at the Court-house ; but, Mr. MORLEY adds—" I say there Was no multitude, and I saw the whole affair at close quarters. One report said that there were only 40 or 50 persons who accompained us. I can- not commit myself as to whether there were 40 or 60, but my own impression is strong and clear upon this that, including the squad of rod-coats and add- ing them to the constabulary, my impression is strong and clear that the armed men on that after- noon at the door of the court-house was at no time less than three to one against the civilians and un- armed men." Referring to the attack upon one of the Irish members who was present, he continues: —" Mr. HARISON says—and I believe that what , Mr. HARRISON says is perfectly true—' I was en- gaged in trying to prevent further violence, and Was endeavouring to get near a policeman whom I saw strike a man in the face. While so engaged, I saw a constable on my right raise his baton, and he struck me on the head.' The result was that Mr. HARRISON, his head all dripping with blood, was brought inside the gate, and I went with others With him into the court." "Thus bad begins but 'worse remains behind." Mr. Morley proceeds:— But now I have a worse incident, which was as close to me as this gentleman here is. Upon the -wall inside the enclosure was a certain reporter for some newspaper, Mr. Keating. I see in some of the reports that he is charged with having struck a blow st a policeman. I saw it all, and this is absolutely untrue. Mr. Keating called out something, I did not catch what it was, but I understand that he said, pointing to the constable who had batoned Mr. Harrison, "I know who you are, you ruffian." Very -well. Now mark this. This exclamation, right or Wrong, was inside the enclosure where we were all as tranquil, we were all as peaceful, as we are on this platform to-night. A constable close by Mr. Resting then and there struck him a murderous blow across the mouth, and sent him, with the blood flowing from him, sent him flat on the ground on the other side of the wall.—(" Shame.") lam pre- pared to testify to that in any court of justice that they like to select.—(Cheers.) I say deliberately that there was no more justification for that Murderous blow than there would be if some one were to conic into this room now and strike me a Murderous blow as I am speaking to you here. Well, hatoning went on outside the gate. From time to time persons dripping with blood were pushed inside the gate. At last, Colonel CADDELL—in a lucid interval, we suppose—acted on Mr: MonLEv's suggestion that the people should be let in the court-house just as would be done in an English town. "What , followed? When the gate was opened and every- body who liked went into the court, even then the Court was not absolutely filled, and when they did get into the court, this tumultuous and terrible throng, when they got into the court they were as quiet and as orderly as if they had been at church." What more need he said? Is it not obvious that tho police were the cause of all the disturbance ; that there was: in fact, no disturbance at all except

that caused by the police; that they broke the law in breaking the heads of the people ; and that they would themselves be in gaol if it were not that they are suppOrted in their illegality and brutality by the worst Irish Secretary that the country has known? Twenty years of such resolute Government for- sooth! It would be a lasting disgrace to English- men if they permitted it for a day beyond the next General Election. Englishmen are in an especial degree responsible for the inequities that are being perpetrated under the Coercion Act. Irishmen, Scotchmen, ivid Welshmen have already sent majorities to the House of Commons to protest against and to put an end to this villainous state of things ; and it is for English electors, when the time comes, to do their duty. Let St. Helens, and Warrington, and Widnes, and neighbouring consti- tuencies discredited by Tory representation see to it that they wipe out the stain when the oppor- tunity is given them. The majorities to be faced are not large; and all things are possible to men who are up and doing and ready to fight manfully in a righteous cause.

The Church IT is a significant sign of the times and that amongst the questions for dis- The Workman. cussion at the Church Congress which was opened at Hull, on Monday, the most prominent were related to Socialism and the labour movement. The clergy have begun to realise that they are losing their hold upon the masses, and they are disposed, if they can possibly manage it, to get in touch again. But it is too late to do anything of moment. The employer will not have what he calls "the meddling of the parson " ; and the labourer knows that he must depend upon him- self for working out his industrial salvation. The Church, as a Church, has hitherto been on the side of the classes as opposed to the masses; and it is only ' now that she is being left high and dry that she is beginning to perceive that, somehow or other, she is "not in it." At Monday's evening sitting, the Rev. C. W. STUBBS of Wavertree acknowledged how it had been in the past by saying—" Now, I do trust that if we are to have in our rural districts a revival of the labour agitation of 1873, we shall not see the country clergy taking up the atti- tude of fifteen years ago." And what was that attitude? It was an attitude of hostility to the efforts for bettering their condition in the world of men living in hovels, and trying to bring a family up on eight shillings a week and Christmas doles of blankets and breeches. There has been some improvement in the position of these serfs of the soil; but this has been due to the labours of such men as Mr. Jos. ARCH, and in spite of the combination of squire,parson, and farmer. It is true that here and there a clergyman risked his present position and future prospects by advoca- ting the claims of the labourer ; and it is due to the Rev. C. W. STUBBS to say that he was amongst the honourable few. It is the weakness of the clergy that they are disposed to patronise the poor rather than help them to right their wrongs ; and that, as Mr. RusiaN has pointed out, they do not bring their influence to bear upon the rich who rob the poor. They must take Emerson's advice— _ .

Go, put your creed into your deed, Nor speak with double tougue. It was stated at the Congress, on the authority of Mr. JOHN BURNS, that "there were 2,000 strikes last year, of which the men at the most, lost only thirty, and that in twenty months up to date, 117 new trades unions have been formed." Granted that strikes are not always as successful as they have proved of late, and that it is a crude way of adjusting differences, it is still, under good organization, the most powerful weapon which the labourer holds in his hands. We have , strong hopes that Boards of Conciliation and lArbitration will before many years are over be the means of averting the majority of threatened strikes; but even they can only be successful where workmen are well organised and act in unison. It is amongst the bast paid and best organised trades to-day that reference is made to arbitration, and proves acceptable to employers. The " sweaters" despise arbitration, because the " sweated " are disorganised. But it is beginning to be seen that improvement must be from the bottom, if it is to be permanent ; hence the tendency towards soli- darity on the part of all classes of workers. The half-starved agricultural labourer tramps into the town to see if he can get a job, and thus enters , into competition with those who are only a little better off than himself. If he were better paid—and there is a margin for better payment in reduced rents—he would stay at home. As Mr. STUBBS pointedly observed :—" The key to the solution of most of the social problems in our great towns in reality lies in the country. There are few of these problems whose solution is not largely dependent upon such a revision of the English land system as shall permanently raise the social and economic condition of the English rural labourers, and this elevation can only be effected as the result of trade orgahisation." But is the Church prepared to assist in this work of reform ? We doubt it;

it is contrary to her traditions, her history, her connections. She is better used to laying by a large store of loaves and fishes for herself than ad- vocating their distribution amongst the people. We shall have "words, words, words" at this, that and the other ,Church withering ; but so long as Church and State are in alliance we shall have no- thing more than words. Still, it is som3thing that such things are talked about; it is, we repeat, a significant sign of the times.

Division THE new scheme, under the of Warrington Improvement Act, Wards. for the re-arrangement of wards has been sent to the Corporation by Mr. C. N. CRESWELL, the Commission appointed to inquire and decide; and it will be found in full in our advertising columns. It has excited a great amount of interest, and it is so much different from the proposals adopted by the General Put- poses Committee, as well as from the alternative scheme suggested by the Liberal members of the Town Council, that it comes upon the public in the nature of a surprise. It is evident that Mr. Cxxss- WELL has a way of his own in these matters, and that he is not to be led either by one party or another. The weak point of the proposals of the General Purposes Committee, who were, however, very much divided, was that it was not intended to enlarge South-West Ward—the si-nallest ward in the town. It was suggested that it should re- main untouched, although under the Corporation scheme it would still be less than half the size of South-East Ward. To permit an anomaly of this kind when the object was to get rid of anomalies was, in the face of it, absurd. The counter proposal to add to South-West Ward by taking a portion from South-East Ward was obvi- ously reasonable; and there is no denying that the scheme submitted by the Liberals would have in- troduced something like equality in numbers and representation. The Commissioner has not, how- ever, crossed Bridge-st. to add to South-West Ward, but—to the astonishment of everybody—he ; , has crossed Horsemarket-St. to add to Town
t tin", • -7 - , T 11F, EXAM INFP *SA.. ur D Y , OCTOBER 4, 18.90.

Hall Ward. Then as to North-East Ward he has not merely taken a piece out of it—he has prac- tically cut it in two. South-West Ward is en- larged by adding the district between Green-st. and Buttermilk Bridge. It is still the smallest ward in the town ; and is less than half the size of the new ward of St. John's ; but there is this to be said for the apparent freak of the Commissioner that there is less roam for growth in St. John's than many of the other wards. It is not improbable that, a dozen years hence, the normal additions to population will lessen the disparity as to members which is at present so striking a feature of the new schema. We append statement as to the rateable value of each ward and the number of ratepayers with the remark that the number of electors wili be increased when the inhabitants in the parts added to the borough, under the new Act, have by effluxion of time, become qualified to be placed upon the burgess roll : Wards No, of Rate- Estimated Rateable payers Electors Value No. 1 Town Hall 1,339 1,100 25,285 „ 2 White Cross 1,006 750 16,639 „ 3 Bewsey 917 750 20,561 „ 4 Orford 801 500 6,738 5 St. John's 1,695 1,300 15,184 „ 6 Fairfield 985 700 12,813 „ 7 Howley 1,247 1,100 21,835 „ 8 St. Austin's 778 660 24,754 „ 9 Latchford 1,104 900 13,100

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
The " Glasgow Herald" says the exact cost to the " Times " of " the Parnellite business " is £lBO,OOO. This is paying rather dear for one's whistle—and such a whistle! Alas poor Pigott I

It does not always happen that because scales are at fault there is an intention to defraud. At Ruthin, on Tuesday, the Mayor and Corporation were fined £3 and costs for haying in the market for the use of traders a scale faulty and against the purchaser. And quite right too. What is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander.

Goose suggests the feathered tribe touching which Mr. Jefferson, the actor, tells a capital story in the October number of "The Century." There was a retired tragedy-queen, named Mrs. Drake, who was invited, on one afternoon, to meet a number of people who had been brought together to honour the occasion. Unfortunately, the hostess, who had a notoriously bad memory for names, intro- duced Mrs. Drake as Mrs. Duck. The tragedienne ' frowned ; and the hostess overwhelmed with confusion, exclaimed—" Oh, I beg your pardon; I mean Mrs. Goose." Capital! The story is too good not to be true.

The Contract Labour Law of the United States was designed to check the wholesale immigration of Chinese labourers ; but its operations are at times of a curious kind. Two priests engaged to teach at a Catholic College have been detained, under the Act, on their reaching the States from Europe. It will be odd if it should be found that the law applies. It will be a case of Protection with a vengeance.

"The Federal Council has received a letter from Castioni, who shot M. Rossi, the Councillor of State, during the late revolt in Switzerland. It is dated from England, and in it he declares that he committed the crime as a 'free citizen of Helvetia." M. Rossi will certainly be a very " free citizen" if he is allowed to pop off those who differ from him as to forms of Government. Perhaps when his extradition is effected, he will find that he is" free citizen" in imagination only.

• The Corporation of St. Helens have faith in Free Libraries, and have just sanctioned the expenditure of £550 on a branch library at Thatto Heath. It is understood that other branch libraries will have to be erected. The Town Council are looking ahead ; and are disposed to give facilities for think- ing as well as drinking. Warrington has got power to levy another halfpenny for library and museum purposes; and it is understood the Com- mittee are preparing to make the library really free early next year.

A young workman appeared at a London Police Court, on Tuesday, and complained that "his gal," whom he was about to marry, had "gone away with another feller." He had given her a gold chain, and he thought under the circumstances that he ought to have it back. It was explained that nothing could be done, as the chain was a gift; and the young man went away sOrrowing. But ought he not rather to rejoice that, in being jilted by "his gal," he has escaped being bound by that matrimonial chain which sometimes "lengthens as it goes and clanks behind?"

The Spiritualists do not succeed in getting hold of the people of Warrington, who take rather to things spirituous. Still they keep trying, and the latest experiment has been made in the shape of a visit from Mr. J. B. Totlow, who is appallingly des- cribed as "a trance speaker and psychometrist." It almost lifts the hair to think of what might come of listening to a man of such occult powers, and yet the audience survived it. Perhaps they did not understand the "trance speaker and ' psychometrist," and were therefore unafraid.

Trance speakers are supposed to be "controlled,' by disembodied spirits who are ready to give quite an encyclopeedia of information as to matters and things which cannot be put to the test. Some years ago we had a little experience of one. The "controlling spirit" professed to be able to seo everything and everybody in the room, using the medium's organs of speech as a means of expres- sion. By way of testing this, we challenged the "spirit" to say how many fingers we held up be- hind the medium's head. The " spirit " could des- cribe all things on earth and in heaven, but oouldn't or wouldn't count three. Our faith was small when we entered the room ; it was less when we came out.

John Reginald Birchall, the murderer in Canada of Frederick Benwell, is the son of the late rector of Church near Accrington ; but in his case the adage has been exemplified=." nearest to church and furthest from God." He is young in years, but old in villainy both to woman and man. Nothing could be more cold-blooded than the way in which he lured his victim from England until he got him in the swamp near Princeton, where he shot him, and then robbed him. He has been found guilty, and if ever capital punishment was justified it will be justified in his execution.

The postmen who agitated with a view to im- proving their low wages were dealt with as though the Department "could not stand it," and as if they were trying to rob the public. It transpires from the year's balance sheet which has just been issued that the increase of profit this year is £146,000; and that the total profit is £3,340,000. But what do we want making an enormous profit out of public business ? Let us pay our way by all means; but a big profit at the expense of poorly- paid servants of the public—that is a species of sweating against which everybody should pro- test.

Mr. John Morley's speech at St. Helens has caused the Unionists to wriggle like ,eels that have been pinned to the ground. The "Birmingham Daily Post" admits the facts, which is something gained, and then tries to console itself by saying: —" After all, the 'Unionist cause is not ruined by the 'admission that upon a small occasion, under circumstances of great irritation; a few Irish police- men, acting without orders, lost their temper for two or three minutes and behaved with lamen- table violence and indiscretion." The " cause" is not perhaps " ruined " ; but it is on its last legs, and it totters to its fall.

Sir John Gorst is an astute sort of man, and it was deemed an astute sort of thing to put up Mr. Lewington, Secretary of the Dock-yard Labourers Protection League, to propose a vote of thanks after an address to constituents at Chatham. The Secretary moved, and then moved on to tell the audience that Sir John as a member of the Govern- ment had been party, for a long time, to paying labourers on public works a minimum of 15s. per week. He thought such a Government was not worthy of support. This made Sir John unhappy, and ho pleaded that his relations with the Govern- ment were confidential, and consequently he had more influence in what he did privately than if he advocated their claims publicly. In other words— "Open your mouths and shut your eyes, and see what I will send you." But working-men are getting tired of being treated like children.

The Rev. E. Lloyd Jones delighted his audience on Thursday evening, by his powerful lecture on "Pilgrim's Progress.' The discourse is original, picturesque, and humorous, and keeps the atten- tion of the listener from beginning to end. It is the same too, with Mr. Jones's sermons; he does not allow his hearers to go to sleep. He was leav- ing a northern town on one occasion, when a stranger came up to him and said he was glad he was going, for he had "lost him a lot o' brass." Asked to explain, the man said he was a shop- keeper. Ho had two little shops; he was nearly run off his feet • and it was his custom to book all his weeks' "orders," and enter note of all he had "trusted" in a memorandum book which he used at chapel during the sermon ! " But," he said, " aw connot do it neaw ; yo make me listen to your sermons, and aw connot get on wi' my booking, and eh I mon, I've lost a lot o' money." The hardened sinner couldn't attend to his silver for thinking of his soul. ; •

The choir rendered special music. In the afternoon the children rendered in a very creditable manner, the service of song "The Christian's Progress." Collections were made in aid of the fund. BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, RUNCORN, The 55th anniversary of this place of worship was celebrated on Sunday, when the Rev. H. Harries, of Stockport, chairman elect of the Cheshire Congregational Union, occupied the pulpit, and preached eloquent ser- mons to large etongregations. The choir sang specially selected music in good style, and Mr. J. Clough presided at the organ, a position which that gentleman ably ful- filled at the ordination service, on the previous Thursday. Collections were made in aid of the Chapel Funds. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. &W. DUTTON'S Sankey-et., Warrington.—Advt. HARVEST THANKSGIVING AT RUNCORN PARISH CHITRCH. A thanksgiving service for the ingathering of the harvest was held at the Parish Church on Thursday night, when the sacred edifice was crowded. The in- terior of the building had been beautifully deccrrated by the ladies of the congregation. The first lesson was read by the Rev. G. St. Patrick Garrett, vicar of Widnes; the second lesson by the Rev. J. Ff. Wilcockson incumb- ent of Weston Point and the prayers were read by the Rev. Canon Wood, vicar. The Bishop of Chester preached a sermon, in which he dealt mainly with the forthcoming mission services.

BURGLARY AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court, on Saturday, Ernest Bee and Alexander Ruddiman, of Mersey-road, were charged with breaking and entering the shop of William Melvin, furniture dealer, Mersey-road, and stealing goods of the value of Bs.—The prosecutor wished to withdraw the charge, but Superintendent Noblett objected, and the Bench decided that the case must proceed. The shop was securely locked up on Thursday and next morning it was found that a window at the rear of the premises had been broken and a number of articles stolen. It was proved that the prisoners sent a boy to pawn the articles, and received 2s. upon them. They were committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. CHURCH ARMY RUNCORN. On Sunclay,harvest thanksgiving services were held in connection with this mission. The room presented a beautiful appearance. At the east end were three panels fringed with oats. In the centre panel was the text in red letters on a white ground, "The Harvest truly is plenteous"; over this reclining on a shield, was a large bunch of grapes; in side panels were crosses wrought in flowers. In the front of these were tables tastefully decorated,upon which were many kinds of fruit, flowers, vegetables, Sm. On the walls were crosses wrought in wheat, and in the middle of each was displayed some choice flower. The preacher in the afternoon was the Rev. G. A. Kingston, 8.A., and in the evening Mr. D. Worthington. The services were continued on Monday evening, when Captain W. Duerden preached. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.-7. &W. DUTTON'S Sankey- st., Warrington.—Advt. FOOTBALL MATCH.—WIDNES V. RUNCORN .—These teams met at Widnes, on„Thursday, before 3,000 spectators and an exciting game ended in a victory for Runcorn by two goals and two minors to Widnes one minor. Davies and Riley scored the tries. On the Widnes side Plumpton bad to retire through an injury to his back, and Davies for Runcorn left the field with a sprained ankle. Both teams were fully represented. WIDNES TRADESMEN'S CRICEF.T CLUB. The annual meeting of members was held at the Rail- way and Commercial Hotel, on Tuesday evening, Mr. T. Smith presiding. The report of the Secretary (Mr. H. G. Powell) showed that the club had played 16 matches, won 9. lost 3 and drawn 4. Mr. F. Mitchell and Mr. T. Laws headed the l•atting list, and Mr. B. Brookes and Mr. A. Fletcher divided the bowling honours. Mr. T. Smith was elected president, Mr. T. Laws, captain, Mr. H. G. Powell, secretary, and Mr. J. Mitchell treasurer.

RUNCORN TONIC SOL-FA CONCERTS. The first concert of the season in connection with the Runcorn Tonic Sol-fa Society will be held in Runcorn Public Hall, on Monday evening next. The vocalists are Miss Ada Lee, and Mr. J. W. Maltby of the Manchester concerts; Miss Nunn, L.R.A.M., solo pianoforte and Miss Gordon Nunn, solo violin, and the choir will render several part songs and madrigals. A most attractive programme hag been arranged, and the efforts of Mr. Halton', the conductor, in the advancement of musical culture, deserve recognition at the hands of the Runcorn public.

ROBBERIES AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, Job Heath, Major Cross-street, and Joseph Mularkey, Chapel-entry, youths, were charged on remand with having stolen 45., belonging to James W. Towers, chemical apparatus dealer, Widnes. The evidence disclosed that on the afternoon of Saturday last, the shop was locked up, and that at that time there were several shillings in the till. Or Monday morning it was found that the contents of the till had gone. Prisoners were apprehended by Con- stable Thompson, and incriminated each other, it ap- pearing that they had divided the money between them. They now pleaded guilty, and, in consideration of their youth, the magistrates only directed that they should be bound over to come up for judgment if called upon.— Mary Ann Robinson, New-st., Widnes, was charged with having stolen two gold rings and a quantity of wearing apparel, value £3 fis., the property of Thomas Edward- son, of Farnworth. Prisoner was employed by the pro- secutor as a charwoman, and it was alleged that she stole the articles when acting in that capacity. She pleaded guilty, aad was sent to jail for a fortnight. SCARLET FRVInt EPIDEMIC AT EARLESTOWN. The medical men of Earlestown and Newton at present have their hands pretty full of cases of juvenile sickness, from scarlet fever. A great many children are kept indoors, but fortunately the dis- ease is of a light character, and is not such as to utterly prostrate the sufferers. The number of cases steadily increases, but no steps have been taken to- wards the closing of the schools. UMBRELLAS BE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. St W. DUTTON'S Sankey-it., Warrington.—Advt. PRESTON BROOK PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL. Harvest thanksgiving services were held in this place of worship on Sunday and Monday. The sermons were preached to crowded congregations on Sunday, by the Rev. H. Davenport, Circuit minister. The chapel was also well filled on Monday evening, Mr. Frodsham presiding. The choir contributed some anthems, and there were recitations by scholars of the Sunday school. After an address by Mr. I Gyton, of Warrington, and votes of thanks to the Chairman, choir, ttc., the meeting closed with the singing of the Doxology. COLLIERY ACCIDENT AT COLLINS GREEN. On Monday, a collier named William. Walker, em- ployed at the Yard Coal Colliery of the Collins Green Colliery Co., and living in Regent-st., Earlestown, received injuries which necessitated his removal to the Providence Hospital, St. Helens. He was engaged filling his box With coal, when he heard the bank from which he had been hewing slip. He stepped on one side to avoid it, when he stumbled ever a piece of coal and fell, anil the working giv- ing way, it fell on one of his legs, breaking it in two places. lie was at once extricated and conveyed up the shaft, and then to the hospital.

CRIMF.S AGAINST CHILDREN. Every humane person will read with interest the growth of the practice of Courts in the matter of the drunkenness of parents in relation to their crimes against children. When we first began our work it was no uncommon thing for the fact of a parentis being drunk when a crime was committed against his child, to be allowed as some sort of excuse for, even a defence to, the charge. There was no law on the subject, and this was the "un- written "practice. In the police courts of the Metropolis that has almost gone. Next the "drunk" fact began to count for nothing. Now it as come to be an evidence in support ot a charge of neglect, and an evidence of means, without the necessity of adducing evidence of wages.—Child's Guardian. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at, the shortest nottee.—J . A W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st.. Warrington.—.Advt. ' EXCITING BOATING ACCIDENT AT WIDNES. Shortly after noon on Tuesday, a number of men, who were standing on the shore at Widnes, ob- served a buoy floating up the Mersey on the in- coming tide. As there is a reward of ss. for the re- covery of these drifting buoys, the men obtained a boat, and quickly reached the object of their search. Instead of allowing one of their number to make the capture, the whole of the occupants attempted to seize the buoy, with the natural result that the boat was capsized, and the men thrown into the water. Fortunately, the accident was witnessed from the shore, and a boat was sent to the assis- tance of the men, who were all rescued. One of them, however, was in a very exhausted state, and he was conveyed to the Accident Hospital, where he was quickly restored, but he was an inmate of the institution for a couple of days. THE LINE BETWEEN LOWTON AND GOLBORNE. There seems to be a brighter prospect for the Liverpool, St. Helens, and South Lancashire Rail- way Company, which started so auspiciously and yet came to a sudden standstill after constructing two miles ot line between Lowton and Golborne. It is, however, understood that Sir Edward Watkin has promised that the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway will raise an extra £20,000, if the railway company can • raise locally another £20,000. It is stated that this £20,000 has practi- cally been raised, and although the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Company, will have o obtain Parliamentary sanction to increase their subscribed capital, the directors promise to proceed at once with the raising of their subscrip- tion, so that the work may be gone on with immediately. EWBANIC CARPET SWEEPERS,—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge-St., Warrington.—Advt. MARRIAGE AT LYMM.

The marriage of Miss Ada Warburton, eldest daughter of Mr. John Warburton, grocer, Lymm, to Mr. William Horton, of Wilderspool-road, Warring- ton, was solemnised at the Lymm Parish Church, on Tuesday morning, theßector (the Rev. G. W. Guest) officiating. The bridesmaids were Miss Annie Warburton (sister of the bride), and Miss Annie A. Winton (cousin of the bride). Mr. Thomas Hor- ton, brother of the bridegroom, acting as best man. The bride who carried albeautiful bouquet, was at- tired in a fawn coloured dress of cashmere and silk, the bridesmaids wearing dresses of muslin delaine, 'with hats to match. As the party left the church, Mr. J. E. Blakemore, who presided at the organ, played Mendelssohn's " Wedding March." Later in the day the newly-married couple left Lymm en route for Windermere, where the honeymoon will be spent. A large number of presents were re- ceived. Lamps, choice designs.—Garland's Lamp Shops, Earlestown and Warringtpn.—Advt. THE HOME IRON TRADE. There is no doubt that the crude iron market is still seriously disturbed by the dispute between the Scotch ironmasters and their men; but the general market is steady and there is a considerable business doing in finished iron and steel. The Glasgow warrant market has been greatly excited, but its tendency, on the whole, has been upwards, Scotch makers' iron is higher in price, but irregular. Middlesbrough pig has been somewhat similarly affected, but there is nh increase in price compared with last week. The other pig-iron markets are also unsettled, hematite pig being the least dis- turbed. The demand for finished iron is well main- tained, and prices are strong. The enquiry for steel rails and shipbuilding material being better, there has been a further stiffening up of values. Manu- facturers both of iron and steel, however, are rather backward in taking orders. Shipbuilders have secured more work. Engineers continue well em- ployed.—lron. CRITCHLEY'S Tailoring meets the times.—Advt.

EARL/MOWN BATOR? FOOTBALL CLUB.' A general meeting of the members of this newly- formed organisation was held at the Prince of Wales Hotel, the headquarters of the club, on Satu- day night. Mr. H. F. Gooch, an old Rugby enthus- iast, presided, and he was supported by lir. Sam Williams, there being also a large attendance of members and intending members. Mr. C. H. Lea, secretary, read the minutes of the last meeting, which were duly confirmed. The Chairman said the club appeared to be in a fair way to succeed, and the members could count upon all the assistance he could give them. If they all -worked together, and preserved a united front, he had no doubt They would form a strong organisation, and enjoy a suc- cessful season. Already they had 115 subscribing members. which he considered most satisfactory. Mr. H. F. Goach was then chosen president of the Club, and Mn S. Williams, vice-president. A pro- position was brought forward to alter the. colours of the club, and it was definitely settled that the colours be red jerseys and white knickers. Several good fixturqp have already been arranged. Blowy.* V. TAYLOIL. Mr. Justice Vaughan Williams, sitting as vacation judge in the Chancery Division of the High Court of Justice, on Wednesday, had before him a motion to restrain the defendant, his servants, and agents till the trial of the action, or further order, from selling as Beecham's Pills or Beecham's Patent Pills, pills not manufactured by the plaintiff. Mr. Marten, Q.C., and Mr. Martelli appeared in support of the motion. Mr. Justice Vaughan Williams said he had received a letter from the defendant in which he emphatically denied that he had ever sold as Bee- cham's Pills any substitute for them, but stated that he had been in the habit of opening the plain- tiff's two-and,zunepenny packets for the purpose of retailing the pills in small quantities. The writer expressed a hope therefore that the judge would in- sist upon clear proof of the charge made against him.—Mr. Marten stated that he had the affidavits of nine purchasers, who had been to the defendant's place of business in Colne-road, Burnley, and on ask- ing for Beecham's Pills had been supplied with pills which were not Beecham's. The defendant did not appear, and Mr. justice Vaughan Williams made the order on affidavit of service.
