FOOLISH CONDUCT OF A CARTER: A SINGULAR

ESCAPE. On Saturday, a man in chaige of a spring cart belonging to Messrs. Boddington, brewers, of Man- chester. had, together with the horse he was driv- ing, a most wonderful escape from death or very serious injury. The man, who was said to be under the influence of &ink, was driving the horse up "Emmett's-brow," having attached to it a spring cart laden with barrels of beer, upon one of which he was sitting. When near the top, he began tug- ging at the reins from some cause or other, and the horse severed round, and commenced backing to- wards the precipice-like bank at the bottom of which is the "dingle." The man, unaware of his danger, still pulled at the reins, and the horse, answering to the call, backed the cart over the hank, when the strain of the heavy cart on the brink of the incline, proving too much for the horse, it was pulled headlong down to the bottom, where it lay a confused mass of horses legs, beer barrels, &c. Several people who saw the affair at once rushed into the valley, and found the man nearly buried by the barrels and the horse on its back struggling for freedom. Strange to say, both had escaped with slight injury and the only damage that appeared to have been done, was to the cart which had a shaft broken. The horse was released, and the cart put into its proper position. The animal being again yoked, the load was pulled on to the main road again, and the man who had been sobered by the fall, drove off, not much worse for his adventure.

AN EXPOSITION OF CONGREGATIONAL PRINCIPLES. In the ordination service of the Rev. John Simp- son at Bethesda Congregational Church, Runcorn, last week, an important feature was an address- by the Rev. S. B. Handley, of Stafford, who had for his subject an, "Exposition of Congregational prin- ciples." In the course of the address, Mr. Handley said : In the formation of our churches we aim to give effect to and to realise the definition contained in the 19th article of" the Book of Common Prayer," viz.: "The visible Church of Christ is a congregation of faithful men in which the pure word of God is preached and the Sacraments duly administered, according to Christ's ordinance in all those things that of necessity are requisite to the same." By "faithful men" we under- stand those who are genuine Christians' pardoned through faith in their Saviour, Jesus Christ, born again of the Holy Spirit, giving all diligence to make their calling and election sure, rejoicing in life to the glory of God. Thus interpreted this definition very fairly sets forth, as we believe, the most frequent meaning of the word church in the New Testament. There is another use of the word which has lately come Into fashion among us. Our forefathers used to call our places of worship meeting houses. For some time past we have been accustomed to call them chapels; now, however, our people copying the example of our Episcopalian and Presbyterian friends, are getting into the way of calling them churches. And for this last name I must confess my own decided preference. The name meeting house is an awkward and cumbrous one; besides which it surely has a sound too commoti and familiar to be a happy designation of the house of God. The word chapel has also, I think, associations which disqualify it for appropriate use at any rate by us. Its origin is involved in some obscurity. The most probable account of the matter is as follows :—lt was applied first to the arched sepulchres constructed in the walls of the Catacomb of Rome which contained the boxes of the confessors and martyrs of the faith, then to any receptacle of such sacred relics, then to those structures round about the choir and cathedral chancel, all of which were built to receive the relics with befitting honour; then, because worshippers often went to pray there, any subordinate place of worship attached to a larger and more central building; hence the origin and meaning of the phrase," Chapel of ease." Now, I expect that in their modesty our great grandfathers scarcely presuming to regard their plain and simple sanctuaries as on the same level as the parish churches were thus led to call them chapels. But the time had surely come for discontinuing the use of a word which is in effect a badge and confession of inferiority. The per- suasion of this, together with the fact that chapel has such a shady and sunerstitious history, strongly inclines me, for one, to prefer the word church. And then, too, church has something to say on its own account. What more natural than that the place where the church—the congregation of faithful men—meets to meditate and pray should itself be called a church. In primitive times the term synagogue was applied to the building and to the assembly which gathered there ; and in still earlier days the term temple was similarly used. For these reasons I give my vote for church rather than chapel. Coming back from this material application of the word church to its strictly proper and spiritual meaning. I proceed to remark that with respect to individual churches or congregations of faithful men, we believe that each is complete in and of itself ; that Jesus Christ the. Lord, is the head of each, as He is of all ; that, in the case of each, the Holy Scriptures are the sole statute book and rule of life; that the members of each are at once free and bound to interpret those Scriptures ac- cording to theie private judgment, in dependence, of course, upon the illumination of the spirit of God; that in the choice of officers, in the admission and dismission of members, and the general administration of its affairs, each church is sufficient for itself, and independent of the authority of Pope,prelate,presbytery,Prince or Parliament. Taking the New Testament into our hands we hold that the Kingdom of Christ amongst men is purely spiritual in its character. Hence for any secular gevernment to take that Kingdom under its patronage, and to usurp the administration of its affairs, is to step altogether beyond its province. Whilst for any government to select any particular religious creed and any particular form of ecclesiastical polity, and to declare these to be the law of the land, and to inflict upon those who con- scientiously object to their civil disabilities, seems to us a gross injustice. Moreover, we are convinced that the Union of the Church and State has been fruitful of no little harm to the cause of spiritual truth. We are not schismatics in relation to the Established Church, for we have come out it, and by God's grace we have been able to stand alone. If there is any schism at all it is in the Established Church itself in its many parties and divisions. Of these, the three principal ones, the high Churchmen or Ritualists, the broad Churchmen, and the low Churchmen or Evangelicals—or as they have been somewhat disrespectfully called—and not by a Dissenter either—the attitudinarians, the latitudinarians, and the platitudinarians—are, as is notorious, so mutually discor- dant not to say repellant that they commonly refuse to have any dealings with one another, except indeed at a Church Congress, or when they band them- selves together against what they call the common enemy and who that is. Having referred to other matters in which they differed from the Church of England, Mr. Handley added All these things and others that might be mentioned we conscientiously think te be wrong. We regard them all as unscriptural, some we look noon as mischievous if not positively perilous to the soul, and as the fuel of superstition and heresy. These things would of themselves suffice to keep most of us aloof from the Episcopalian Church in this land, even though the mandate had gone forth—that like its sister , across the channel, it should cease to be an establish- ment. We are denominated Independents. Of this name I for one am proud. It has descended to us from our honourable ancestry. It is imperishably associated

with the stand which more than 200 fears ago, was so heroically made against the attempt to fasten upon the nation the yoke of despotism. civil and religious alike. Lastly, we are called Congregationalists. This name Implied the democratic character of our Church Govern- ment. The denomination Independent expresses the fact that each church manages its own affairs. The denomination Congregationalist, sets forth the right and duty of every church member—every member of the " congregation of faithful men"—to take part in this management.

div.head: WIDNES REVISION COURT.
div.p: WIDNES REVISION COURT.

On Wednesday evening, Mr. J. T. Foard, revising barrister, held a court at Widnes Town Ball, for the revision of the list of voters in Widnes and Crouton polling districts. Mr. IL B. Shores, appeared for the Liberal party and Mr. W. B. Woodworth acted on behalf of the Conservatives.

div.head: MAJOR WAREING GETS HIS VOTE.
div.p: MAJOR WAREING GETS HIS VOTE.

Major Wareing,of Bedford Bouse,Mill Brow,Appleton, claimed to be placed on the ownership list in respect of leasehold land and building—the Widnes Grease and Oil Works, Ellison-st., Widnes. In reply to Mr. Shores he said he had owned the works for 27 years and they were worth over LS a year.—Mr. Woodworth : All right, sir. —The vote was allowed.
AN INDIGNANT _IR/SHMAN.

Patrick Scanlan, of 44, Midwood-street, a chemical labourer, appeared to claim his vote. He said be had been in the house two years and he came on the same occasion last year, and as he had to work night and day he could not lose his time.—The Barrister : How is it he was left off.—Mr. Goff (assistant overseer) : The house was returned empty.—Scanlan: It was never empty sitSce I was in it, and I never had the bailiffs. (Laughter.)—The Barrister:. I don't know. It was left off but you have claimed and got your vote.—Scanlan : What about the time I have lost 2—The Barrister: I don't know anything about it.—Mr. Goff: Who is the landlori 2—Scanlan: Mr. Lancaster.—Mr. Goff: Then ask bins why he did not send your name.—Scanlan: I gave it here myself last year.—Mr. Shores: It is a frivolous objection Scanlan, and if you had come to-mor- row youwould havegot your expenses.—Mr. Woodworth: He is not objected to.—Mr. Shores: I beg your pardon —all right—Scanlan (turning to Mr. Goff) : Who told you the house was empty. (Laughter.) There is as much in it as there is in yours, if I am not here in good clothes. (Renewed laughter.)

THE TESTAMENT CALLED FOR. Denton Sherlock, 59,Lonsdale-road, claimed a vote as occupier of these premises and was objected to by the Conservatives.—Mr. Woodworth : We must have the testament here.—Mr. Shores: You don't object.—Claim- ant : No.—Mr. Shores: It is a true statement.—Claim- ant : Yes.—Mr. Woodworth: Have you a rent book.— Claimant : I have, but it is not here.—Mr. Woodworth: Who is Mrs. Urquahart ?—Claimant : My mother-in- law.—Mr. Woodwerth : And she pays the rent.—Claim- ant : I pay the rent and have done for five years—Mr. Woodworth: Why don't you have your name on the rent book.—Claimant: It is on the book.—Mr. Woodworth: Why didn't you bring it with you.—Claimant: Because I thought my word was good enough.—The Barrister: Does John Urquahart live in this house?—Claimant: Yes, he is there at present.—Mr. Shores : Are you the tenant of the house.—Claimant : lam the tenant and have a five years' lease.—Mr. Shores (to Mr. Woodworth) : Will you have him sworn P—Mr. Woodworth: No, but it is very funny that Mrs. Urquahart says her husband is the tenant.—Claimant : How can he be when .I have a five years' lease from Mr. Holland ?—Mr. Shores: It is clear that Urquahart comes off the list and this man goes on.—The Barrister agreed—Claimant: There has been a lot of bother about this vote one time or another.—Mr. Shores : Tell the rent collector to give your name to Mr. Goff so as to save this bother in future. The Court was resumed on Wednesday morning. A FRIVOLOUS OBJECTION.

James Murray, 29, Moss Bank-road, was objected to by the Conservatives, on the ground that ho had not lived in the house twelve months. Mrs. Murray, the wife, said they had lived there eleven years, and asked for expenses. The Barrister instructed Mr. Woodworth to give her half a crown.
SUBSTITUTION.

John Walker, 11, Luton-st.,claimed a vote as occupier. —Mr. Goff said Mary Basnett was down on the list for this house.—Mrs. Walker said Mary Basnett had been dead eight years, but the property agent had neglected to alter the name.—The Barrister, in striking off the name of Mary Basnett, and substituting John Walker's, I said the property agent ought to take more care.
SPOILING THEE ENEMY.

Mr. W. W. Gossage, 13, Hargreaves-road, Sefton Park, Liverpool, reclaimed in respect of his Widnes property. and was objected te by the Conservatives.—Mr. Shores said Mr. Gossage had made a reclaim in consequence of changing his address from Camp Hill, Woolton, to 13, Hargreaves-road.—Mr. Woodworth: I objected to the reclaim.—The Barrister pointed out that Mr. Gossage had altered the register by reclaiming.—Mr. Woodworth: There is no objection to the reclaim; my clerk has made a mistake.—Mr. Gossage : Costs, if you please, sir.— The Barrister: What do you do ?—Mr. Gossage: My business is in Liverpool now, and I have had to come here specially to prove this.—Mr. Woodworth : You ought to have sent your clerk.—The Barrister : I sup- pose you are a contractor between here and Liverpool: —Mr. Gossage: No, sir. I only come once a week.— The Barrister (to Mr. Woodworth) : You will have to pay a guinea in this case. • The business of the Court was resumed on Thursday morning.

div.head: STARR BOWKETT CASE.
div.p: A STARR BOWKETT CASE.

John Midwood, Elizabeth-st., Ditton, claimed a vote for leasehold property in Widnes. In answer to Mr. Shores, applicant said the property was worth more than £5 a year.—Mr. Woodworth pointed out that the appli- cant was a member of the Starr Bowkett Building Society, and the property was obtained by the claimant by ballot. It was for the barrister to decide what the property was worth at the present time.—The Revising , Barrister, after examining the books of the claimant, said there appeared to be a magin of above £5, and he there- for allowed the vote.

div.head: FRIVOLOUS OBJECTION.
div.p: A FRIVOLOUS OBJECTION.

John James Murray appeared to answer an objection by Mr. Sl.,,res. The objection was that the name was wrongly stated on the list.—The Barrister said it was a frivolous objection. He overruled the objection, and allowed Murray 3s. 6d. as expenses.

- A SUSPICIOUS RENT ROOK. John Keogh, 2, Hope-st., claimed a vote for occup- ancy of that house.—The Conservatives objected on the ground that the applicant's sm-in-law was really the tenant of the house, and had been in receipt of parish. relief.—The name was struck off, the Barrister remark- ing that the rent book which applicant produced looked as if it had been filled in.

div.head: FIRE ENGINE STATION FOR WIDNES.
div.p: FIRE ENGINE STATION FOR WIDNES.

On Tuesday morning, Colonel W. 31. Ducat, R.E., Local Government Board Inspector, held an inquiry at Widnes Town Hall, into the application of the Widnes Local Board for permission to borrow .£3,000, for the purpose of building a new fire station and cottages on some land belonging to the Board in. Lacey-st. There were present Messrs. W. J. Hargreaves, and J. Taylor, J. T. Allen (clerk). Sinclair (surveyor), and Carr (engineer, and superintendent of fire brigade). '—Mr. Allen said the population of Widnes, in 1881, was 24,000, and at a census made by the Board in 1888, it was 29,723. The population was now estimated at 31,000. The rateable value in 1881 was £101,943 and at the be- ginning of the present year it was £132,885. During the last few months it had been increased by about £8,500. The Board were £65,324 in debt on the General District Rate, but the total amount of the debt was £72,324, of which £7,000 was for street improvements, and was being rapidly paid off. It was the Board's in- tention to erect a new fire station and 14 cottages—eight for the use of firemen and the remaining six for other workmen under the Board.—Mr. I. Carr said at present the brigade were scattered over the town, and when a fire broke out only one or two men could be got to go ia charge of the engine, which fie thought was a very un- satisfactory state of things. In the past five years the brigade had attended 24 fires. The damage done was £44,886 and the amount at risk was £228,429.—Mr. Allen said the Board asked that the repayment of the loan should be extended over a period of 50 years.—The In- spector: I think 30 years would be sufficient.—The in- quiry then concluded and the Inspector afterwards visited the site of the proposed buildings and intimated that his report would be placed before the London Board in due course.

div.head: CHURCH CONGRESS.
div.p: THE CHURCH CONGRESS.

The discu;sions at the Church Congress, on Wednesday morning, were mainly on religious subjects, but at night one section discussed Socialism, the claims of Socialists to be answered being pretty generally admitted. While one section of the Congress at Hull, spent Thurs- day forenoon in discussing the nature of the inspiration of the Holy Scripture, the other and larger one was oc- cupied with the topio of Anglican Brotherhoods and the recent proposals tor their formation. The speakers in favour were led by Archdeacon Farrar, and those against were headed by the Bishop of Liverpool. There was great variety of opinion, some blessed and some banned the project energetically. The Congress spent the forenoon mostly in a common devotional meeting. The afternoon was occupied in considering the ethics of commerce, with disquisitions on the Christian conception of trading, and on speculation in relation to Christian morality. The difficulties and needs of country parishes were also considered.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

PERSISTENT FRAUDS ON THE RAILWAY COMPANY. On Wednesday morning, at the Warrington Police Court, Alexander Malcolmson was charged in custody, with having defrauded the London and North-Western Railway Company, by travelling from Liverpool to War- rington without having paid his fare. It was stated that this was the tenth appearance of Malcolmson for offences of this kind, and that he had only been out of prison a week, he having been serving imprisonment for a similar offence at Newton. Ha was now fined 40s. and costs, and in default of payment was seat to prison for a month.

div.head: VIOLENT ASSAULT ON POLICEMEN AT RIXTON.,
div.p: VIOLENT ASSAULT ON POLICEMEN AT RIXTON.,

At the \Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednes- day, Thomas Blears, a labouring man, was charged with drunkenness and disorderly conduct at Rixton, on the 27th ult., and with having, at the same time, as- saulted Constables Schofield and M'Collough. Prisoner, who was in a fighting humour, refused to go home at the request of the officers, and threw Scholfield to the ground by catching hold of his legs. He also struck M'Collough several times, and made attempts to bite him. Ulti- mately he was put under arrest, and it now transpired that he had been convicted four tim.s for assault. The magistrates fined him 10s. and costs for the drunkenness. and sent him to jail for three months with hard labour for assaulting the officers.

div.head: ASSAULT BY. A STEPFATHER:.
div.p: ASSAULT BY. A STEPFATHER:.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Wednesday, a scissors-grinder, named Emmanuel Smith, was brought up in custody, charged with having assaulted Margaret Connolley on the 25th September, and other dates. Mr. Hunt, the Chief Constable, said that complainant, who was nine years of age, was the prisoner's stepdaughter. On the 25th ult. he beat her with an umbrella stick until she was covered with bruises. On Monday morning, he again brutally illtreated her, and kicked her on the head, causing a wound. On the evening of the same day prisoner went home drunk, and the child told a policeman that she was afraid to go home. This led to inquiries being made, and to the arrest of the prisoner. A witness who afterwards examined the child said that her body was one mass of discolouration. Prisoner was sent to prison for a month, with hard labour.

div.head: MORE ASSAULTS ON THE POLICE.
div.p: MORE ASSAULTS ON THE POLICE.

On Monday, at the Warrington Police Court, severai charges of assaulting the police were investigated. John Stirrup, for being drunk and disorderly and assaulting P.C.'s Corbett and Hardy at Market-gate, on Saturday evening, was committed to gaol for a month without the option of a fine—James Miskell was charged with being drunk and disordisorderly on Saturday evening, in Buttermarket-st. ; with assaulting Police-constables Critchley, Harrington, and Fish; and with assaulting Catherine Taylor. The evidence was to the effect that the prisoner was pursuing the woman Taylor down Buttermarket-St., when she ran into a shop. The prisoner followedher, knocked her to the floor, and kicked her several times on the head. The police Officers had great difficulty in taking him to the police station. He kicked them all, and was very violent. As this Was the prisoner's 51st appearance, he was committed to prison tor four months' hard labour. The prisoner: " I shall be out again at Christmas, and I'll see you again." A PASTEBOARD HALF-SOVEREION PASSED IN A PUBLIC ROUSE.
and

On Monday, at the Warrington Police Court, a young man named James Higgins, was charged with stealing by means of a trick, from George Crawford, of the "Old House at Home," Friars'-green, the sum of 9s. 811, glass of stout, and a glass of beer, The Chief-Constable said the prosecutor served the defendant and a woman with some drink about half-past ten, on Saturday night, -and soon afterwards they called for more, tor which de- fendant tendered what appeared to be half a sovereign. The landlord having given change, put the coin in his mouth, and defendant, having consumed the liquor, rushed out, followed by the woman, who left her shawl. Mr. Crawford felt the supposed coin go rather soft, And

on examining it, found i was cardtioard covered with gilt. The woman returned for her shawl on Sunday, and the defendant's whereabouts were then ascertained. He was appreheuded by Police-constable Monaghan.—Defend- ant, who denied the offence, was sent to jail for one mouth, with hard labour. A FACTION FIGHT IN ANGEL YARD.

At the Warrington Borough Court, on Friday, the following persons were charged with having committed a breach of the peace in Angel-yard, Warrington, on Sunday, viz. :—Martin Burke, Charlotte Burke, Lawr- ence Mannion, Richard Chadwick, Edward Sauce, John McDonough, sen., John McDonough. jun., Thomas Douce, and Ellen McLoughlin. The evidence went to show that there had been quite a "free fight "between the parties named, they having ranged themselves into two conflict- ing parties. Some of the defendants had received cuts und blood had flown freely, and in addition to this damage had been done to some windows and doors. Charlotte Burke, Lawrence Mannion, and J. McDonough jun., were bound over to keep the peace, and the others were dismissed. A claim for damages done to property was dismissed.
TRESPASSING ON RAILWAYS.

At thelWarrington Borough Court, yesterday morning, two lads, named Patrick Moran and John Burton, were charged with having trespassed on the London and North-Western Railway Mr. Preston of Liverpool, who prosecuted on behalf of the Railway Company, said that there had been complaints about boys trespass, ing on the line and a detective was told off to watch in the neighbourhood of Pierpoint-st. On two occasions he saw the lads put something on the metals in front of trains and also throw stones at trains. Mr. Preston said he was informed by the Chief Constable, that a large stone had on the previous night been thrown by some boys at a train, from the Park. Moran's mother said she was willing that her son should be birched, and the magistrates directed that he should be kept in goal till six o'clock at night and receive twelve strokes with a birch rod. Burton's mother said she would rather pay the full penalty of 40s. and costs than that herson should be birched, and the magistrates imposed the full penalty. Later on Mrs. Burton changed her mind and consented to the birching, and the fine was therefore remitted.

div.head: MINOR CASES. WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
div.p: MINOR CASES. WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
MONDAY.—Before the Mayer (Alderman Francomb), and Alderman Harrison.

AN UNMOVED Eman—o-s—.-----iTrile-s--tiValsh came up on rem Ind he having been admitted to bail, from Saturday, on a charge of having assaulted a young woman named E. Lawrinson. Mr. A. Browne, who appeared for the de- fendant, said that the charge was a trumped-up one, and had been brought in spite. The defendant had a good character. As the complainant did not appear, the case was dismissed.

DRUNKENNESS—The followingpersons weredealt with for this offence :—T. Lloyd, in Legh-st.' on Saturday, fined ss. and costs; Patri-A Dempsey, in Whittle-st., on Saturday, was dismissed; B. Brannan, in Silver-st., on Saturday night,fined ss. including costs; Emma Howard, in Bewsey-rd., on Saturday, sent to prison for a month: M. A. McGuire, in Berry's-yard, on Sunday morning, fined ss. including costs; Sarah O'Brien, in Buttermarket-st., on Saturday night, sent to prison for a month; Annie Duffey, in Winwick-st., on August 25th, fined ss. and costs; Joseph Corcoran, in Rose and Crown-st., on the 27th January, fined ss. and costs; James Traynor, in Corporation-st., the same morning, fined ss. including COstS.

A DESERTER.—Thomas Grigg, labourer, was charged with having deserted from the Ist Regiment of Foot, stationed in Ireland, on the 14th inst. Prisoner was committed to Walton to await escort. CARD PLAYING. Cornelius Ward, a youth, was charged with with playing at cards for money in Williams-yard, Church-st., on Saturday afternoon. The magistrates ordered that the lad be locked up until six o'clock in the evening. SLEEPING our.--John Adams, charged with sleeping out in a shed belonging to Elizabeth Monks, at Arpley, on the same morning, was sent to prison for seven

days. "SCRIMMAGING."—AIfred Hargreaves was summoned for disturbing the peace by fighting in Brick-st., on the 21st September, and William Hunt and Charles Derby- shire summoned each other for assaults alleged to have been cz.mmitted on the same occasion. The charge against Hunt was dismissed, and as the evidence was not clear with regard to the other two defendants, their cases were adjourned.--Edward Brown and Robert Forest were bound over, and ordered to pay costs, for having disturbed the peace by fighting with each other in Bewsey-road, on the 19th ult. DISORDERLY CONDUCT.—Elizabeth Lewis, summoned for having been disorderly in Egerton-st., on the 22nd
llism=
ult., was ordered to pay costs.—William Bate, summoned for having been disorderly in Catherine-st., was dis- missed.

PITCH AND Toss.--Patrick Murray and William Beckett, lads, were summoned for playing at pitch and toss in Crown-st., and were ordered to undergo imprison-. ment until six o'clock the same day. CHIMNEY ON Ft Preston was ordered te) pay a shilling for having allowed the chimney of his dwelling-house to be on fire. BAD LANGUAGE.—EIIen Smith, summoned for having, used bad language in the market, was fined 55., including costs'. TULLDAY.—Before Aldermen Holmes and Chandley, and Mr. R. Garnett.

DRIINHENNES.9.—John Galway, for having been drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road, on the night before, was fined ss. and costs.—Martin Burke, for having com- mitted a similar offence in Church-street, on the previous night, was also fined ss. and COAL SLEEPING °GT.—George Jones, charged with this offence, was sent to prison for seven days with hard labour.

SCTIOOL ATTENDANCH CASES.—SeVeraI persons were summoned for neglecting to regularly send their child- ren to school, and the usual fines were imposed. Mr. George Riley, school attendance officer, proved the cases.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Holmes and Chandley, Capt. Nicholson, and Mr. John Fairclough. DRUNKENNESS.—Thomas Bryers, charged on warrant with having been drunk and disorderly, in Winwick-st., on the 22nd of March, was fined ss. and costs.—For the same offence Jane Connell was fined 55., including costs; 1 Sarah Ann Hillier was sent to prison for a month; Joseph Warburton, two charges, was fined 10s. and costs; Michael Rourke was tined ss. and costs, and William Street was fined 55., including costs WIFE ASSAULT.—George and Julia Storer, husband and wife, were charged with having been drunk and dis- orderly on Town Hill, on the night before. The male prisoner was also charged with having assaulted his wife. Inspector Spinks said that he saw him strike his wife a violent blow on the face. Prisoners were each fined ss. and costs. ABSCONDING FRO3I THE WOBKHOUSB.—WiIIiam Taylor, charged with having absconded from the Union Work- house, on the 9th ult., and for having left his two chil- dren chargeable to the common fund of the Union was sent to prison for a fortnight. VAGBANCY.—WiIIiam Smith and William Bostock, charged with sleeping:in a haystack at Arpley-fields, were each sent to prison for a week. THEFT IN A PUBLIC-House.—Stephen Collins was charged with having stolen 95., the property of a navvy named James Low, whilst in the Roebuck Inn, on the previous night. He was sent to prison for three weeks. FIIIDAY.—Before Mr, John White (chairman), Alderman
Harrison, and Dr. Gornall.

REFUSING, TO QUlT.—Charles Fudge, apparently a navvy, was charged with having been drunk at the Old Crow Inn' Fennel-st., and with refusing to quit. It was stated that he had been violent because he was refused drink, and that he had broken a window. A fine of 20s. and costs, or one month's imprisonment, was imposed. INDECENT BEIZAVIOUIL.—Ann Smith was charged with having been guilty of indecent behaviour in Rattersby- lane, and was discharged on promising to leave the town. RIDING WITHOUT A TlCKET,—William Smith, a haggard looking individual, was charged with riding from Liver- pool to Warrington by the Cheshire Lines without a ticket. He stated that he had been drinking heavily and he could not tell how he had got into the train at Liver- pool. He had no business at Warrington whatever. He was fined ss. and costs or a week's imprisonment. ALLEGED THREATS.—EIIen Corfield was charged with having used threats towards Richard Lomax, but the case was dismissed.—William Marjin, of Wellington-st., was bound over for having used threats towards William Williams.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. Edward Greenall, G. Comber, and J. Crosfield.

MISCELLANEOUS.—EIIen Hatton and Esther Martin. for disturbing the peace at Sankey, were bound over to be of good behaviour.—John Hughes, for having been drunk at Sankey, on the 20th ult., was fined Sc. and costs.—James Baxter, for having been drunk whilst in charge of a horse and lurry, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. —Joseph Carter, for having been drunk in charge of a horse and cart, on the 24th September, at Rixton. was fined ss. and costs.—Thomas Couglie, for a similar offence, was fined is. and costs.—JamesFazackerley was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for riding a bicycle on the footpath on the sth inst.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. J. Brundrit and Mr. James Handley. JURY LISTS.—For the townships of Aston, Acton Grange, Halton, Norton, Runcorn, Stockham, Sutton, Weston, and Clifton, were presented and signed by the

magistrates. HALTON CASTLE HOTEL.—Mr. F. A. Lake said last week the license to this hotel was renewed on the understand- ing that Wolstencroft went out and a new tenant was provided. Since that time Messrs. Baker and Sons had arranged with Messrs. Bell and Sons, brewers, Peover, to take over the house, As that firm had been unable to get a suitable tenant up to the present. Mr. Lake asked that the application for transfer should be postponed until they had a man in whom they could place full re: liance.—The Bench agreed. DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence William Thomas was fined 2s. 6d. and costs.
Do° AT LARGE.—Ed ward Johnson, Bridge-street, was fined 6d. and costs for allo wing his dog at large unsecurely muzzled.
DISCHARGING FIRIAWORICS.—SamueI Lythgoe, 10 years of age, was summoned for discharging fireworks in Waterloo-road, and he was dismissed with a caution.

STREET OBSTRUCTION.—James Owen and John Spencer were each fined 6d., and costs 9s. 6d., for wilf ally obstruct- ing the footpath in Bridge-st. IN FEAR OF HErc HUSBAND.—SamueI Massey, labourer, Norfolk-street, was summoned for using threats towards- his wife Maria, en the 22nd September.—The complain ant said the defendant came home drunk, ran her out of the house, and threatened to take her life. He would not work and keep the family, because of his drunken habits, and her life was in danger.—She had had to take her three children to a neighbours and sleep there.—The de- fendant I will tell you what I think she is tired of me and wants a separation.—Mr. Brundrit : There is nothing surprising about that, when you are drinking all the time and won't work.—Defendant : They won't let me have drink in Runcorn without paying for it, and I cannot get money without working for it.—The Bench bound the defendant over to keep the peace for six months, himself in £lO and one surety of £5.

STUPIDLY DRUNK.—Joseph Davenport was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st. P.C. Crowder said he was driving Superintendent Large over Delph Bridge, the prisoner, who was drunk planted him- self in the roadway and would not move. Witness had to descend from the trap and take him away or he would have been run over. Defendant used disgraceful lan- guage. The magistrates imposed a fine of 103., and costs Bs. 10d. _ _ . .

THEFT OF A COAT.—John Bums, a labourer, was charged on remand with stealing a coat value Bs. 6d., from the shop of Arnold Unsworth, High-st.—The defendant said he had injured his leg, and been taking morphine and did not know what he was doing.—He was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. CRUELTY TO COLTS BY BOYS.—Robert Peers (10), and David Pownall (11 ),were summoned for cruelly ill-treating horses.—P.C. Woodrow said on Wednesday the 17th September, he saw the defendant and other boys throw- ing stones at two horses in a field belonging to Mr. Morris. He watched them a quarter of an hour. One of the colts was almost run into the Big Pool.—Mr. Morris said that during the summer considerable dam- age had been done to his crops and cattle. He had brought this case as a caution. The defendants were each ordered to pay the costs, 4s. 6d.

div.head: WIDNES PETTY. SESSIONS.
div.p: WIDNES PETTY. SESSIONS.
TEITIRSDAY.—BeiO-r-e•Me;;;;.-..E-.JK7M-u-;p-r-a-tt (chairman)
and H. Wade Deacon.

DRUNKENNESS. William Kenny, Lancaster; Thos. Grice, 12, North-st. ; and James Gagham, for being drunk and disorderly, were each fined ss. and costs, or in default seven days.—John Doherty, 19, Midwood-st., and John Reynolds, 12, North-st. were fined 7s. 6d. and 10s. and costs respectively, for like offences. BREACHES or THE PEACE. —Margaret Wall, 8, Caroline- St. ; Mary Ann Smith,Peel-st. ; and Mary Dunn,Caroline- st., were each summoned for committing a breach of the peace, and the defendants were each bound over for three 1 months, or go to goal for seven days. , OBSTRUCTING THE FOOTPATII.—Austin Ball, Mersey- rd.; Amos Beswick, Hurst-st. ; George Wilson, 7, Beech- terrace, three youths, were summoned for obstructing the footpath, in Mersey-st., on the 23rd ult.—The defendants were discharged with a caution. Doa AT LARGE.—John Williams, Ball-lane, Ditton, was summoned for allowing his dog to run at large, and a fine of 2s. 6d. and costs was imposed. DISAGREEABLE Nniammuns.—Elizabeth Finn, 20, Elea- nor-street, was summoned for using threatening language towards Jane Dooley, on the 28th ult. The complainant said she resided at 36, Eleanor-st. On Sunday night, the defendant, without any provocation, said she would "knock her two eyes into oue."—The defendant was bound over to keep the peace for three months. Assema.—Martin Dunn, 9, Caroline-street, was sum- moned for assaulting Mary Murtha, on the 27th ult.— The complainant stated that on Saturday night she saw the defendant quarrelling, and asked him to go home and not to fight. The defendant turned round, caught her by her hair, and kicked her about the body.— Several witnesses were called who gave corroborative evidence, and the defendant was fined 10s. and costs, or seven days.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. H. Wade-Deacon. BREACH OF nix PEACEL—Thomas M'Grevr, 11. Davies- st., was summoned for committing a breach of the peace and he was bound over to keep the peace for two months, or go to goal for seven days. DRUNKENNESS. ••••-• Edward Shaw, 4, Waterloo-road, Domoniac Kelly, St. Helens, Anthony Walsh, Duke-st., Ditton, and Elizabeth Grennan, Watcr-st., were each

div.head: EXAMINER,, SAT
div.p: THE EXAMINER,, SAT

fined 55. and costs for being drunk and disorderly on the highway at Widnes on Saturday night. ASSAHLTING THH POLICE. —James Fitzpatrick, 3, Hutchinson-st., was brought up in custody charged with assaulting P.C. Tweddle, on the 18th inst., and also with threatening Benjamin Naylor. The prisoner pleaded guilty to assaulting the police, and on the appli- cation of Superintendent Noblett, this charge was with- on the prisoner promising not to offend again, and agreeing to pay the costs.—Benjamin Naylor. a foreman in the employ of Messrs. Mort, Liddell and Co., said on Sunday night he was ejecting the prisoner, when he threatened him, and said he would "swing for him yet." For this offence the defendant was bound over for three months, or seven days' imprisonment.

div.head: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.
TussDAY.—Before Messrs.
Edward Greenall (in the

chair), W. Long, and H. Neild. Tns JURY LISTS.—The assistant overseers for the various townships in the Daresbury Petty Sessional Division presented the names of persons qualified to serve on juries. The lists were confirmed.

DRIINYEINNESS.—The following persons were charged with this offence and dealt with in the manner stated.— Samuel Littler, Antrobus, 31st August, fined ss. and costs; and Michael Dowd, Walton, 22nd September, fined ss. and costs.

A FESTAL " CABBY."—A cab-driver, named Wm. Car- ney, of Warrington, was charged with being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cab at Walton Superior, on the 31st August.—Sergeant Booth said that the cab was standing right across the road--so that no vehicles could pass. Both the doors were open, and the defend- ant, was lying drunk on the top of the cab.—The defend- ant, who said that he had been out to a wedding party, was fined ss. and costs. STRAYING ANmits.—John Asker was summoned for allowing a donkey and mule to stray on the highway at Little Legh, on the sth September, and was fined ss. and costs.—Joseph Plumb, for allowing his mare to stray on the highway at the same place, on the 29th August, was fined is. and costs.

CONTRAVENTION OF TAR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) ACT.—A HEAVY PENALTY.—WiIIiam Brown, cattle dealer, of Manchester, was summoned for allow- ing 16 bullocks to be driven through a pleuro-pneumonia infected area at Walton on the 28th August, without having a license authorising him to do so. William Kirk was also summoned for driving the cattle through the area. Several constables proved the case. The defend- ant said he wanted to remove the cattle from Norton Park to Carrington, but did not think he was contraven- ing the regulations, or he would have got a license.—A fine of £lO and costs was imposed. The case against Kirk was dismissed.

DANGEROUS Doos.—Mary Barker was summoned for allowing her dog to be at large on the 26th August, at Antrobus. She was also charged with keeping a dan- gerous dog' aud not having it under proper control. A lad named William Blain, said that on the day in ques- tion the dog, which was unmuzzled, bit one of his legs. The dog, which is a fox terrier, had previously bitten him, and was a source of danger. Peter Hankinson and William Hankey also swore that the dog had bitten them. A fine of Is. and costs (£1 Bs. 6d.) was imposed, and the dog was ordered to be destroyed.—Charles Foulkes was summoned for allowing his dog to be at large and not sufficiently muzzled, at Daresbury, on the 14th August. It was proved that this dog also had bit- ten a school boy on the leg, and the defendant was fined Is. and costs-13s. Bd. in all. THEET OF Pararoas.—Two labourers, named Samuel Rustage and James Earl, were charged with stealing, at Appleton on Sunday morning, the 21st September a quantity of potatoes. value 6d., the property of Mr. , Joseph Knowles,farmer.—P.C. Brett proved the case, and said he saw the defendants taking the potatoes from Mr. Knowles' field.—Mr. Knowles said he had suffered a great deal recently from pilfering. —Earl was fined £1 and costs, or in default one month's imprisonment and Rustage ss. and costs, or fourteen days. SCHOOL CASES.—Mary Delooze was summoned for not sending her son regularly to school, and was fined 55.; for a similar offence William Henry Owen was fined 103. (two cases.) TRESPASS IN PURSUIT OF GAME.—A man named James Davidson was charged with trespassing in search of game on land, the property of Mr. William Turner, of Walton, on the 9th August. A gamekeeper said that on the day in question he heard the report of guns, and on proceed- ing to Mr. Turner's field he saw the defendant and three companions each carrying a gun, and they had dogs with them. He saw the defendant shoot two partridges, but the other men ran off with the birds. , . . .

Defendant refused to give his name to witness.—The defendant said he was only on the river bank waiting to shoot peewits. He was not two yards from the water.— A fine of 20s. and costs was inflicted. A GRAPPENHALL FARMER FlNED.—Thomas Ditchfield was summoned for having on the 29th August, at Grap- penhall, acted in contravention of an order by driving two cows through a pleura-pneumonia infected area, without having a license authorizing him to do so. P.C. Millington, who proved the case said that he met the de- fendant on the day in question driving his cattle from the fields to the house. He asked him if he had renewed his license. On its being produced, it was found to have expired a fortnight ago.—A fine of ss. and costs was im- posed.
FRODSHAM POLICE CASES.

TRESPASSING IN PURSUIT OF GAME—George Bontoft I was summoned for trespassing in pursuit of game, at Flelsby, on the 24th September. Richard Tweedle was out on the date named. on some land in the occupation of Mr. George Hulme, when he saw the defendant in a potato field, with a gun. On being questioned as to his- name and address, he threatened to give him the contents of the gun. Mr. Reynolds had shooting rights over the land.—Fined 10s. and costs.

THEFT. - David Aston, labourer, Frodsham, was charged on remand with stealing a gantry, value 45., the property of Arthur Foster, of the 'Albert Inn, Frod- sham, on, or about, August 25. h. Mr. Fletcher repre- sented the defendant. The larceny was reported to PS. Turner, who, as the result of enquiries, found the gantry in a stable belonging to the prisoner. He charged Aston with the theft, when he replied, "I did not steal it; I found it in a field, and took it, and locked it up for safety." A fine of 20s. including costs was imposed, in default 14 days' imprisonment.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

- Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

RUGBY. RUNCORN JOCKEYS V. SIMMS' CROSS RANGERS.—On Saturday. Score :—Jockeys, 1 goal, 2 tries, 3 minors; Rangers, 1 'try. RUNCORN OLD BOYS V. WARRINOTON-ROAD ROVERS.— This match was played at Widnes in fine weather, and ended in a victory for the Old Boys by 1 try,3 minors,to 3 minors. Caldwell scored the try, but Bolton failed at goal. FRODSILAM V. WIGAN ROVIIRS.—The referee not putting in an appearance in this Alliance fixture, it was decided by the teams to play an ordinary game. Both teams played a splendid game. Just on half-time W. Tudor got over the line for the home team, the kick at goal failing. Final result :—Rovers, 1 try, '4 minors; Frodsham, 1 minor. WIDNES ST. MARY'S Y. SIITTON.—This match was played on Saturday afternoon, at Widnes, before a large number of spectators. After some give-and-take play, Hardman scored a try, and registered the first goal. Play was even for a while, and Johnson dropped aigoal for Sutton. In the second half WCafferty and Donoghue scored for St. Mary's, and Flardman placed a second coal. The game ended :—Widnes St. Mary's, 2 goals, 1 try, and 4 minors ; Sutton, one goal.

, WARRINGTON RANGERS V. IMOSDALE (Widnes).—This match took place at Widnes, on Saturday, and after a hard game resulted in a win for the Rangers by one try, two minors, to one minor. Potts, after a grand run from half way, secured the try for the winners, the same player failing at goal. The home team tried hard to equalize, but failed, owing to the combined play of the visitors, who had the best of the game throughout. Plinston had a try disallowed. WATERLOO WHITE STAR (RI7NCORN) V. WIDNES OLYMPIC.—This match was played on the ground of the latter, and resulted in a win for the former by two goals, four tries, and four minors to nil. Douglas got a try for the Stars, which he failed to convert, and another try was scored shortly afterwards, with the same result. Cross dropped a splendid goal, and Lockett got a try, from which Dyer landed a goal. Tries were also ob- tained by Knight and Faulkner. Wimms V. TUEBROOK.—Tuebrook journeyed to Widnes in their opening encounter, where about 1,500 spectators turned out to witness the game. Both sides were well represented, and the visitors winning the toss elected to play with the sun behind them. From the start the ball was rushed towards the Brook quarters, Laws leading a dribbling movement to the quarter-flag. Whelan at length had an opportunity, of which he took full advan- tage, but Plumpton failed to convert the point. The drop out brought no relief, for Plumpton soon got posses- sion, and, but for a timely nudge into touch, wouldhave scored. The visitors could not stem the rushes of their opponents, who severely penned them in their quarters. From a line out Laws obtained the second try, and Plumpton again failed to do the needful. A flying visit ' to the other end was readily repulsed, and Laws was again to the fore with his second try, but the place kick- ing was at fault. With the score 3 tries to nil in favour of the Chemicals the teams crossed over. The second half had not been long in progress when a try was se- cured by the visitors, and, the point being converted, the teams were once again on even terms. The last point fairly roused the Widnesians, and after a combined rush Laws placed another unimproved try to the credit of his side. Two others followed, by Peters and Farmers. the first being converted by Plumpton. No other points were added, Tuebrook meeting with their first reverse by 1 goal, 5 tries, and 2 minors, to 1 goal. RUNCORN V. ROCHDALE HORNETS.—This important and time-honoured fixture was brought to another issue at Runcorn, before 3,000 spectators. The home team were
UR

poorly represented, Broady, Wainwright, and W. Hughes being absent from the ranks. At exactly four o'clock Faulkner started, and Smith and Mellidew did a neat bit of passing. Runcorn got a footing in the Hornets' quar- ter. Crompton and Davies made a grand exchange, when, after an effort by Rigby, Davies again received the ball and sprinted over the Hornets' line, Houghton mis- sing the goal. For a long time play fluctuated until Crompton gave Davies a chance, he putting in a grand run. Play was then under the Hornets' posts. Rigby tried hard to score, but H. Hughes gained a smart try. Crompton however, missed the goal. Riley and Faulk- ner assailed the the Hornets' line, but failing to hold the ball, lost good chances of scoring until Crompton ran over the line, and kicked a goal. Score at half- time :—Runcorn 1 goal 2 tries. Hornets 2 minors. Smith restarted, and Gayter returned to touch. Play was now fast. Crompton, starting the running, got to the Hor- nets' quarter. Mutch, trying to relieve, was soon pulled up by Gayter. Houghton then showed excellent form, his kicking to touch being much admired. From a centre Pendlebury, picking up very smartly, grounded over the Hornets' line, no goal being scored. After resumption of play, the Hornets were hard pressed, some flashes of fine passing by the Runcorn Hornets making the play warm around the visitors' line, until Riley ran over strongly, Crompton kicking the goal. Following up this success, Houghton, running up, passed back to Rigby, who crossed, Faulkner kicking a goal. Against such odds the Hornets kept well to their work, though the play of the home pack, led by Faulkner, who played most promin- ently, gave them plenty of collaring. The home for- wards pressed, Crompton crossing the line, Faulkner kicking a goal. For a time the Hornets, by the aid of Mute, got to the home quarters, but Dolan ran the ball back. Final result :—Runcorn 4 goals, 3 tries, Hornets 3 minors.

WARRINGTON A. V. MILNROW.—This match, the first meeting of these teams was decided on the Wilders- pool enclosure on Saturday. The start was considerably delayed, owing to the late arrival of the visitors, and it was past four o'clock when Isherwood started the oval. An attack was at once made on the visitor's citadel by Beard, Neild. Dillon and Davies, a minor being conceded to avert further disaster. The drop out failed to clear, and for a few minutes the Milnrow lines were in consid- erable danger. Then came a grand bit of play on the part of Warrington. It was started by Lawless, and the ball went through the hands of Daniels, Bate, Jolley and Webster, until it finally reached Jolley, who had no difficulty in scoring. This was succeeded by an equally fine piece of play, which fairly roused the enthusiasm of those present, Isherwood, Turner, Jolley and Webster handling the leather, the last-named securing a try. Suc- ceeding the drop out, a pass from Jolley to Daniels en- abled the latter to put in a fine run through the thick of his opponents; but although Grime and Ambler cleared the danger, another rattling run by Daniels again raised the sei,ge, but only a minor was obtained. From the drop out Milnrow were enabled to gain a foothold in neutral territory, but were quickly repulsed by the splendid combination of the home team, the forwards giving the backs any amount of of opportunities. Directly after- wards Russell broke away with a rattling run, and when close to the line, threw to Beard, who rushed over near the posts, Webster converting. In nowise disheartened, Milnrow now played up harder than ever, and succeeded in getting well into the home quarters. Russell, Moly- neux, Knowles, and Davies cleared their lines, and then Jolley was very prominent by a strong run right through his opponents. A free kick to Milnrow gave welcome re- lief, which, however, was only temporary, for a tre- mendous punt by Jolley was mulled, and Nield scored a try immediately after this, a magnificent run by Bate from midfield resulted in a try, after completely baffling his opponents, but no goal was kicked, half time arriving with Warrington.l-4-2, to nil. Restarting, some lively play ensued, Sunderland by a long kick sending the ball to touch at midfield. Isherwood retaliated by galloping too near the line, and when the homsters were looking dangerous, Howarth got possession, and running round a scrimmage, averted disaster. Following this a wide pass from Lawless to Daffiels ended in the latter securing another good try, which Turner converted by a splendid ' kick. Some good forward play by Davies Neild, Dillon, and Molyneaux were next witnessed, and from a free kick to the visitors, Bate gathered the oval, and getting, away in surprising fashion, handed over to Lawless, who ran over grandly, no goal accurring. From a scrim- mage some capital passing ensued between Lawless, Bate, and Webster. which almost ended in a drop- ped goal. Jolley directly afterwards crossed the line. and Webster converted,and another try was immediately obtained by Daniels. Some interesting forward play, in which Dillon, Russell, Knowles and Isherwood were conspicuous, ended in a further minor being added to the list. During the last few minutes, however, the Milnrow forwards woke up, Rigby and Schofield distinguishing themselves, and got right up to the home line, a minor, being conceded. From the drop out the Warringtonians amongst whom Beard, Neild, and Turner were notable, came away with a rush, and amid some loose play Web- szer picked up, and ran right through hic opponents and obtained the last try, the score being Warrington 3-7-5 to 1 minor.

div.head: WARRINGTON V. BARROW.
div.p: WARRINGTON V. BARROW.

This match was played at Cavendish Park, Barrow, on Saturday. Fine weather favoured the match, but only a model.? te number of spectators witnessed the game Barrow made a special effort for the occasion, placing their best team in the field. Unluckily, Warrington could not boast of this privilege, for Fair Turner, Dillon, Antrobus, and Massey, the latter of whom has not recovered from his accident against Lancaster, were all absentees. Capital substitutes were provided, and ss the final result plainly shows, they acquitted themselves admirably. Starting against the wind, and with the sun in their eyes, Warrington kicked off, and no reply being made, the first scrimmage was formed at the Bar- row twenty-five. Passing across the pack between Mather and Bate ultimately found the oval in the pos. session of Barnes, who dodged Milner, and after a pretty run and kick caused the game to be waged on the Bar- row line. From a pack the visiting forwards soon had the oval out, and Bate, puzzling Dickinson with his tricky play, dodged over, and only two minutes had elapsed before the first 'try was claimed by Warrington. Frank Turner's kick at goal was a poor attempt. Along drop out was got away by Barnes, who punted well, and placing the forwards "on side," Bowker had an uneasy time of it. The home custodian was at fault on many occasions, but Warrington failed to take the many op- portunities offered them. Bate easaycd the rushing tactic, but to no purpose, for Sands and Dickinson getting possession passed well along the touch, Boscow eventually relieving with an excellent screw kick. Barnes, , Evans, and Lawless in succession frustrated movements of the home forwards. Play was located at half way for a considerable time until Mather by an exceedingly pretty run,in which time, made ground by feigning to pass, though the effect was spoiled by a bad pass, transferred the game to the home quarters. Sutherland came to the rescue of the Barrovians, ard a dodgy run and kick gave his side the upper hand for the first time, and Bos- cow having his kick charged under the posts, Cowell rushed the leather over, and secured a try, Milner giving his side the lead by converting. This sudden change of affairs had cvidently its effect on the wirepulters, for on the restart we found them attacking in strong force. Nevins, Ashton, and Thornley- repeatedly showed up with useful work, but the defence was equal to any em- ergency. A grand pass from Berry to Lawless afforded the latter a rare opportunity, which he failed to take, and then a moment later Mather Bate, Barnes, and Lawless passed finely along the line, the last-named grounding the wrong side of the line, this piece of hard luck bringing half time with the score as follows Warrington, 0-1-0; Barrow, 1-0-0. The visitors had now the advantage of the strong wind, and on the re- startj Barrow unexpectedly rushed the oval dawn the field, compelling their first and only minor. The attack was only momentary, for a long drop out by Frank Turner met with no response, and the Warrington for- wards realizing the situation beat their opponents back on their lines, and it required all the energies of the Barrow backs to prevent them from scoring. Bowker was again at fault, and from a succession of scrimmages 011 the mouth of the Barrow goal, futile endeavours to cross the line were made by Evans, Mather, Bate, and Nevins. However, the defence was eventually broken through, for after a display along the line, Lawless made no mistake this time, grounding near the corner flag. The coveted goal was not scored, and as Warringt3n failed to notch this point the enthusiasm of the specta- tors was intense. Following the drop out, Bate, Frank Turner, Barnes, and Povey passed well, and Barrow again defended. Milner got away, but the safe grasp of Evans easily accounted for him, Evans next ran through the thick of his opponents and kicked across to Lawless, but the oval unfortunately gravitated in touch. A drop by Lawless added a minor. Barnes next became pro- minent with a good run, and the oval, now that it had been set travelling, was quickly taken over, and Mather scored a clever try, Frank Turner this time placing the issue beyond doubt by scoring a fine goal. Barrow rallied after this, but they had little or no chance with their opponents who easily beat off any impending danger, the latter portion of the game being of a scram- bling description. The whistle sounded "no side," Warrington winning by one goal, two tries, two minors, to Barrow one goal and one minor. Teams :—Watring- ton : Boscow, back; Evans, T. Barnes, and Lawless, three-quarters ; Mather and Bate half backs; Ashton (captain), Frank Turner, Bandies, Povey, Nevins, Holmes, Thornley, Berry, and A. Barnes, forwards. Barrow Bowker, back; Lawton, Milner, and Suther- land, three-quarters; Sands and Dickinson, half backs; Leake, Weatherall, Cowell, Tureek, Dickinson, Shaw, Warley. Bliazard, and Jones; forwards. Referee :Mr. Walker, Kendal Hornets.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

WARRINGTO!s7 A SSOCIATION-F00;11-AIL CLUB.—The mem- bers of the Warrington Association Football Club played their opening match at Warrington, on Saturday, their opponents being Whiston Reserve. 'rho result of a well- contested game was a draw, each side scoring twice. Parry and Simkins scored for Warrington. The follow- ing were the Warrington team :—Goal, Jones; full backs, Phillips and Davies ; half backs, Mather, Ayling, and Parry (captain) ; forwards, Wyatt, Clayton, Onions, Sankey and Simkins.

div.head: AY, OCTOBER 4, 1890.
div.p: AY, OCTOBER 4, 1890.
CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES.

The Canadian Premier and two members of his Cabinet delivered important speeches at Halifax, on Wednesday, on the question of union with the United States. Sir John Thompson, Minister of Justice, said they did not mean to allow the American flag to wave over Canada, or to give the Canadian market to the Americans. Sir John Macdonald, the Premier, denied that Canada had anything to gain by union with the United States, "with its mass of foreign ignorance and vice." He rejected the idea of annexation to the United States or the erec- tion of Canada into an independent republic. He had un- bounded faith in the ability of Canada to survive Yankee commercial hostility.

GREAT FIRE IN SYDNEY. 1 DAMAGES £1,500,000. A Reuter's Sydney telegram states that a fire broke out on Wednesday, in Pitt-st., one of tile principal thoroughfares of that city, and soon assumed immense proportion., extending to Castlereagh-st., which runs parellel with Pitt-st. to the east and to Moore and Hunter streets, which join these two thoroughfares. A large number of houses, used as offices and warehouses, have been destroyed. The following premises have been completely gutted :—The head offices of the City Bank in Pitt-st., the Athenseum Club, Castlereagh-st., and the warehouses of Messrs. Lack, Sons, and eneral mer- chants. Moore-st. ; Messrs. Feldheim and C0.,d0., merchants and importers, Hunter-st. •, Messrs. H. Bull and Co., I warehousemen, Pitt-st. ; Messrs. Gibbs, Shallard, and Co., printers and stationers, Pitt-st. ; Messrs. Lawler, and Messrs. Richardson and Wrench, auctioneers, Pitt-st. A number of other buildings were seriously damaged. The loss is estimated at £1,500,000.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. FOOTBALL-RUGBY.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. FOOTBALL-RUGBY.

Several matches on Saturday were remarkable for heavy scores. New Brighton, for instance, ran up four goals,and six tries,to the Free Wanderers a try ; Runcorn, four goals and three tries to Rochdale Hornets nothing ; Wigan three goals and two tries to the Manchester Rangers a try; St. Helens Recreation, three goals and a try to Aspull a goal.

Saturday was a black day for many of the leading Rugby clubs of Lancashire. Nearly all, if not quite all, the teams that were engaged with oppenents from other shires were beaten. Swinton opened their brief tour with a match at Cardiff, where a very hard game saw the Welshmen victorious by a goal to nil. The visitors could make no impression on the Cardiff defence. Harold Murray could not undertake the journey, and Herbert Cooke, late of Salford, took his place at full back, doing fairly well in his new position. Bradford beat Salford by a goal and a try,to a try, and after the dressing down the Yorkshire men gave Runcorn the previous week the Salfordians were perhaps lucky. Is there form in foot- , ball ? Runcorn severely beat Salford and are then beaten by quite a pile of poixts by Bradford, but Brad- ford only beat Salford by a rather lucky goal. Where does the form come in here? _

Another suspension! The Yorkshire Rugby Union, at a. meeting held in Leeds, on Monday night, suspended the Leeds Parish Church ground for play until the Ist of November, because a referee had been illtreated by the spectators during a match. A Bingley player was at the same time suspended for foul play.

div.head: ASSOC/ATION.
div.p: ASSOC/ATION.

All the Association League clubs were on the warpath on Saturday,five of the six games being remarkably close contests. It took the champions all their time to shake cff the Bolton Wanderers at Deepdale, only one goal being scored throughout the match. Gal!ocher, the latest " catch " of the North End, fell far below expectations. Sutcliffe, the ex-Yorkshire Rugby three-quarter, kept goal brilliantly for the Wanderers, for whom Jarrett, of Ruthin, was also prominent on the right wing. Everton added another victory to their list, and are still at the head of the League. They had not much to spare at Accrington, wheresthey won by a goal only. Blackburn Rovers, although on their new ground at Ewood, failed to hold their own with Wolverhampton Wanderers. The latter were at ene time two goals behind, but they played up with great pluck and came out victoriously. The Revere lack much of their old dash. A very stub- born game took place at Turf Moor, where Burnley and Sunderland where each credited with three goals. Notts just managed to defeat Derby County, but West Brom- wich Albion ran away with Aston Villa, at Birming- ham.

Notts Forest are a point in front of all their Alliance rivals. Next come Sunderland Albion, Walsall Town Swifts, and Stoke, the latter of whom had a hard task with Newton Heath. Arwick somewhat easily asserted their superiority over West Manchester, who have not yet won a match this season. They have strengthened their defence by securing Ferguson, formerly of the Pres- ton North End and latterly of Gorton Villa.

The Scottish Association are bestirring themselves in the matter of professionalism. Edinburgh St. Bernard's have been suspended, and a large number of the fore- most clubs have been ordered to produce their books for examination. The order has created consternation in certain localities where the payment of players is more than suspected.

DEATH FROM STARVATION AND EXPOSURE. "DADDY CHRISTMAS" DEAD.

An inquest was held on Tuesday, at the Horse and Jockey Inn, by Mr. Brighbuse, relative to the death of the man whose body was found on Friday morning last week, in a ditch on the Winwick road, near Clambrook Farm. Deceased was about seventy years of age, and had been in and out of Warrington for a good many years past, but no- body knew his name. To the children he was known as "Daddy Christmas," a sobriquet which was given to him because of his long white beard and hair. He earned a living—a very poor one, as the evidence showed—mainly by begging. One of the witnesses, John Smith, a farmer, of Sands-lane, Orford, said the man wanted to sleap in his outbuildings on Thursday night, and he let him lie down for a while, and his wife offered him some tea, which he did not take. Witness said he could not go to bed comfortably knowing the man was on his premises, but he had to send for P.C. Whittingham before he would leave. After this, about nine o'clock, the same night, Mr. Fisher, of Clambrook Farm, heard his dog barking violently, and on going into the yard, he saw the deceased prowling about. On be- ing asked what he wanted, deceased replied, "A doss," but Mr. Fisher told him he could not sleep there, and he left. Early neixt morning he was found lying dead in a ditch not far away, by John Savage, one of Messrs. Walker's draymen. Dr. Adams, who had made a post-mortem examination, said the deceased's body was in a state of extreme emaciation, there not being a particle of fat through- out the whole structure. The stomach and bowels were absolutely devoid of contents, the liver and kidneys were in a state of chronic disease, and the lungs presented signs of long standing congestion. The man had no doubt suffered from chronic bron- chitis for 20 or 30 years. The cause of death he held to be pneumonia, accelerated by starvation and exposure.

THE BIJRULARY AT THE BATTEN ARMS HOTEL. At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, Josoph Birchall, cabdriver, Cartwright-st., and John Dickenson, tailor,also living in the same street,were brought up on remand, Birchall charged with fel- oniously and burglariously stealing from the Patten Arms Hotel on the 29th July, a portmanteau, two suits of clothing, and other articles, value £22 18s., the property of Hr. Harry Cope Morley, a commercial traveller, who resides at Burslem, and Dickenson with receiving part of the property knowing it to have been stolen.—Mr. Arthur Browne prosecuted, on behalf of Mr. Kiernan, landlord of the hotel, and Dickenson, who had been allowed out on bail, was de- fended by Mr. Percy Davies. It was alleged that on the night in question Mr. Morley went to the Patton Arms Hotel. He gave his portmante-tu to a servant, who took it upstairs to a bedroom. When Mr. Morley retired to rest, however, between twelve and cne o'clock, the port- manteau was missing. Nothing further was heard of the affair until last Sunday week, when Joseph Birchall was arrested in Manchester on another charge, viz., that ' of stealing a coat. On searching his house the police found several of the missing articles. When charged with the theft Birchall said " I took them, but threw the portmanteau into the river." Inspector Spinks and P.C. Monaghan subsequently went to the house of BirchalPs father-in-law—Diekenson. The latter saio that the port- manteau was not in his house, but it was subsequently discovered in the cellar. Se veral of the stolen articles were also found in the house, which Mr. Browne thought Mr. Dickenson must have known to be stolen, as he had pawned a pair of trousers and altered a number of the articles. Mr. Browne, in conclusion, said that Mr. and Mrs. Kiernan were at first at a loss to imagine how the burglary had taken place, but a glass which was broken on the roof confirmed their opinion that Birchall had got through the window. Birchall afterwards admitted having gained admission to the room by the skylight. Evidence having been called, the prisoner Birchall was committed for trial. The magistrate (Alderman Harrison) ruled that no prima facie had been made out against Dickenson, who was discharged.

A SCENE. In the course of cross-examination, Mr. Davies asked Inspector Spinks why he did not apprehend Binliall's wife, if he thought it necessary to arrest Dickenson.— Witness : What husband and wife ?—Mr. Browne : Don't answer the question.—Mr. Davies repeated the queotion.—Mr. Browns: Don't answer it.—Mr. Davies: —I think Mr. Browne is the most bumptious advocate I ever met. I had proof of that last Tuesday.—Mr. Browne : I don't make such an ass of myself as you do. (Laughter.)—Mr. Davies : You cannot make an ass of yourself ; you are a donkey to start with.—The cross- examination was then resumed. After some time had elapsed, Alderman Harrison said he hoped Mr. Davies would try to make the case as short as possible. He had an engagement at a quarter to two o'clock.— Mr. Davies: I think you are anxious to see justice done.—Alderman Harrison : Certainly ; but I think we are spending an unnecessary length of time. —Mr. Davies: I think this is a very serious charge against my client, who is charged with receiving stolen property.—Later on, Mr. Davies said the only other witness he had anything to do with was P.C. Monaghan.—Alderman Harrison (to Mr. Browne) : If you can accommodate Mr. Davies, please do so.—Mr. Browne : Not after what he has said about me.—Mr. Davies : Why not call Monaghan now P—Mr. Browne : I shall call Herbert Darvell.—Mr. Davies : That is retali- ation.—Herbert Darvell was next sworn. He said he was employed at the Patten Arms Hotel. He took the portmanteau up to Mr. Morley's bedroom on the day in question.—P.C. Monaghan, who was the next witness, substantially corroborated the evidence of Inspector Spinks, and added that he apprehended the prisoner in Manchester, on another charge, on the 21st September. He brought the prisoner to Warrington. On the way the prisoner (Birchall) asked him not to go near his wife, as she was ill. That aroused his suspicions, and he sub- sequently searched the house and found a portioa of the property produced. When charged Birchall said, " I took them ; if you will look over it for this time I will see that it does not occur again. I sold some of the articles to my father-in-law, but he did not know they were stolen. Dickenson said to witness, " I did not know the articles were stolen when I bought them." Mr. Davies then addressed th,e Court on behalf of his client. He was present to endeavour to show that no prima fdcie case had been made out against the prisoner Dickenson of receiving goods knowing them to have been stolen. Mr. Browne had had an easy task to per- form, as Birchall had admitted Hs guilt. His client had been admitted to be a most • respectable man, and had been in one situation 14 or 15 years. The very first time his client knew his son-in-law had been guilty of stealing the articles was when the officers came into the house. They also informed him that his son-in-jaw had been locked up. He was naturally put out of the way when he heard the news. He contended that the prosecution had been very unfair to Dickenson, as he had received nothing from Birchall except those things which he had given up. The things he gave up afterwards he got from Mrs. Birchall's by the instruction of Inspector Spinks.—Mr. Browne: It is not correct that Inspector Spinks sent him to the daughter's house. Mr. Davies: It was admitted that that was the case.—Alderman Harrison : If the police permitted Dickenson to go to the bridewell alone it would seem that they had not made up their minds that he was guilty.—The Chief Constable: They walked behind him, sir.—Mr. Davies, continuing, said this was not a prosecution of his client, but a persecution. His client's mouth was closed, and he could say nothing. He had voluntarily taken goods to the police station; and Inspector Spinks and Constable Monaghan gave him time enough to receive from his daughter certain things. For the time Dickenson was one of the police and helped them to recover the missing things. He contended that the charge of receiving goods knowing them to have been stolen had not been made out.—Alderman Harrison said this was a case of strong suspicion. The prisoner Dickenson had been guilty of a great want of 'dis- cretion ; still he had a difficulty irk saying that his neglect was of a criminal character. He could not persuade himself that there was such a case against Dickenson to justify him in committing him for trial. It was the duty of a magistrate when adjudicat- ing upon a case like the present to give the prisoner the benefit of any doubt which existed in his mind. The police treated Dickenson not as a criminal, but as some- one who was endeavouring to assist them in their inves- tigations.—The prisoner Dickenson was then discharged. —Mr. Browne: We have the power to indict him to the assizes without your aid.—Mr. Davies : That is a down- right insult to yourself (Alderman Harrison.)—Alderman Harrison : I said it was a strong case and I say so now; and that Dickenson has been guilty of the greatest im- propriety.—The Assistant-Clerk : There has been no case made out against him.—The prisoner Birchall was then committed for trial to the next Liverpool Assizes.—He was then charged with stealing two carriage rugs from the Pattern Arms Hotel, and a gentleman's overcoat,the property of Captain Stapleton Cotton, from the Barracks at Orford, and was committed for trial on each charge.

The Marquis of Ripon, addressing a Liberrl meeting at York, on Wednesday, said the brewers' compensation proposals and the Parnell Commission ruined the last session, and the Tipperary outrage had ruined the corn- ing session. It would be the duty of the Liberal party' to ask the deliberate judgment of Parliament, and ult!-., mately that of the country, upon these proceediogs. it was not too serious a matter, hovv they ought to ir joke and be thankful at that event, and to bless four for for having provided such an overwhelming argu- ment in favour of Home Rule!
