But there 10,1' another thing to consider, and that was that after eenl:Years of coercive Government such a course of con- e 44, should be necessary. The comfortable hopes of set kion had been cruelly blighted by the Tipperary pro- tv,..ons. He had suet Unionists in Ireland who had 1 . teZeivings of the Minister who had instituteide tthesielptrit:- • t t iags, because they knew they gave h coloured pictures which he had painted an resulting kV Coercion. (Cheers.) Every Unionist in Ireland, , hilt, every sensible Unionist in England, if such there be, * at know that the inevitable effect of these proceedings ele th. d be to rally the Nationalists and make them close tei lr ranks. (Cheers.) What could be the motive in the hsalci, of Mr. Balfour in instituting the proceedings? He own opinion as to that, though he did not mean te.o-"ay to examine the reason then, but to state what the teDeeedings were in themselves. The prisoners contained ther,Seentatives of the national and the clerical party and the ;fess. The Government had now had one-fourth of teb"l'lle which they asked for in which to bring Ireland , the 'ace, and vet the three great forces of the people, , I Thelerr— , ey and the Press were almost dead against them. ' Moo`ers.) He should' be sorry to be connected with any . rorernent which showed such a result. But another illg e, Was against them in the prospect of an approach- , fe, "aniine in the West of Ireland. Within the past , tlee daYs landlords and others having no connec- With the Nationalist cause had described the vson-eaching calamity as certain, and the Government ' eisi'l;.d have to take action to deal with the congested t hiefiets speedily and strongly. He had hoped that the , ~)0 ~, ,Secretary would have remained in the mood for , It,s l?'!ering the calamity and the means to be taken for tNp:bllef, , but what was the use of asking men who were tie). le of the criminal folly which was now being perpe- ttic'ted in Ireland to do anything for these suffering dis- e 8 ? L ov, (Cheers.) A party so infatuated as the present .'el-nrnent with regard to Ireland were past being It "'"• He had been criticized for going to Ireland, but see e„ riled rather a do,,in the-manger policy if the Chief arY would not go to Ireland nor allow- anyone else os ai,; (Cheers.) For himself he did not play golf, and i ttqd `4. not profess to lessen his ignorance of Ireland by 8 Yule roe, e the wants of the country from the east coast of Was tuti• He never was more surprised than when he 00°d he went to Ireland to intimidate the Coercion awl it was just as silly an observation as if he qa en '° say that the Channel Fleet which he saw in Dub- "Y was sent to intimidate him. (Laughter.) The

-reason he went to Tipperary was because he felt that the ' Government were going to drive a good strong nail into their own coffin, and he wanted to see the first blow. (Cheers.) Proceeding to describe what he saw at Tipper- ary, Mr. Morley said he found himself hustled and pushed and menaced by constables with uplifted arms 11 and faces of menace. There was no sort of obstruction, and no approach to disorder, and yet this harmless knot of people seemed to enrage the police, and he had never I , seen such an act of folly as the attitude of the authorities on the occasion. (Cheers.) It was quite right that the two members of Parliament who had been arrested should be protected from any attempt at molestation, but he said, with a sense of the responsibility from which' he should not shrink, that the attitude of the authorities I was such as to put the constabulary in a state of mind most likely to lead to disorder. He denied that he and his friends vrcre followed to the Court-house by a great multitude, and said the armed force present were at all periods ot the day three times larger than the crowd in numbers. (Cheers.) There was no opposition on the part of the crowd, and without a shadow of jus- tification or reason from an English point of view the police drew their batons, and blood began to flow. Were the Irish police the only people who could not protect a court entrance without bloodshed ? He ventured to say that a couple of village constables in England would have managed without any trouble to have kept order among that crowd. (Cheers.) He confirmed the account which Mr. Harrison had given of the melee, and said he was prepared to testify to the assertion that without any provocation whatever a constable struck a newspaper reporter named Keating a murderous blow in the mouth, and sent him flying across the court-yard. He went on to say that it was not necessary to close the gate of the court, because when all the people were allowed to go in they did not fill it, and were as peaceful and as orderly as if they had been at church. (Cheers.) The whole thing was a piece of disgraceful blundering, but blunder- ing when you are dealing with armed men was a crime. (Cheers.) He hoped the country would believe that it was with great reluctance he said a word against some of the members of the Royal Irish Constabularia„ He did not forget that four years ago he and they we the sub- jects of certain childish charges at Belfast. He knew too well the difficulties with which the constabulary in Ire- land had to contend, and he would be the last man to try to make political capital out of their conduct. (Cheers.) He had never understood Radicalism to mean that they should not defend the partizans of order, but he must say that the action of the police authorities on this occasion could only be described as a deplorable and lawless and cowardly outrage, and a wanton and unprovoked outrage. (Cheers.) The strongest Tory in Lancashire would have felt as much outraged as he felt at this brutal outrage. (Cheers.) Who was responsible for these indiscretions? The system pursued by the Chief Secretary for three and a half years was responsible. He had defended every act of the authorities, whether right or wrong, and this was the result. From the odious and wicked slaughter at Mitchelstown onwards the Chief Secretary had refused all open inquiry, and the Irish people had been left to the mercy of the authorities without help and without hope. (Cheers.) We would now see whether he would listen to knglish members across the table of the House. (Cheers.) He could only say that he was prepared to stand by every word he had said that night, and he should not Only be able,but ready to justify it,when he stood face to face with the Government in the House. (Cheers.) How could they wonder in the face of scenes like this if the Irish people did not reverence the law, but hated the English Government who wielded such a force? Cheers.) He would put it to any man, Tory or Liberal, whether the case in the Tipperary court-house, which involved momentous issues to the accused, should have been tried by such judges? It was tried by two men, one of whom was still an executive officer of the police, and the other nominally a barrister. What scandal could be worse than such a proceeding? Whatever the legality of it might be, we all knew what the common sense and equity of it were. (Cheers.) If we were to have coercion courts, by all means let them be covered with decency and equity. The whole scene in the Tipperary court- house was one of bewilderment. The two judges seemed to him to feel their position acutely. (Laughter.) But he did not come there to blame the officials; it was the system of which he complained. We had not heard the last of it, and he believed the people of Eng- land would, by these proceedings, be convinced that they had embarked on a path which led nowhere. and from which no good could come, and those repon- sible were in the first place the Government, who put in motion the machinery of which all complaint was to be made, then the Parliament, and then the constituencies who had placed in power a Government whose policy was one of coercion and tyrannous force. (Cheers.) But, as he said before, we have not done with this matter. We should hear much of it in the future. He said at the beginning that this would be a turning point in the dark history of coercion. (Cheers.) He thought it was a point from which we should date our speedy and direct approach to the point at which we should convince the people of England and those who voted for the present Unionist composite majority in 1886, that they had embarked upon a path which led newhere, and from which no good could follow. (Cheers.) He believed that the people were now beginning to see the folly of the course upon which the Government had entered. St. Helens was one of the constituencies which had helped to put the present Government in power, and to them, as to the whole nation, he appealed in the name not only of the law, but in the name of goed govern- ment and in the name of order, as well as in the name of peace between two countries and two peoples who had no quarrel—(cheers)—to put an end, by their voices now, by their votes by-and-bye, to the system and to the policy, and to the Government, which inflicted a cruel wrong upon unfortunate Ireland, and which also in- flicted the greatest dishonour and disgrace upon justice- loving England. (Loud cheers.) Mr. W. R. Kennedy, Q.C., the Liberal candidate for St. Helens, was then called upon, and ;he was greeted with loud cheers. He said they felt honoured, and that the town of St. Helens had been honoured by the pres- ence of Mr. Morley that night. (Cheers.) They knew him and had respected him as a historian, a philoso- phere, and as a statesman, but they had learned his highest worth as the one who, after the great chief himself—(cheers)—had stood in the foremost place in endeavouring to redress the relations between England and Ireland, and strengthen the United Kingdom by giving it real and permanent union, and now, after four years of Tory government, to redress the cruel wrongs by trying to put an end to the coercion policy which at present ruled that country. (Cheers.) He asked them to assist the Liberal party in putting an end to the present Government for until that Government was ended no Liberal Government could come in, and until they had a Liberal Adminstration they should con- tinue to have the miseries and the wrongs of Ireland. (Cheers.) Mr. Lloyd George, M.P., said there was no politician whom the Welsh people honoured more than Mr. Mor- ley. The new movements in England and Wales were the result of the simple inspiration that had come from Connemara, and in the spirit of the new democracy everywhere they found nothing but the inspiration which the struggle for freedom in Ireland had given to them. (Cheers.) Councillor John Forster, in moving a vote ef thanks to the Right Hon. J. Morley and Mr. Lloyd George for their presence and addresses, said that there had been times when epochs of history commenced in that hall—as, for instance, when Mr. Gladstone opened the campaign for the disestablishment of the Irish Church. (Cheers.) So , the incidents of the Tipperary s.iene, as told by Mr. Morley, would make a mark on the whole civilised world, and mark the turning point for the Government, and ultimately end in the success of the Liberal party at the poll. (Cheers.) Councillor H. Martin seconded the motion, and asked the electors to bring this " damnable Government " to an end. The motion was carried by acclamation. Mr. Morley briefly responded, and the meeting then concluded with a vote of thanks to the chairman.

div.head: OVERFLOW MEETING.
div.p: OVERFLOW MEETING.

An overflow meeting was held in the Town Hall, and was presided over by Councillor J. B. Leach. There were also on the platform Mr. Lloyd George, M.P., Mr. W. R. Kennedy, Dr. O'Keeffe, Councillor T. Snape, Councillor Mearns, Mr. G. W. Rawlins, Mr. S. Taylor, &c.—Mr. T. Snape moved—" That this meeting expresses its condemnation of the Irish policy of the Government, and demands an early appeal to the country, feeling sure that the early return to power of a Liberal Government would conduce to a satisfactory settlement of the Irish question." (Loud cheers.)—Councillor Mearns seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.—Mr. Lloyd George, M.P., Mr. Rawlins, and Mr. Kennedy also addressed the meeting.—Mr. S. Taylor moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman and the speakers.—Dr. O'Keeffe seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.— The proceedings were then brought to a close.

Mr. John Morley, M.P., left St. Helens Junction' at 9.20 a.m., on Tuesday, for Chester. He was the guest of Mr. Arthur Sinclair, J.P., Waterdale, Sutton, during his visit to the town. Mr. Lloyd-George, M.P. for Carnarvon, who had been the guest of Councillor J. Forster, chair- man of the Executive of the Liberal Association, left St. Helens in the forenoon for Nelson, where arrangements had been made for him to give an address at night. The arrangements at the St. Helens Post Office for a rapid despatch of the telegraphic reports of Mr. Morley's speech on Monday night were of a most complete charac- ter, and were carried out without the slightest hitch or mishap. Mr. Pearce, of Shrewsbury, was in charge of the staff, which had been increased for the occasion by 15 clerks from Manchester, five from Chester, and two from Warrington. [he 6,400 words contained in Mr. Morley's address were all transmitted in several different messages, and these, with condensed reports, made a total of about 34,000 words which were telegraphed from St. Helens. To prevent any delay three Wheatstone in- struments had been brought from Liverpool, and in less than 40 minutes after the right honourable gentleman had concluded his speech the whole of the messages had been despatched to the Liverpool office, as the centre from which they were "wired "to their respective des- tinations. On no previous occasion had there been such a vast amount of work accomplished in one night at the St. Helens office.

div.head: – – – THE CHARGE AGAINST RUNCORN SANITARY – –
div.p: - - - THE CHARGE AGAINST RUNCORN SANITARY - -
OEFICIALS.

- - Sir,—ln reference to the letter which I sent to theßun- corn Rural Sanitary Authority, and the discussion there- on, as reported in the "Examiner," allow me to offer the following explanation. Dr. Adams at the meeting said he replied explaining exactly how the whole thing had arisen. This reply was received by me on the day after the meeting. Before sending my communication to the Sanitary Authority. I gave Dr. Adams four days to reply to the letter which I sent to him in which I stated the facts of the case, and asked an explanation. Raving received no answer, I came to the conclusion that he did not intend to vouchsafe one ; hence my subsequent action. I was not aware that he was away fer his holidays, and consequently thought I had to deal with Dr. Adams himself, but it seems it was his locum tenses who caused the trouble. In reference to Mr. Aaron's statement that "there were some hovels is Weston that needed ransacking both upstairs and downstairs," perhaps that may be so. In justice to Mrs. Lightfoot, however, I must emphatically say that her cottage is not a hovel. On the contrary she keeps her cottage very neat and clean, and took every possible precaution to prevent any spread of the fever. It has not been a pleasant matter for me to take the course I have in this affair, but the interests of my patients in a humble position must be respected, and I considered it my duty to bring the case before the Autho- rity.—l am yours truly, A. MACLENNAN, M.D., Edin. and C.M. 107, Church-place, Runcorn.

FEASTING RUNCORN OFFICIALS. Sir,—Since writing hereon, I have been looking over the Returning Officers' expenses for the past six years, and I find they have been increasing out of all proportion to the number of electna. T•he figares are as follows : s. d. 1885, Mr. Shaw 6 4 0 „ 6. Mr. Dobson 8 9 0 „ 7. do 8. Mr. Fisher . 9, Mr. Lightburn 1890, do It will be observed they have almost trebled since 1885, I and quite doubled the cost in the two years when our respective and worthy representative, Mr. Doleson, was the returning officer. Leaving out the cost of the feast for our gastronomic friends, the expenses remain too high, and I think the ratepayers ought to know why the elections are not now conducted on the same lines as they were in the first three years when the arrangements for the polling were efficient, and every credit was given both to Mr. Shaw and Mr. Dobson for the manner in which they had dis- charged the duties of their office. Then what necessity is there to deviate from so good an example? If the rate- payers do not set their faces against such needless I expenditure it will undoubtedly grow. I should like to suggest that the officials be not em- ployed at any future election. It would be far better to confine them to the duties for which are paid as servants of the Board. As for the Law Clerk, he is not required under any circumstances, as the Assistant Overseer is the man to say who is and who is not entitled to vote, and whether the voter has one or more votes. The Nuisance Inspector would be better occupied in devoting the whole of his time to the removal of those noxious smells which are so frequent in the town, and which doubtless are the cause of fever being so prevalent. There are many tradesmen, who even in these times, find it a struggle to live, and who would be glad to do the work for the ordinary remuneration, without the feasting expenses as extras, and who are quite qualified ; indeed, almost any schoolboy who has passed the fifth standard, could discharge the duties with celerity and accuracy—Yours, &c., Runcorn, October Ist, 1890.
SACRED MUS IC. &c.

div.head: RATEPAYER.
div.p: RATEPAYER.

Sir,—A fortnight ago there appeared in the columns oi your paper a letter entitled " Sacred Music," and signed " Order." Why your correspondent should have adopted such a nom de plume, I know not; " Disorder " would have been more appropriate, for the judgment ot the writer is not only warped, but the subject matter of his letter most confused. To his sneer about the Salvation Army there is a ready answer. He will find it in "The Parable of the Lost Sheep," which he may have read often, but evidently to little advantage. "To do good," different men adopt different means. As to the bands which on Sundays perform in our Park, " Order's " remarks are offensive. lam sure the bandsmen and their conductors, who ungrudgingly give their services, have more good sense than to be influenced by such stupidity. With respect to the other portion of his letter, having reference to "Sacred Concerts" on Sunday evenings, and the "Almighty Dollar," this concerns me, per- sonally, and others with me. A series of concerts are being given of a private character in the Public Hall ; . but there is one to be given on Sunday week,which seeks the "Almighty Dollar" in aid of our local hospital. The choir have given during three months, much of their spare time in its preparation, and the members of the orchestra have diligently given as much of their time for four weeks. Our case stands as follows: if there is a surplus over expenses,our hospital will have it; if there is not, the loss will fall upon the promoters. Can anything be more disinterested? Should there be a loss, Mt. Thomas Morris insists upon bearing one half; but we hope our townsmen will give such support as will render this generous offer unneces- sary. I ask pardon of Mr. Morris for using his name, but under these circumstances, I know he will grant it. The character of our programme is as " sacred" as it can be, as a perusal of it will testify; and we shall exe- cute it to the very best of our ability. It is the "Al- mighty Dollar" we, the choir and band seek, not for our- selves, but for "the poor and needy, . . . in the time of trouble." lam not aware that the Founder of Chris- tianity when He enforced moral lessons, such as" To do good, to distribute, forget not, that with such sacrifices God is well pleased," which most of us too often conveniently forget, named any special day or hour when to exercise the highest of Christian virtues— " Charity." It was He Who uttered that sublime saying "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath."—Yours truly,

div.head: GEORGE WOODS.
div.p: GEORGE WOODS.
THE GRIFFIN LICENSE, EARLESTOWN.

Sir,—ln one respect " Pluto's " letter in your last issue is like the racks in railway carriages, that are made to hold light articles only ; and, what is worse still, he has placed his parcel of tender goods so carelessly that I can already see their foul contents of rotten eggs descending on his own unlucky pate. In the first place he generously assumed that I was

aware that the publican's business is as legal as my own. I answer that I am fully aware of that, and of more than that. I may say that, although I myself hold a commission in her Majesty's service, the publican has a special privilege which I have not, and which all ordin- ary people and tradesmen have not. But" Pluto" over- looks the other side of the question, which is the legality of withholding this privilege. It is incorrect to describe

that withholding as pillage or stripping of rights. Let me give an instance in order to drive my argument home. It is quite legal, and dignified because legal, for "Pluto" in his journeys between Newton and Earlestown to scramble through hedges and over fences so long as the farmer permits him, but it would be equally legal for the farmer to prohibit him from taking such a short cut, and thus cause him to walk along the ordinary Mesnes path or Crow-lane. The farmer can permit or prohibit at will, and does nothing illegal in using his power either

way. Then, again, " Pluto " said that teetotallers are utterly worthless from a commercial point of view. Allow me to inform him that in all public services, especially the department I happen to be in, preference is shown for such abstainers. Ho also says that the blue ribbon is not the best mark of a saint. I entirely agree with him there, but surely he will admit that it is a surer sign of a saint than a red nose is. I hope that in admitting this neither he nor any of your readers will fly to "the glass" and poke his nose into it, neither mirror or tumbler. lie is quite right when he says that this teetotal craze will go on. It has gone on so far as nearly to upset the present Government. I trust it will continue to go on

so as to set up a Government whi'zla will give us genuine Local Option instead of the pres ent sham, and thus help to bring in an era of sobriety VA. the whole nation. I am not much of a puzzle, reader, but I have had nol difficulty in tracing " Plu*,es” real identity. Let me remind him of the old sch,oolboy motto "Honesty is the best policy," especially in these enlightened days of thought-reading, hypnotism, and other secret sciences. I should like further to know why he changed "Stead" into "Samuel." I Pope it was for the purpose of imitat- ing at this present juncture Samuel of old, for" He ran I unto Eli and said here am I, for thou calledst me. And he said, I called not: lie down again. And he went and lay down." Sensible Samuel, *. go thou and do likewise." Luckless Stead! Twice luckless Samuel ! ! Thrice luck- less " Pluto" !! ! "Pluto" and "Griffin" both belong I to the heathenish realms of myths. "Pluto" is said to reign in the nether infernal regions. I sincerely hope " Pluto" did not choose his newest name under the madly ambitious spell which stirred Satan to say he would rather "reign in hell than serve in heaven."— Yours truly, Earlestown, 29th Sept., 1890.
J. H. PROFIT.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

VISIT OF STOCKBROKERS. A visit was paid to the Manchester Ship Canal works by stockbrokers from Manchester, Leeds, Bristol, and other towns. Sir Joseph Lee, deputy chairman of the Company, stated that the progress of the canal was satisfactory in every way. The Bridgewater undertaking was paying handsomely. In about three months the length of the canal between Runcorn and Ea.stham would be completed and in operation, and the joint in- come would probably not be less than £lOO,OOO a year, which would amply cover the borrowing powers of the Company.

RUNCORN MISSION HALL. On Sunday harvest thanksgiving services were held at the Ship Canal Mission Hall, Runcorn. Mr. D. Elam, of Manchester, was the preacher both morning and even- ing. At the evening service the large hall was quite packed, some having to go away as they could not get in- side. On Monday evening a public meeting was held in the same hall, and a large congregation assembled. Ad- dresses were given by the Canal missionaries. Mr. Wes- ton, agent for the Runcorn section, presided. An impor- tant item in the programme was the presentation of prizes to the Sunday school scholars by Mrs. Weston, who, as she gave each one their prize, spoke a few well- chosen words of encouragement to them. Solos were sung by Mrs. Grame and Miss Brown in good style. Mrs. Joynson presided at the organ. THE VOTING RIGHTS OF SHIP CANAL EMPLOYES. The Revising Barrister, Mr. H. F. Blair, held a court on Monday for the Urmston, Flixton, Davyhulme, Irlam, and Cadishead districts of the Eccles Division, at the Victoria Hotel, Urmston. Mr. B. L. Green appeared for the Liberals, and Mr. E. Gabriel for the Conservatives. The business was for the most part formal. Mr. W. J. Froone, engaged on the Ship Canal works at Flixton, put in a claim as occupier of one of tho huts, for which he said he paid a rent of £l6 Bs. a year. The question raised was whether the place was rated or not.—Mr. Smith stated that ho had not got it on the rate-book.--The Re- vising Barrister said that although not specified cn the rate-books, yet the claimant might have a right to vote. —Mr. Andrew said that Mr. Walker, the Ship Canal con- tractor, was not rated at all, but the Manchester Ship Canal Company paid a deficiency rate during construc- tion. Mr. Walker had the land during construction and had a right to erect workmen's huts or hospitals thereon. —Mr. Smith stated that MY. Walker was rated on the land, but not for the huts.—Mr. Andrew observed that Mr. Walker would not pay rates on the huts.—The Barrister replied that that did not njure the tenant, who in this case alleged that he tried to pay rates. If no de- mand had been made on the tenant for the rate lie was in the same position as though he bad paid them with regard to a vote. The point was a very knotty one. The question whether the rating of the land on the deficiency principle, and not the rating of the buildings, was strong enough to bear the franchise. Ultimately the Barrister said he would reserve his decision. Several claims of a similar character were made and will abide the decision n this case. ASSAULTING A SHIP CANAL GATEKEEPER.— A HEAVY FINE.

At the Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Messrs. E. Greenall (in the chair), W. Long, and H. Nield, George Stanley Harrison, a mechanic employed on the No. 6 section of the Ship Canal at Thelwall. was summoned for having, on the 29th August, assaulted George Bennett, a gatekeeper, employed on the Ship Canal at Thelwall, and living at the Huts. There was a cross-summons charging Bennett with assaulting Harri- son. Mr. Percy Davies, who appeared on behalf of Ben- , nett, said that about a quarter to eight on the night in question, Bennett was on duty at the Thelwall New-road crossing, when he noticed Harrison riding a bicycle on the footpath, from the offices, in the direction of the crcssing. Bennett shouted to Harrison (who had not a light) to get off the footpath. The latter did not take any notice of the order, and was going at a quick speed. ! The result was that Harrison's machine grazed Bennett's right leg, which caused the bicycle to turn over on the road. Harrison, it was alleged, then struck Bennett a violent blow on the ear, which knocked him across the road, cutting his head. Harrison then said to Bennett, "You are drunk I'll report vou." Bennett corrobo- rated Mr. Davies's statement.—.. John Smith, a gateman, Margaret Bowers, Mr. Eggleton, and Mr. Manning gave evidence to the effect that Bennett bore an excellent character, and was sober on the night in question.— Harrison denied striking Bennett at all. He threatened Bennett, and said that if he had been a young man, he would have given him something for his trouble.—Har- rison said that Bennett deliberately took hold of the handle of the machine and threw him to the ground. Harrison, during cross-examination by Mr. Davies, said he was " downy on the lawyers." (Laughter.)—PC. Millington also gave evidence.—The magistrates deter mined that the assault upon Bennett had been proved, and fined Harrison 10s. and costs, £2 2s. 6d. in all. The cross-summons was dismissed.

RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS. The monthly meeting of the members of the above- named Board of Commissioners was held on Thurs- day morning, at the Town Hall, Mr. Samuel (chair- man) presiding. There were also present—Messrs. F. Wiswall, E. Imison. J. Pritchard, W. Ilankinson, J. W. Lightburn, IL White, R. Able, H. J. Grice, Dr. MacDougall (medical officer of health), Mr. F. A. Lake (law clerk), Mr. E. Marshall (secretary), and Mr. Barker (surveyor). THE HEALTH OF THE TOWN. Dr.MacDoug,all (medical officer of health) reported that the number of deaths registered during the past month amounted to 51. Of these two were inquest cases, and of the remaining 49 deaths, 12 were due to diarrhcea, 5 to bronchitis, 5 to inflammation of the lungs, 4 to mesentric disease, 6 to fever, 2 to cancer, 3 to heart disease, and one each to blood disease, disease of liver, paralysis, convulsions, premature birth, inflamma- tion of the lining membrane of the brain, disease of bone, disease of skin, apoplexy, debility; one each from consumption and disease of the brain. The above 51 deaths showed an average death-rate of 34 per thousand of the estimated population, and exclusive of the inquest cases, of 32.6 for the twelve months. Mr. Lightburn observed that the death-rate was very excessive.—The Chairman : Is there any particular cause ?—Mr. Lightburn said there were six cases of death from fever. He also referred to the deaths from cancer, and said that the valley of the Mersey was known as a cancerous valley. Mr. Grice said the deaths from cancer were not due to any defects in sanitary matters, and he expressed the opinion that it was satisfactory the deaths from cancer were so few. HIGHWAYS AND BUILDING COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended that the footway in Greenway-road, from the end of Salisbury-st. to the rail- way bridge, be made with granolithic pavement, and that the tender of Messrs. Stuart's Granolithic Paving Company, to do the work at 4s. 3d. per superficial yard, be accepted. It was further recommended that, as the Burial Board had consented to give up a strip of land for the purpose of widening the end of Victoria-road, the Surveyor be instructed to proceed with the setting back of the fence.—Mr. Grice moved the confirmation of the minutes, and referring to granolithic pavement, said he did not think that the Board could do better than try the experiment at that place, to ascertain whether it gave satisfaction or not.—The minutes were adopted. FINANCE. The Finance Committee reported. that the treasurer ' had received the following sums during the past month: —General fund, £606 10s. 6d., which included £562 13s. 6d. on general district rate account, and on library fund account, £1 18s. 2d. Accounts as follows were re- commended for payment : General fund, £277 153.8 d.; loan account, £9 9s. ; library fund,' £ll 12s. Bd. The treasurer's balances were—General fund, £934 18s. Bd. ; unspent loan, £554 us. id.; district fund, £4 2s. 9d. ; sinking fund, £192; library fund, £l9 3s. 4d. The Committee recommended that the general district rate made on April 21st last, be amended by raising and re- ducing certain assessments, as set forth in the schedules submitted, the net increase amounting to £597 12s. 6d. rateable value ; that the irrecoverable arrears of the first instalment of the general district rate, amounting to £3O 17s. Bd., be allowed.—Mr. Imison moved the confirma- tion of the minutes, and remarked that the irrecoverable arrears were smaller than in former years, and were causal in consequence of property which was not habitable remaining on the rate book.—Mr. Hankinson seconded the proposition, which was carried. NIGHTSOIL REMOVAL. The Health Committee recommended that a nigh tsoil foreman be engaged at 28s. per week, and that handbills he printed and "distributed drawing the attention of householders to the need of the duly flushing of cellar grids. Mr. Lightburn moved the confirmation of the minutes,and said the Committee had found it really neces- sary to appoint a nightsoil foreman, as Mr. Percivil had discovered that he could not do the work satisfactorily in addition to his ordinary duties. If he had sufficient to do before he undertook the nightsoil work he must

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 4, 1890.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 4, 1890.

necessarily have too much to do now. The Chairman did not consider the appointment would mean much extra expense, and said the work was not being satisfac- torily carried out. It was more in the way of making a satisfactory alteration that the recommendation was made rather than increased cost. The minutes were adopted.

Tng FISHERMEN AND THE SHIP CANAL. Mr. Hankinson expressed the opinion tkat the Board should take some action with reference to the preserva- tion of the privileges of the fishermen with regard to 1 moorings.—The Chairman explained that a petition was signed by a number of fishermen to the Manchester Ship Canal Company. This petition was sent to him, and Mr. Marshall had forwarded it to the Ship Canal Com- pany, asking them to give it careful consideration. He was sorry that the petition did not come earlier, as a question ought to have been taken up at the time when other matters were considered. Mr. Marshall had had a letter from the Ship Canal Company stating that they would give the matter their careful consideration, and as soon as the Board got anything definite they would take the matter up.—Mr. Lightburn said there was a condi- tional arrangement at Ellesmere Port.—Mr. Grice said it ! was a very important matter to the parties, and in their interest the Board ought to see that all the privileges enjoyed in the past were maintained. This was the whole of the business.
THE POLLUTION OF KECRWICK BROOK.
LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD INQUIRY AT

PRESTON BROOK. - On Thursday, at the Red Lion Hotel, Preston Brook, Colonel Walter Marden Ducat, R.E., an in- spector of the Local Government Board, held an inquiry as to the alleged pollution of Keckwick Brook, by Messrs. W. R. Earp and Co., tanners, of Preston 3rook, by the discharge of liquid refuse into the drain. The proceedings were taken under part 111. of the Rivers Pollution Prevention Act 1876. The Rural

Sanitary Authority, by whom the complaint was made, were represented by Mr. H. Linaker (clerk), Mr. A. Linaker (solicitor), Mr. H. G. Linaker (assistant clerk), Dr. Adams (medical officer), J. Farrington (sanitary in- spector). Mr. Robert Davies, solicitor, appeared on be- half of Sir Gilbert Greenall, the owner of the Tannery, and Mr. H. J. Longton, solicitor, Warrington, represented Mr. Earp. who was present. Mr. C. L. Evans, who had

made the complaint was also present. Mr. A. Linaker made a statement showing that Mr. C. L. Evans complained of the conditions of the Brook on the 19th May and the proceedings that were taken by the Rural Sanitary Authority, ending in that inquiry. M. C. L. Evans, was the first witness, and said Keck- wick Brook ran through the Norton estate for nearly four miles. He alleged that through the pollution of the Brook by the tannery, cows had cast their calves at about seven or eight months.—By Mr. Longton : Before the stream reached Sir Richard Brooke's land it was joined

by the Preston Brook. James Ferguson, bailiff to the Norton Estate for ten years, said seven sheep and three cows had died, which had access to the brook; and they were in the habit of drinking water from the stream. He had not had the cows examined. Joseph Jones, keeper to Sir Richard Brooke, said a portion of his ground abutted on the brook. He took three samples of water from the brook at Keckwick a fortnight ago. He had known the brook for 24 years from the Mersey to the Tannery. He had caught trout and eels from it 18 years ago, and had also drunk from it. There were no fish in it now.—By Mr. Longton: He had fished in the Preston Brook.—Mr. Longton : That's where all the poison comeS from. F, Weir, farmer, Norton, said he had known the brook six year, and it was in much the same condition then as it is now. The stream was badly polluted. He had several fields abutting on the brook, ore of which was fenced off. He had one cow which died in a field adjoin- ing the brook. She was "gone in the lung ".—By Mr. Longton: There was a spring in the field and the cattle could drink out of that or the stream. Mr. Earp had been there four years and the brook was much in the same condition two years before.—By Mr. Evans : He could not say that the cattle died of drinking from the brook.—Mr. John Weir, farmer, Lower Walton, said he known Keckwick Brook 35 years ago, when the brook was perfectly clear up to the fields of Mr. F. Weir abut- ting the brook. About 20 years a pollution began, and it was supposed to come from the Tannery. The tannery drained into the brook at that time, but he could not say whether the tannery was occu- pied or not. His father lost eleven cattle which were kept in fields abutting on the brook. His I father supposed it was tannery water caused their death. I The cattle wasted away and no kind of medicine could cure them.—By Mr. Evans: His brother had the farm at one time and he lost a considerable number. When he saw the brook twelve months ago the water was not so bad as it was 20 years ago, although it was not a good I colour. Mrs. Haslam, Warford Farm, Norton, said she had three fields adjoining the brook. The fields were all below the juncticn of the brook with Preston brook. since she took the farm, three years ago, she had lost five I cows and three calves. They all had access to the brook, and " swelled and became black directly " ; but she did not know what they died of. Whenever she turned cattle I into those fields, she had some one to take charge of them, Samuel Done, of Keckwick. said he had four fields adjoining the brook, but all except one had other water in addition to the brook. During the four years he had held the farm, twenty cows had "picked their calves." They were all pastured in the fields named, which were. below the junction of the two brooks. Cows would take polluted water, when they would not drink clean water. He attributed the " picking" of the calves to the drink- ing of the water. Mr. J. Farrington said he had been inspector to the Rural Sanitary Authority for 14 years, and the brook was then highly polluted. The pollution came from the tannery. The colour of the matter discharged into the brook was sometimcs white and sometimes brown, and sometimes a mixture of the two. He had frequently inspected the brook, and its condition varied. The stench from the brook varied according to the weather. Two of the samples analysed had been taken above the junction of the two streams. He had had many verbal complaints of the condition of the Keckwick Brook.— By Mr. Longton : The samples were taken on Whit- Tuesday, after the tannery had been stopped for several days. There was more water in the brook when the tannery was working. The drainage from a number of places went into the brook through sewers. He took the first sample after this sewerage had altered the brook. Before he took the second sample the Preston Brook had joined the Keckwick Brook. There were about 32 houses drained into the Preston Brook, Reynolds' Tannery, in the Union, drained into a brook, but he was not prepared to say that they turned more pollution into it than Mr. Earp discharged into the Keckwick Brook. They had no complaint against Messrs. Reynolds, and therefore no proceedings had been taken. Proceedings had been taken against Mr. Earp because of complaints. Mr. Evans said if he had had complaints from Mr. Finch or any other tenant about Mr. Reynolds' tannery, he should have reported tothe Authority just in the same way as he had with regard to Mr. Earp. In answer to Mr. Longton, the Inspector said the other day there was a larger volume of refuse turned out of Messrs. Reynold's tannery than was discharged from Mr. Earp's tannery, but the quantity varied.—Mr. Farring- ton added that the whole of the sewage from Preston-o'- th'-Hill passed into the brook.—Mr. Longton: Then this brook is a sewer for Preston Brook.—Mr. Farrington : I make that statement because it is a fact.—By Mr. Evans: Be took a sample of the water in 1879, and Dr. Carter Bell, the county analyst, said the water was not destructive to fish. The drainage he had spoken of was slops, &c., and did not include excreta. On behalf of Mr. Earp, Mr. Longton contended that Keckwick Brook was not a stream within the Rivers Pollution Act; that it was mainly used as a sewer ; that Messrs. Earp had at common law a right to foul the stream because they had done so for 20 years. That they had used all practicable and available means for rendering harmless the liquids discharged into the Brook: and that it was to the industrial interests of the locality that Messrs. Earp and Co. should be permitted to carry on their trade. He pointed out that all the evidence, with two exceptions, had been given by servants and tenants of Sir Richard BrOok ; and said it was a very one-sided prosecution. Mr. E. G. Guest. 8.A., J.P., tanner, of Warrington, said there was much greater pollution by using lime than there was by the use of soda. Mr. Earn was taking all practicable and reasonable means for rendering, harmless the liquid falling into the stream.—By Mr. Linaker : The liquid draining from the tannery into the brook would be sulphide of sodium and tannic of gallic acid. It would close the place if Mr. Earp did anything more to prevent pollution than he was doing at the pre- sent time.—By the Inspector: He knew of no other means except absolute evaporation, but it would be such a costly process that it would not be worth while carry- ing the place on. Mr. W. R. Earp, said he was a tanner by trade, and a chemist, and he was also the County Coun- cillor for the Daresbury District of Cheshire. In order to diminish the pollution of the stream ht had erected a series of five settling tanks at a cost of £lOO, and had also substituted soda instead of lime for tanning operations. The use of soda instead of lime was more expensive, and cost him about £4 more per week. He had erected a furnace at a cost of £lOO to burn the refuse tan, and in time the whole of the refuse heap would be destroyed, and the benefits would be found in time. He was an expert in tanning, and his books would show that within the past four or five years he had received several thousand pounds in fees, ranging from £lOO to £2OO, and he did not think tanners would pay him if he did not know something about the business. If the stream ran as formerly, he did not think the pollution from his works would be noticed, but either the stream had been diverted, or the syphon under the railway did not work. The tannery had had the right to use the stream for certainly one century, and probobly two or three centuries. When Mr. Farrington took the samples from the stream no liquid had been pumped into the stream for about two months. From the analyst's certificates. Mr. Earp argued that they showed, that there was five times as much poisonous

matter coming down the Preston Brook as there was down the Keckwick Brook. Mr. Longton said his other witnesses would prove the use of this stream for the purposes of the tannery for many years. Mr. Linaker stated that the stream had been used by the tannery for 46 years to his knowledge, and these witnesses were threfore not called.—After Mr. Earp had been cross-examined by Mr. Evans, the inquiry concluded, and the Inspector proceeded to inspect the tannery.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT RUNCORN, &c.
BY AN "OCCASIONAL OORILESPONDEN`e

That a very encouraging commencement has been made at the night classes instituted by the Run- corn School Board. That there are now about 50 students enrolled for the several subjects to be taugh t,and the head master Mr. Moulton, has some very good material to work upon. That Mr. Howitt and Mr. Taylor deserve every credit for the persistency with which they advo- cated the classes, and had them established. That, as the readers of this journal will be aware, the Widnes Local Board have adopted the Technical Education Act, and have taken control of the Wid- nes Science and Art School,and they have signalised the inauguration of the event by charging double fees to those students whose parents are not rate- payers of the town, or who are not ratepayers themselves. That in previous years a number of students have attended the school from Runcorn, and this rule will have a very harsh bearing upon them. That the Runcorn Board of Improvement Com- missioners, it they do their duty will adopt the Technical Education Act and put the youths of their town in a position for obtaining a scientific and artistic e iucation equal to the young men of Widnes. That the Act limits the local authority from spending more than a id. in the .£, and no rate- payer who has the interest of his town at heart will grumble at that expenditure. That at the inquiry respecting the proposed Wid- nes Fire Brigade Station, Mr. Allen, the respected clerk to the Local Board gave some interesting figures which will be found in another column. That the scheme is highly necessary and desirable if the Brigade are to be efficient and do their duty. That Greenway-road, Runcorn, has to have a length of granolithic pavement after all. That the Commissioners sanctioned the experi- ment at their meeting on Thursday, without any opposition being raised. Where was Mr. Smith ? That during the coming winter Mr. H. Wade Deacon, the Liberal candidate, will address a series of meetings on political subjects. • That Mr. T. C. Edwards Moss will carry out a similar campaign. That the election whenever it takes place will be a keen and exciting contest, and it is the general opinion that Mr. Moss has received notice to quit.
"THE PILGRIMS' PROGRESS."

LECTURE BY THE REV. E. LLOYD JONES. On Thursday evening the Rev. E. Lloyd Jones, of Rhyl, but formerly of Warrington, lectured in the Bold-st. schoolroom, Warrington, on the subject : " The Christian Life, according to • Pilgrim's Pro- gress : ' Is it a passing phase or a permanent type." There was a fairly large and enthusiastic audience. The chair was taken by Mr. E. J. Guest, J.P., and there were also on the platform, the Rev. J. Gunnell

and Dr. gornall. The CHAIRMAN, in his opening remarks, said that Mr. Jones needed no introduction from him. They knew him as a preacher and they knew the power he had in the pulpit. As a lecturer he appeared be- fore them in a somewhat different character but his praises in that respect had gone before him. Mr. Jones had a magnetic power and influence that very few men had. His past had been a series of successes, but he (the chairman) believed that the future, if he had his health, would be a series of greater successes still. (Applause.) He supposed he held his position there as chairman that night be- cause he had the honour to recognise Mr. Jones as a friend. He'trusted that he would have better health in the future than in the past. (Hear, hear, and ap plause.) I The Rev. E. LLOYD JONES then gave an eloquont and most interesting lecture on the subject of B un- yan's " Pilgrim's Progress." In his prefatory re- marks he said he had been speaking for 25 years and had been talking for 45 years. but he had only been lecturing for six months or so. (Laughter.) For 20 years he had steadily resisted lecturing, and indeed it was one of the vows he had to make before his wile would marry him. (Laughter.) He had two reasons besides that for not lecturing before. One was that he he had never known a man yet who took to lecturing and im- proved his preaching. He had known several who had nearly lost all their spiritual force by over-work in lecturing. There was another reason. He determined he would never lecture, if he lectured at all, unless the lecture was as much like a sermon as possible (hear, hear.) lie would not lecture unless fully convinced that it was quite as likely to be the means of grace as any 'sermon he could preach. (Applause.) Mr. Jones then gave a vivid and powerful sketch of the period in which Bunyan lived, and of the "immortal dreamer's" early life. The lecturer's subsequent delineation of some of the principal characters of the " Pilgrim's Pro- gress" was of the most masterly and fascinating kind. The appreciation of the audience was clearly evidenced by very frequent applause. The Rev. J. GUNNELL, in moving a vote of thanks to Mr. Jones, said that after that night the Pilgrim's Progress would be to him a better and more in- structive book. The book would be a greater power in their christian life than they had yet known it. (Applause). Mr. Moss seconded the vote of thanks which was heartily accorded, and a similar compliment to the chairman brought the meeting to a close.

FARM FIRE.—£S,OOO DAMAGES. Damage to the extent of £5,000 was caused yesterday, by a fire which raged for several hours at Stokesay Farm, near Ludlow.
WRECK OF A COLLIER. The barque Larissa, coal laden, was wrecked on the Gunfleet Sands yesterday morning. The crew abandoned her, and were picked up by the lifeboat.

. . _ . TROOPS AND THE GAS STOKERS. I A special messenger arrived :at Chatham on Thursday night with orders for troops to be held in readiness to proceed to Woolwich, if the gas stokers created a de- monstration. Seven hundred men of the Marines and
Hampshire Regiment-paraded yesterday morning.

HANLAN DEFEATED BY TERMER. A Halziel telegram from East Liverpool (Ohio), dated I to-day, states that Teemer and Hanlan competed yester- day in the Ohio River for a purse of 1,000 dols., the dis- tance being a mile down the stream. Teemer won easily, but the time made is unknown, as the judge's boat was obstructed and could not overtake the scullers and allow
the timekeeper to see the finish. TERRIBLE TRAGEDY IN LIVERPOOL.

In Liverpool, yesterday, Robert Jones was charged with causing the death of Sarah Scarisbrick, a widow, aged 30, with whom he cohabited. The parties had been drinking all day on Wednesday, and in the evening they quarrelled, when it is alleged the prisoner stabbed the deceased several times in the body. She died last night from her injuries. When arrested the prisoner attempted to cut his throat. He was remanded. THE ORMONDE CLUB FIGHT. Yesterday, Frank Patrick Slavin and Joseph Patrick M`AulitTe, again appeared on bail at Lambeth Police Court, charged with a breach of the peace by fighting at the Ormond; Club. Mr. Polann prosecuted. M'Auliffe had lost some of the traces of the punishment he received in the encounter. Both defendants sat in the dock. Mr. Poland said the defendants were charged with a common,prize fight. If it had been a boxing match and mere trial of skill, it would have been perfectly legal, but these men entered into a contest in order that one might knock the other out of time. Had M'Auliffe's la - juries had a fatal result, several persons would have found themselves at the Old Bailey charged with man- slaughter. He should apply for a summons against aiders and abettors. Other evidence having been given, the defendants were remanded until Tuesday next. Bail was again allowed. THE TIPPERARY PROSECUTIONS. Yesterday morning fully half an hour was lost by the late arrival of two defendants from Clonmel. The first witness on the table was Sergeant Andy Griffin, who gave an emphatic denial to the statement made at the last sitting that he intimidated one of the boys called to prove tho purchase of the "Tipperary Nationalist." Evi- dence was the,' taken in reference to the Thurles meeting in September. Two poticemen were called to prove that several of the defendants took part in the gathering. In cross-examination one witness said he did not know that the address presented to Mr. O'Brien referred to that gentleman's wedding. Mr. Healey said the Crown were endeavouring to makean act of conspiracy out of an ad- drees presented on a man's marriage. Ultimately the magistrates refused to hear further Mr. Harrington, because he said the Crown was on the Bench, and the court adjourned until next day amid much excitement. MIL GLADSTONE AND TIPPERARY. Mr. John Ogilvy, secretary of the Dundee Radical Association, having addressed a letter to Mr. Gladstone strongly condemning the proceedings at Tipperary, has received the following reply :—" Dear Sir,—Before reaching Midlothian, I hope to be provided with all the facts of the Irish arrests, and to be able to give a deliberate opinion upon them—Yours, W. E. GLADSTONE, Hawarden, September 30th."

GREAT GALE IN THE NORTH SEA. LOSS OF FOUR SHIPS. BERLIN, FRlDAY.—Telegrams received here announce that a heavy north-westerly gale raged in the North Sea yesterday, during which four vessels foundered.

div.p: LYA.IM.

Lynx Cnuncn BRASS BAND.—This band rendered a selection of sacred music at the Cross, Lyintn, on Sun- day afternoon. BAND OF HOPE MEETING.—A meeting in connection with the Wesleyan Band of Hope was held in the schoolroom, on Monday evening, conducted by Mr. Brown. ' A COTTAGE FIRE.—An alarm of fire was raised in the village on Friday evening.i It transpired that the out- break was at a cottage n Rush Green, occupied by Mr. Henry Moston. Several firemen, together with the fire engine, proceeded to the place, but on their arrival discovered that the flames had already been sub- dued. ALLEGED ASSAULT.—On Tuesday evening, at the Lymm Police Court, before Mr. Charles Lister and Dr. Brabazon, an Irish farm labourer, named John Wade, who lives at Lymm, was charged with having on Sunday night last committed an assault upon Rebecca Bates, 17 years of ago, a domestic servant in the employ of Mr. J. Shake shaft Cherry-lane, Lymm.—P.C. Griffiths gave evi- dence in support of the charge, and the prisoner was remanded. WESLEYAN HARVEST TRANKSGIVING.—The local Wes- leyans held special services of thanksgiving for the safe ingathering, of the harvest on Sunday. Owing to the chapel (which is undergoing re-decoration inside) not being available, the services had to be conducted in the schoolroom, which was tastefully decorated for the occa- sion with choice fruit, flowers, and vegetable produce. The morning preacher was the Rev. John Gunnell, super- intendent of the Warrington circuit, the pulpit in the evening being occupied by the Rev. T. Ross, also of War- rington. The congregations, especially in the evening, when the schoolroom was packed, were large. A QUICK RIDE ON A TRICYCLE.—On Saturday morning, at eight o'clock, Mr. Fred Evans, the Cross, Lymm, started on 100 miles race in twelve hours on a tricycle, under the rules of the Bowdon Cycle Club. The start was made from the Nag's Head Hotel. Lymm, thence to Prescot, back to Warrington, and through Chester to Whitchurch, where a rest was taken. The rider came back through Chester, arriving at Lymm at 7-45, thus covering 110 miles hi a quarter of an hour under the stipulated time. The actual riding time did not exceed nine hours. Mr. Evans has by this performance gained the gold medal of the club. REVISION COURT.—The court for the revision of the lists of voters for the polling district ot Lj,mim was held in the Police Court, before Mr. Parkins, the revising barrister, on Thursday. The business was of a routine character. An objecticn was taken by the Conservative agent to the vote of Mr. Wm. Henderson, head coach- man tc Mr. Dewhurst, because of his absence in Scotland with his master. It was contended that though he was the tenant of the house for which he was on the list, yet he did not occupy within the meaning of the Act, which required that he should be at liberty t. come back at nleasure without breaking his contract of service. The Barrister took time to consider his decision,which will be given at Cheadle Dulms. FUNERAL OF AN OLD RF.SIDF.NT.—The funeral of the late Mr. William Green took place at Warburton Parish Church on Saturday. The deceased, who was 76 years of age, had been a tenant on the Warburton estate for many years, and was held in the greatest esteem. The following members and relatives of the deceased's family were present—Mr. James Green; Mrs. Longshaw, Miss Green. Miss Ada Green, Mr. and Mrs. Cowan, Mr. and Mrs. White, Mr. and Mrs. Tinsley, and Mr. and Mrs. Green. Others who attended were—Mr. and Mrs. Dykes, Mr. Perrin. Mr. Leigh, Mr. Edwards, Mr. Williamson, Mr. :fames Beekitt, Mr. Coleshill, Mr. Newton, Bent Farm; Mr. A. Barff, Saracen's Bead; Mr. R. Jones, Mr. Apple- ton. and Mr. Whitelegge. The burial service was read by the Rev. G. E. Warburton. ,WEP

-- DEDICATION OF THE CHURCH TO \ The new and nandsome tower of St. Mary's, Lvirim, was formally dedicated on Tuesday afternoon, by the Lord Bishop of Chester, when a special service was held. The corner stone of the new tower was laid by Mrs. Dewhurst, of Beechwood, on the 16th May, 1889, al- thougn the work of taking down the old tower was COM- menred as far back as September or October of the previous year. The Rev. G. W. Guest, M.A., rector; Messrs. William Bailey and Thomas Jones (wardens), together with Messrs. John Dewhurst and Colin MaClver. constituted the Tower Building Committee, the archi- tect being Mr. Joseph S. Crowther, of Manchester; the builders Messrs. Geoffrey Gosset Holmes and Charles Wm. Green, of Liverpool, and the clerk of the works, Mr. John Jenkinson. The cost of the construction of the new tower, exclusive of the hells and clock, is pot down at about £4.500. The tower, which is about 100 ft. high, is in the old Cheshire style of architecture; and, except in certain details, it has been built on the lines of the old one, which is said not to have formed a true square; hence its rapid decay. The present structure stands on a rock and four feet of concrete. The carving of the west door—said to be one of the finest in the country—is quite a work of art, and it has already been much ad- mired. it was done by Messrs. Herpson and Hobbs, of London and Manchester. The service of dedication commenced at three o'clock, and the congregation was a large one. The clergy pre- sent were the Bishop of Chester, the Rev. G. W. Guest, the Rev. Canon Greenall, the Rev. W. G. Knocker, the Rev. H. C. Wilkinson, the Rev. H. A. D. Surridge, the Rev. J. Edwardes-Evans, and theßev. G. E. Warburton. A shortened evening service was used. The Bishop of Chester preached from the words "A goodly heritage." His Lordship is the course of an able sermon, remarked that the congregation were no doubt proud of the ancient history of the church. Eight hundred, years ago, there was a church and a parish in Lymm. They had the testimony of the Domesday Book, that there was an Anglo-Saxon Church at least to begin with. Later on in the afternoon the members•of the Lymm Church of England Brass Band—who had escorted the children from the Parochial Schools to church—ascended the tower and played the Halleluiah Chorus. The dedication of the tower was further celebrated by the discharge of a canon.

CYCLING CLUB HANDICAP. A 25-mile club handicap was held in connection with the Warrington Cycling Club,on Saturday. The course was from a point at Grappenhall, on the Knutsford-road, to the first milestone past Lostock Gralam. and back again. There were 23 entrants, 18 of whom started. ,The prizes which were of the value of £5 10q., were the gift of the Vice-President (Councillor William Pierpoint). The following were the successful comnetitors, viz.: —Mr. W. H. Bellian (captain) Ist, Mr. W. V. Brown 2nd, Mr. W. Rath- hone 3rd. Mr. W. Boyle 4th, and Mr. W. Collier sth. 3,1 essrs. C. H. Wood (hon secretary), and James , Critchley (hon. treasurer), officiated as starters.

div.head: PENKETII.
div.p: PENKETII.

ACCIDENT TO A BOV. On Wednesday evening, a little boy named Isaac Lloyd, aged six years, was swinging behind a lorry when his leg became entangled in the wheel. The little fellow was carried home and Dr. Murray was called. It is thought no bones are broken, but the injuries are very severe. HARVEST TEIANKSGIVING SERVICES. On Sunday, harvest thanksgiving services were held in connection with the Wesleyan Chapel, renketh. The pulpit was occupied by the Rev. Mr. Clayton, of Didsbury College. In the evening the sacred anthem, entitled "Ye shall dwell in the land,' by Sir J. Stainer, was effectively rendered by the choir, the bass solo being sung by Mr. D. Garnett. Collections were taken after each service in aid of the circuit fund. There were large congregations both morning and night.

TRIPS FROM PENKEnt. On Monday, the members of Mr. D. Garnett's Sun- day school class had a trip to Windermere, Mr. Gar- nett defraying.the expenses. The party left War- rington (Bank Quay) at 7.10 a.m., and arrived at Bowness about eleven o'clock. Immediately upon arrival lunch was partaken of, after which every- one took the steamer to Ambleside, and on ths re- turn to Bowness boats were procured for a: sail on the lake. A walk round the town and view of the lake were indulged in, and about 4.30 p.m., tea was partaken of. The return journey was com- menced at 6.10 p.m., and Warrington was reached about 930.—0 n Saturday the employ& of Messrs. Ti. Garnett and Sons journeyed to Hale for a picnic. The party, numbering about 27 in all, left Penketh in wagonettes about 1.30 p.m., and arrived at Hale about three o'clock. At five o'clock tea, which was provided at the Child of Hale Hotel, was partaken of. Afterwards Mr. Thomas Garnett explained the object for which the picnic had been got up. Ile said it was to celebrate the completion of the ap- prenticeship of Mr. A. Dunabin. Mr. Dunabin had gained the esteem of both his employers and fellow- workmen during the time he had been in their em- ploy, and he hoped that they would never have reason to change their good opinion of him. He wished him long life and happiness. Mr. Dunabin replied in suitable terms, after which an enjoyable evening was spent. Songs, readings, &c., were con- tributed by various members of the party, and at seven o'clock the return journey was commenced. Penketh being reacted about ten o'clock, all having spent a most enjoyable afternoon.

TRINITY CHAPEL. —On Sunday. morning and evening, the annual thanksgiving services were held in Trinity Wesleyan Chapel, when the Rev. P. Pizey, preached. The interior of the chapel had been richly decorated with an abundance of flowers, fruits, and vegetables. The choir rendered satisfactorily the anthem, "'rue eye of the Lord," and "The earth is the Lord's." The offer- tories were in behalf of circuit .fund, and amounted to £7 12s. ed. UNION CHURCE.—The harvest thanksgiving services in connection with the Union Church, Frodsham, were held on Sunday, morning and evening, the sermons being preached by the Rev. James Irving, of Tunbridge Wells. The Church presented quiet a beautiful sight, the pulnit and communion being the most attractively decorated. , The collections were devoted to the Chester Infirmary, and the flowers, fruits, and vegetables were destined for the Manchester Flower Mission. THE BONA-FIDE TRAVELLER.—At Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday, Sarah Edge, of the Weaver Tavern, Frodsham Bridge, was summoned for having her house open during prohibited hours, on the 10th August, and George Wilkinson and William Jackson, of Runcorn, were summoned for being on the said licensed premises on the day stated. Mr. Fletcher represented the police, and Mr. Brassey appeared on behalf of Mrs. Edge.—ln opening the case, Mr. Fletcher drew their worships attention to the idea that seemed to have crept into the minds of many persons, that because a person chanced to have gone a little over or a little under three miles, he was constituted a bon4;fide traveller. That was a , ridiculous notion, and it was surprising that such an opinion should have gained so wide a currency. The proviso setting forth the exception on the bond...fide traveller question was of a purely negative character,and did not say that a person who travelled three miles should be deemed to be a bond-fide traveller. The detend: ants were seen to go into the house at a quarter to eleven, and there were until nearly twelve o'clock. That of it- self constituted an offence, for after getting the refresh- ' ments they ought to have gone away. It was a emimon practice to go out from Runcorn to FrOdsham Bridge. get drunk, and turn out, when people were coming from places of worship, in a boisterous condition. That was the first prosecution the police had instituted, and they did not wish to bear too hardly on Mrs. Edge. If some undertaking could be given, by which the matters complained of could be stopped, and the costa were paid, lie though they would be satisfied.—P.C. Thomas Breeze, P.S. Costello°. and P.S. Turner proved the case.—Mr. Brassey urged that the men lived about three miles from the public-house, and contended that they did not go to the place for the simple purpose of obtaining refreshment—the wien were not merely out for the pleasure of a walk, but were out on distinct business. The day in question was very wet, and the defendants Wilkinson and Jackson entered the Weaver Tavern more for shelter than anything else. Their coats were drying before the fire when the police entered the public-house. Although he agreed that drink- ing prevailed in Cheshire, on Sundays, he did not con- , sider that they should visit a fine upon his clients, be- cause the police wished to put a stop to that kind of , thing. Re might add that since that case was com- menced Mrs. Edge bad refused to serve anyone who came from Runcorn, and had thereby exercised very great dis- cretion. She had kept the house for years, and had not up to the present had a charge brought against her, and this showed that she was trying to carry out her business in a proper and legitimatemanner.—Aftor the defendants had supported the above statements, the summonses were , dismissed, simply on their merits. The Bench, while admitting that the question of distance was not the only one in the matter, said they did not consider that the , men in question walked from Runcorn to the Weaver Tavern, only for the purpose of obtaining drink; and in their opinion Mrs. Edge believed them to be what they ; represented themselves, namely, bona fide travellers.

LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS, FRIDAY. For beef, fine grades, full prices are asked, and other sorts attract little notice, Pork is steady. In bacon, prices generally are steady, but there is no improvement in the demand, buyers merely pur- ohasing to satisfy their immediata requirements. Ham- fluctuate but little, and the currencies are .unchangeds Shoulders are quiet, and prices favour buyers. Cheese is firmer, and butter without special feature. Lard has a stronger tone though without change. MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDAY. Things are not buoy- ant in this market, and any business of magnitude doing in cloth is at prices that are not attractive whets put into figures. Cotton is somewhat lively. The estimate has been raised from 10,000 to 12,000 bsles, but no at teration is made in prices. Spinners are having a good time. Prices of yarns generally are tending to harden, and welts cannot, as a rule, be bought at prices current a week ago. There is not a large yarn trade doing to-day. Bun dies are steady. A BRILLIANT idea, try what" SUNLIGIIT SOAP" will do next washing day.—Adut. WALTON Cguncil. Harvest thanksgiving services were held at this church on Thursday evening. The chiach was very tastefully decorated, the work of decoration having been done by the Misses Greenall, plants, &c. being supplied by Sir Gilbert G-reenall. T here was a crowded congregation. The preache r was the Rev. L. Gresley, M. A., vicar of Birdsall, York.

A sitting of this Court was held on Thin- before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes. The only caSe" of public interest was one in which George Live, commission agent. Rodney-st., Warrington, sued Miss Emma Wilson resiaing at the Feathers gotel, Bridge-at, Warrington, for payment of IA the price of certain furniture which he alleged he had purchased on her behalf at a sale by Maiuwaring on the 27th February last. Plaintiff said that the articles turned out to be made of common wood instead of mahogony,as was thought to be the case. They were t4eu - to the Feathers Hotel, and placed in a room upstairs. Afterwards they were sought to be exchang,ed.—Defel!cl. ant denied liability, and Messrs. Mainwaring sued plain- tiff, and obtained from him payment of the price. gal now sought to recover the same, and called sevyr :witnesses on his behalf. Defendant denied having giv.eel instructions to plaintiff to bid for her, and also den' • having received a letter from his solicitor, Mr. Arthur Browne, although her own solicitor, Mr. Percy DaclFs,,, produced the letter in court. She also denied 110101, seen the articles in her father's bedroom.—fler brothe._ who was her witness, said that though he was near. hu' sister during the sale he did not hear her give instructio to plaintiff. He admitted having seen the things taker: upstairs, and having gone to Messrs. Mainwaring to ges them exchanged, but he said he went there at the reques of plaintiff.—His honour said it was a very serious and a case which, if supported by adequate evideacw! ought to go before another court. Here was a deliberatu_ concoction on one side or the other to committ grf, perjury. As far as he was concerned he must give 11-1 Jj ment for the amount claimed.—David Garton B. Hood Wright for thrashing amounting £4 10s.--17 Judge gave judgment for the plaintiff for the full ainounoi Mr. Percy Davies was for the plaintiff.—Mrs. Earle, _ the Fox Inn, sued Mr. Draper, of Penketh, for the retut'uo of goods deposited with him.—Mr. Percy Davies, 171 appeared for Mrs Earle, explained that the mother-i_i_ law of the plaintiff lived with Mr. Draper, and that goods were lodged there for her benefit, and he thotEi. perhaps that she really ought to be sued in thia His Honour cc ncurred, and adjourned the case stio

NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY OF CHESTER will be holden at the COURT HOUSE, NETHER KNUTSFORD, in and for the said County, on MotaiAr,the 11th day of October next,at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will ' be empannelled. The hearing of all appeals arising within the Hundreds of Bueklow, Macclesfield, and Northwich, forming the Knuts- ford District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from such Hundreds, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Knntsford District must be in atten- dance at the Court House, Knutsford, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 13th day of October, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. AND NOTICE IS HEREBY ALSO GIVEN, that at the time and place aforesaid, a proposal will be made to the Jus- tices then and there assembled to make a Provisional Order to dissolve the Highway District for the Eastern Division of the Hundred of Broxton, in the said County, which said Highway District consists of the Townships or Parishes fol- lowing, viz. : Agden Egerton Aldersey Farndon Aldford Grafton Barton Hampton Bickley lfarthill Bradley Horton Broxton Handley Bickerton King's Marsh Bulk eley Larkton Burwardsley Ma,efen Caldecott Malpas Carden Newton-by-Malpas Chidlow Oldcastle Cholmondeley Overton Chowley Shocklach Church Chorlton Shochlach Oviatt Churton-by-Aldford Stockton Churton-by-Farndon Strettou Coddington Threapwood (part in Ches- Clutton hire Crewe Tilston Cuddington Tushingham-eum- Duckington Grindley Edge Wichhough Edgerley Wigland and the said Court at the time and place aforesaid will also be moved to make a Provisional Order to dissolve such Highway District in accordance with such proposal. AND NOTICE IS HEREBY ALSO FURTHER GIVEN, that at the time and place aforesaid a proposal will be made to the Justices then and there assembled to vary the High- way District of the West Division of the Hundred of Broxton, in the said County, by adding to the said District the Town- ship of Huntington, in the said Hundred, for the purposes of " The Highway Acts." THE COURT will be Adjourned to the Castle of Chester. on Thursday, the 16th day of October next, at Eleven o'clock In the Forenoon when another Grand Jury will be emPan- nelled. The hearing of all appeals arising within the Hun- dreds of Broxton, Eddisbury, Nantwich, and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last-mentioned Hundreds will take place at such Adjourned Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the opening of the Court on THURSDAY, the 16th day of October next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Peace for the County of Chester. Chester, 23rd September, 1190.

STARVATION WAGES. At an inquest at Cradley Heath, on Tuesday, on a chainmaker's blower named William Narwood, sixty- three years of age, who had been found dead in bed, it Was stated that deceased earned only 4s. a week, out of which he had to pay is. a week for lodgings, and that for =oaths past he could not have had sufficient food. 40. TERRIBLE RAILWAY ACCIDENT. Part of a mixed goods train from Brecon ran off the ?arils near Llanidloes, Montguneryshire, on Sunday, and fell down the embankment, a distance of about 200 feet The driver and fireman were seriously injured, but the Passengers escaped, the couplings connecting the pas- senger carriages breaking and leaving them on the line. RUSSIA AND ARMENIA. ALARMING SITUATION. Adrices from Erzeroum represent the situation there aS very serious. The massing of Russian troops on the frontier continues, and it is even stated that 72,000 men are concentrated there. The Turks fear that an attack Will shortly be made upon them, and are putting the Kurds in readiness to offer resistance. European famil- . ies arrive at Ersingian every day, having fled from Er- zeroum in fear of a massacre. A Berlin telegram says very little credence is attached There to the report of an approaching invasion of Turk- ish Armenia by Russian troops. MURDER, SUICIDE, AND INSANITY. A terrible domestic tragedy occurred on Sunday, at Lacon, Illinois. A man employed at some woollen mills ; in that place was enraged with his daughter for having but a few hours previously got married without his con- sent, and when she catne to ask his forgiveness he shot her dead, immediately afterwards committing suicide. The husband at this moment came upon the scene, and Was so horrified at the tragedy which had just been en- acted that he became insane.; MR. GLADSTONE AND THE TRAFFIC IN CHILDREN. Mr. Gladstone, in the course of a letter which he had written to Mr. W. H. Wilkins, with reference to his re- cent communication to the "Times" on the subject of Italian vagrancy. says :—" I regard with nothing short of horror the traffic in Italian children, as represented in your deeply interesting letter, but want of knowledge and want of time to inquire, disable me from taking part in any engagement concerning it."

THE ELECTIONS IN SERVIA. - --- The final result of the elections gives a return of 111 Radicals, 19 Liberals, and two Progressists ; while in two constituencies there will be second ballots. The Opposi- tion paper state that the greatest pressure has been exerted by the representatives of the Government to pro- cure the election of the Ministerial candidates. A " GLADSTONE " BEDSTEAD. At the sale of Lord Tollemache's furniture in St James's- square, among other lots put up was a mahogany bed- stead at ss. No further offer was apparently forth- coming until it transpired that Mr. Gladstone had slept in it for over seven months, when it became the object of the most spirited competition, and was sold for a large sum. GENERAL BAPTIST CONFERENCE. The 237th annual Conference of the General Baptist Assembly, the oldest Nonconformist body in England, concluded on Tuesday night, in Bethnal Green-road Chapel, London, when resolutions were passed condemn- ing the Government policy in Ireland, favouring free education, and expressing sympathy with the labour movement. The Rev. E. P. Hall, Trowbridge, was elected president for the year, 111. LADY VOTERS STRUCK OFF.
